> I couldn't figure out to make it vectorize (specially the multi-level part) - but unfortunately have a convergence problem. Any recommendation ?

You pretty much have to use a non-centered parameterization for these hierarchical shrinkage priors in Stan and even then, you probably have to crank adapt_delta up to 0.99999... and then get lucky. There is some code for the non-centered parameterzations at

https://github.com/jpiironen/rstan-varsel

Ben

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] How to obtain unweighted mean instead of weighted mean in hierarchical model?
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] How to obtain unweighted mean instead of weighted mean in hierarchical model?
messages.body_plain:
If you have a way of estimating the population distribution
of predictors, then you can do post-stratification to find
an estimate of a population quantity of interest given a model
based on the predictors.  We don't really have that in the manual,
but in a simple case where you just have K groups, then you
calculate some quantity of interest per group, lets say alpha[k],
the you have some knowledge of the size of each group, say size[k].
Then you can just literally calculate the population mean for alpha
as

  alpha_pop = sum(alpha .* size)

if alpha and size are both defined as K-vectors.  You'd usually do
this in the generated quantities block.

A meta-analysis works the other way around, which is what I was
suggesting in early email.  It works out to generate each group
as a different "experiment".  But it assumes a generative model of
some population quantity of interest, which won't necessarily look
like a weighted mean.

- Bob

> On Sep 30, 2016, at 5:18 PM, Henrik Singmann <sing...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> Hi Bob,
>
> I understand your point and appreciate the recommendations about testing ones model. But it does not really answer my actual question, so please apologize that I come back to it.
>
> The parameter I want to estimate is not the (unweighted) mean of the groups, but the mean of the participants (i.e., a weighted group mean). Imagine this like a meta-analysis on the individual level data. And in a meta-analysis it is common to weight the effect by the sample sizes of the individual studies.
>
> So if my parameterization does not allow me to estimate the value I am actually interested in (i.e., mu_mu captures the variations across groups), my question is:  How can I parameterize a model that estimates a hyper-parameter corresponding to the weighted group mean (i.e., groups weighted by their sample size) while including a random effect of group (i.e., adequately accounting for the fact that individuals within my groups might be more similar to the other group members than members of other groups) and possibly other random effects (which are not part of the simple example)?
>
> Cheers,
> Henrik
>
>
> Am Donnerstag, 29. September 2016 23:22:26 UTC+2 schrieb Bob Carpenter:
> Here's how to test that things are working properly.
>
> Simulate data form the model, fit the model, and make sure
> 50% of the parameters are within their posterior 50% intervals.
> Repeat.
>
> If that works, your model's coded properly.
>
> When you have
>
>   y ~ normal(mu[group], sigma[group]);
>   mu ~ normal(mu_mu, sigma_mu)
>
> you don't expect mu_mu to be the mean of the y.  Instead,
> normal(mu_mu, sigma_mu) are trying to capture the variation
> in the mu[k] across groups.
>
> The reason to have the variance components is that you don't expect
> each group to have the same variability, and the variability of the
> mu will play into the variability of the mu_mu estimate.
>
> - Bob
>
>

> > Am Donnerstag, 29. September 2016 15:40:38 UTC+2 schrieb Bob Carpenter:
> > The simple answer is that you need to model the variance.
> > That will produce the kind of weighting you expect.
> >
> > The bigger point is to think about the models generatively.
> > Rather than trying to build a model so that the posterior mean is
> > some preconceived quantity (like mean across individuals) and instead
> > look at calibration.  Simulate data and see if the posterior intervals
> > have the right coverage.  And cross-validate on real data or use a held-out
> > evaluation set to test real-world calibration.
> >
> > Let's say everything's unconstrained and normal.  Assume there
> > are K groups and N observations and that observation n is from group
> > g[n] in 1:K.  Then the generative model is:
> >
> >   vector[N] y;
> >   vector[K] mu;
> >   vector<lower=0>[K] sigma;
> >
> >   y[n] ~ normal(mu[g[n]], sigma[g[n]]);
> >
> >   mu[k] ~ normal(mu_mu, sigma_mu);
> >
> >   sigma[k] ~ ...;
> >
> > You can use whatever hierarchical prior for sigma you think makes sense.
> >
> > - Bob

  sum(alpha .* size) / sum(size)

if the sizes aren't normalized to sum to 1.  Then if you define
it in generated quantities, you get a posterior distribution on
the estimate which you can use for prediction.

- Bob

messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] How to obtain unweighted mean instead of weighted mean in hierarchical model?
messages.body_plain:
Except sample size isn’t always a meaningful concept
depending on your model.  If the group-level likelihoods
are not in the exponential family then there isn’t really
a formal definition of sample size so your request is
ill-posed.

That said, when you do have exponential family likelihoods
and a Gaussian hierarchical model then the hierarchical
mean already acts like a weighted mean over the groups
(modulo the regularization of the hyperprior).  Those groups
with fewer data pull the hierarchical mean less, just as
desired.

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Ideas for Hierarchical Modeling With Partially Ordered Groups?
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Ideas for Hierarchical Modeling With Partially Ordered Groups?
messages.body_plain:
The big aspect that is lost when imposing exchangeability on ordered
groups is the sense of continuity.  Continuity implies that neighboring
groups should have similar values but exchangeability ignores that
implication.  Now if the groups are big enough then this constraint is
weak and the exchangeability assumption is quite good (for example,
with large age or income brackets) but if the groups are small then
this can be a serious issue.  A common example of the latter is when
the groups correspond to small intervals of time.

messages.subject: Re: Using RStan to develop Latent class Multinomial Logit Model
messages.subject_clean: Using RStan to develop Latent class Multinomial Logit Model
messages.body_plain:
See the last post on this thread:

https://groups.google.com/forum/?fromgroups#!category-topic/stan-users/general/SPlQPDH6f6U

That script takes as data a vector (x) which you assume has K latent classes of gaussian-distributed data.
It uses soft clustering, so each individual has some probability, pi, of belonging to each cluster.
Pi is estimated from softmax regression (multinomial logistic) from intercepts, beta0, and predictors, beta.
"predictors" is a matrix WITHOUT a column for the intercept (the intercept is assumed by beta0).

It's not pretty code, but it works.

> One quick comment - I think you have your lags back to front
>
> You have the following code line:
> mus[t] <- mus[t] + B[p] * Y[t+p-1]
>
> Assume you have P=4 lags.
>
> If t is 10, then t in the original data is t+P = 14.
>
> So then:
> p = 1 means you are referencing 10+1-1 = 10 in the original time step
> p = 2 means you are referencing 10+2-1 = 11 in the original time step
> p = 3 means you are referencing 10+3-1 = 12 in the original time step
> p = 4 means you are referencing 10+4-1 = 13 in the original time step.

messages.subject: Re: Sampling from inverted beta/dirichlet
messages.subject_clean: Sampling from inverted beta/dirichlet
messages.body_plain:
Yet another update, but also a bit of a new question.

As per Bob's suggestion, I constrained beta0[1] (arbitrarily) to 0, so that the logits have some sort of scale. I then allowed the beta0[2:K] to be negative or positive (rather than constrained to be positive).
This led to divergent transitions and very wrong, albeit consistent estimates of beta0[2:K] and the latent class means/sds.

Honestly, I have NO idea why that would be the case.

To clarify (and review):
One model uses softmax regression, but constrains the intercept-logits (beta0) to be positive and ~logistic(0,3); with this parametization, several combinations of beta0s are possible, but it does not affect the model because once softmax'd, the probabilities are the same.
The other model uses softmax, but constrains beta0[1] to be 0; the others are ~ logistic(0,3) with no constraint. This should yield the same model as above (intuitively, to me, anyway), but sets a scale for which other logits to be compared to (no more multiple combinations of beta0s should be possible). This latter model suffers from div. transitions and incorrect parameter estimates.

No idea why, and I welcome any input about that.

> Hey everyone,
>

>

>
> However, I noticed today that when using beta(.2,.2) as a prior, for example, that sampling was *slow* (like, 45 minutes later, and only hitting 10%, slow), and I assume that it's because so MUCH probability is over 0 and 1, and the geometry of that is awful to sample from (the negative log of that would be like an inverted U, constrained at 0 and 1).
>
> Because of that, is it preferred to instead parameterize as log-odds and sample from a wide logistic?
>
> That is, is it preferred to use:
> vector[N] pi_logit;
> pi_logit ~ logistic(pi_logit_mean, 5); pi_logit_mean ~ logistic(0,5);
>
> as opposed to:
> vector[N] pi;
> pi ~ dbeta(alpha*scale,beta*scale); alpha = (pi_mean); beta = 1 - pi_mean; scale = .2; pi_mean ~ uniform(0,1)
>
> I assume the logistic is easier to sample from, geometrically, than a beta/dirichlet that is highly pointed near bounded areas (0 and 1). Am I correct in thinking about this?

You can test whether things work with the following example

rm(list=ls())

## These are necessary when sourcing the file with the code for the package
library(flexsurv)
library(INLA)
library(data.table)
library(rstan)
source("survHE.R")

## This is what we'd like to have (and load the dependencies)
library(survHE)

# Reads data in
dat <- read.table("http://www.statistica.it/gianluca/survHE/data.txt",header=TRUE)
# Adds some fictious covariates - for testing
dat$sex <- rbinom(dim(dat)[1],1,.5)
dat$age <- rpois(dim(dat)[1],32)
dat$imd <- cut(runif(dim(dat)[1],0,100),breaks=seq(0,100,20)); levels(dat$imd)=1:5
dat$ethnic <- cut(runif(dim(dat)[1],0,100),breaks=seq(0,100,20)); levels(dat$ethnic)=1:5

## Now you can test whether the survHE functions work
# 1. running MLEs via flexsurv
x1 = fit.models(Surv(time,censored)~as.factor(arm),dat,"weibull")

# 2. running INLA (*NOT NECESSARY* --- but we implement this too, for the survival models that INLA can do)
x2 = fit.models(Surv(time,censored)~as.factor(arm),dat,"weibull","inla")

     [,1] [,2] [,3]
[1,]    5    9   13
[2,]    6   10   14
[3,]    7   11   15What you're asking

What you're asking for goes against the behavior of multi-indexing.

What you can do is write a function:

vector dbl_idx(vector level, int[] ii, int[] jj) {
   vector[size(ii)] result;
   for (k in 1:size(ii))
     result[k] = level[ii[k], jj[k]];
   return result;
}

and then you can use

  dbl_idx(level, student, season)

in place of where you think you wanted to write level[student, season].

We could, of course, build such a function directly into Stan very
easily.

- Bob

> in order to optimize the model (i.e. increase its efficiency) I tried to implement the multivariate non-centered parameterization of the model. Following the examples in the manual and various suggestions in the mailing list the code looks as follows (only the changes are illustrated, the rest of the code is equivalent to the code above):
>
> "
> parameters {
>   vector[J] theta;        //abilities
>   matrix[3,I] xi_tilde;   //parameter matrix
>   [...]
> }
>
> transformed parameters {
>   matrix[I,3] xi;
>   xi = (diag_pre_multiply(tau,L_Omega) * xi_tilde)';
>   [...]
> }
>
> model {
>   //xi ~ multi_normal_cholesky(mu, diag_pre_multiply(tau, L_Omega));//
>   to_vector(xi_tilde) ~ normal(0,1);
>   [...]
> }
>
>
> While model results are equivalent to those of the cholesky-model, the non-centered parameterization substantially increases the effective sample size of all parameters and helps with convergence. Moreover, it eliminates practically all divergent transitions (which was only possible in the cholesky-model by tuning the sampler. Hence, I hope I managed to implement the non-centered parameterzation correctly.
>
> What I am unsure of, however, is the following statement in the model block:
>
> to_vector(xi_tilde) ~ normal(0,1);
>
>  What does this statement imply exactly?

It increments the log density with an independent normal prior on
each entry of the xi_tilde matrix.  So basically, it's the unit
normal basis that provides z scores, which then get transformed by
rotating (correlation) and scaling (scale/variance).

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
> On Oct 2, 2016, at 12:21 AM, ralphe...@gmail.com wrote:
>
>
> > Since foo_raw is always ~normal(0,1) is it necessary to have T versions of it?
>
> Yes---it's characterizing the movement of the elements
> of the time series on the unit scale.  It might be helpful
> for you to try it and see the difference.  It won't be a time
> series model.
>
> I guess my confusion was difference between
>
> for t in (2:Nt){
>   foo_raw[t] ~ normal(0,1);
>   foo[t] = foo[t-1] + sigma*foo_raw[t];
> }

You want to code the above as

  for_raw[2:Nt] ~ normal(0, 1);

  foo[2:Nt] = foo[1:(Nt-1)] + sigma * foo_raw;

but note that this doesn't set foo[1] or give a distribution to foo_raw[1]
as written.

>
> and
>
> foo_raw ~ normal(0,1);

>
> I assume the former necessary to do independent draws?
>
> > If so, to constrain the bounds of foo (upper=a, lower=b), must I now constrain foo_raw to constrain foo indirectly?

If you must have constraints, that's what you'd want to do.

> Are you sure you really want to do that?  Where do the bounds
> come from in the generative process you're envisioning here?
>
> If you do need those bounds, you'd need Jacobian adjustments.
>
> For this problem, I'm fitting multiple peaks with time-varying parameters to a surface. In many cases, those peak parameters (such as the center of the peak) have known ranges (from experiments). For example, let's say peaks 1,2, and 3 can have centers that fall between 0 and 10, 20 and 30, and 40 and 50, respectively. My thought was by imposing a hard restriction on the parameters I could keep peaks from crossing out of their ranges (as they time-varied) and to make sure that the parameters in each chain correspond to the same peaks. Even though the parameters evolve, these bounds would have to be imposed at each time point.

You're probably better off not constraining and letting the data
constrain the shape of the posterior.  A data sample is often consistent
with future draws being outside the observed data bounds (e.g., collect ten
people's heights and it's not unlikely the eleventh person will be taller or
shorter than all of the first ten, but as you get a hundred or a thousand people,
it's still possible, but less likely the new one will be the most extreme).

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Rstan running time
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Rstan running time
messages.body_plain:
Run time is not linear in number of iterations because
the number of calls to log density and gradient calculations
(the real time sinks) changes.  As adaptation runs
during warmup, it changes the parameters of the underlying Hamiltonian simulation.
If the step size and mass matrix produce small steps, it may seem like it'll never
finish.  This is usually done in response to complex posterior geometry,
often arising in hierarchical models.

diagonal matrices as local variables---they should be in
transformed data if you need them.  But you really want to
use the cholesky factor parameterizations of covariance for
efficiency.  See the manual chapter on regression for prior
recommendations and how to code them.

messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Question on multilevel regression with group-level interaction
messages.body_plain:
I've fit similar sort of models on similar types of data.

Do you have plots of the raw data (i.e., distance towards target versus signal amplitude with a linear fit for each subject, with separate facets for each count of electrodes? If not, ggplot2 is great for this). This will help considerably in deciding how the number of electrodes should be incorporated into the model. With 12 subjects you will likely have difficulty in estimating the effect of number of electrodes if estimating for each case of 1 to 5 and will need to include appropriate priors. Depending on the plot of the data, it may be appropriate to do partial pooling for the effect of the number of electrodes on intercept and slope. Alternatively, if the plot shows there is an approximately linear influence of number of electrodes on intercept and/or slope then can make some modifications of your model to hopefully get reasonable estimates.

Numerous other improvements are possible but first need to determine the appropriate structure of the model given the data.

Daniel

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] How to specify a sum-to-one vector with individual component has support on full range from [0,1] ?
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] How to specify a sum-to-one vector with individual component has support on full range from [0,1] ?
messages.body_plain:
The boundaries shouldn't matter because they have measure 0.
That is,

  Pr[theta[n] = 1 OR theta[n] = 0

for any continuous posterior density p(theta | y).

There's a section in the manual on coding sum-to-one constraints.

The simplex type allows 0 or 1 values.  You will only get them
through underflow or overflow in the inverse-logit transforms from
unconstrained space---the manual has a chapter on constraint
transforms near the end that explains how the transforms work for
parameters like the simplex.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Rstan running time
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Rstan running time
messages.body_plain:
Unless you're somehow running out of memory (you can
check your system monitors depending on OS), a more
powerful computer's only going to be an incremental
improvement.  You really need to code the model more
efficiently computationally or find a more efficient parameterization
statistically or work with less data.

Run time is very sensitive to data.  If the model is
misspecified for the data, run time can be very long even
in cases where data generated from the model will fit easily.

We always recommend fake-data testing to start.  Take a small
instance of your problem, generate fake data from the priors,
then see if you can fit it.  If you find yourself saying "the priors
are too wide for simulation", then you probably want stronger
priors in your model.

- Bob

On Wed, Oct 5, 2016 at 3:59 PM, sreenath am <natha...@gmail.com> wrote:
> Thank you very much Bob.
>
> If I define the weight as simplex[3], with a flat Dirichlet prior on it, do you meant to say that theoretically a sample from posterior can be (1,0,0) or (0,0,1)?

Yes. If you write a model as:

parameter {
  simplex[3] theta;
}
model {
}

You'll just sample from 3-simplexes. (1,0,0) has the same probability as every other valid simplex.

(Feel free to throw that into a .stan file and run it.)

Daniel

>
> -Sreenath
>

> > The boundaries shouldn't matter because they have measure 0.

> >
> > for any continuous posterior density p(theta | y).

> > There's a section in the manual on coding sum-to-one constraints.
> >
> > The simplex type allows 0 or 1 values.  You will only get them
> > through underflow or overflow in the inverse-logit transforms from

> > > Putting constrain doesn't seems to work because they are transformed using scaled logit(), behind the scenes, in Stan.
> > >
> > > I am using this vector as weights. Below is a simple representation of the model.
> > > Basically I am trying to define a weighted sum of exposures happened at different time points, this weighted sum would be the effective exposure.
> > >
> > > data{
> > >   int N;                                    //Number of observations
> > >   vector[N] X1;                        //Exposure variables at three time points
> > >   vector[N] X2;

> > >
> > > for(n in 1:N){

> > > }

> > > So if one time point exposure is not contributing anything the corresponding weight should be zero. Also the vise-versa, if there is only one time point contributing everything then the weight for that period should be 1 and all others zero.

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] How to specify a sum-to-one vector with individual component has support on full range from [0,1] ?
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] How to specify a sum-to-one vector with individual component has support on full range from [0,1] ?
messages.body_plain:
Not from a Dirichlet.  See the Wikipedia page.

But due to the vagaries of rounding with floating point,
we will get (1, 0, 0) values out by mistake due to roundoff
during inverse-logit transforms.

Our simplex data type allows values to be 0 or 1.  But it's
not useful as it doesn't provide full support for a categorical
distribution---it puts all the mass on one outcome.

So what I'm saying is that you should be able to ignore the boundaries.

Why do you think you need 1 or 0 values?

- Bob

Hi -- I'm sorry, but I don't think you're understanding the importance of having the exact files that generate the output. The program you sent earlier doesn't line up with both these outputs. The reason I can tell is that in the forloop_output.txt, the exception happens in line 81 and in the vectorized output it happens in line 80. As far as I know, there's at least one difference that you haven't specified. I really can't tell if there are others and there's an infinite number of ways things could be different.

Space is cheap, so please just send both programs and both outputs exactly. If you attach the data, I could try to run it too.

Regarding your slow model, "optimize" isn't the right term. Vectorizing code and making computation more efficient helps, but only by small percentages. Reparameterizing models and writing models that are better fits to your model will make large jumps in time.

So... if you want more help with this model:
1) send the Stan program with the for loop in one file (.stan)
2) send the Stan program with the slicing in another file (.stan)
3) send the output with the for loop as a text file (like you've done)
4) send the output with the slicing in another file (like you've done)
5) send the data that goes along with the runs

I'm actually trying to help, but there isn't more than can be done when there are lurking issues in the background. If your model is showing a bug, that's really important and I want to be able to hunt it down, but it's really hard when I can't replicate and can't track through enough of your changes.

messages.subject: Identifying a constant that may be dropped for sampling
messages.subject_clean: Identifying a constant that may be dropped for sampling
messages.body_plain:
Hi, The following statement in the manual defines a parameter, transformed parameter or local model variable as not constant - and therefore required - for updating the sampling joint log-probability.

"The second difference is that if lambda is not a parameter, transformed parameter, or local model variable, the sampling statement is clever enough to drop the log(lambda) term."

I sometimes get confused as to when something is a constant with respect to updating the sampling log-probability; for example, if i impose a Gaussian prior on a model parameter where the covariance matrix contains no parameters, then it is constant and i can drop the additive logdet term from the log-probability update.

 however, I'm currently building an lpdf function where it is not clear to me.  I want to update the log-probability for the asymmetric lapace distribution, AL(mu,tau,p) with density function, f(x|mu,tau,p) = tau*p*(1-p)*exp(-tau*rho_{p}(x-mu)),where rho_{p}(u) is the so-called check function.   Here "p" denotes the skewness.  mu, x and tau are parameters.  Suppose I bring "p" into the model in the data block.  Then will the log(p) + log(1-p) terms drop out as constants?

Thanks for your insights.

Terrance.

--
Thank you, Terrance Savitsky

messages.body_plain:
Thanks, the plot makes it much easier to see the form of an appropriate model.

Firstly I'd demean the log amplitude: df$logamps <- df$logamp - mean(df$logamp)

Then try this model which has some minor changes to above:

data{
    int<lower=0> N;                     //number of total observations
    int<lower=1> J;                      //number of subjects
    int<lower=1,upper=J> s[N];     // suject ID
    vector[J] e;                            // group-level interactions (number of electrodes)

    vector[N] y;                           // outcome variable
    vector[N] x;                           // predictor(s)
}

parameters{
    real beta_mu[2];                                    // group averages for intercept[1] and slope[2]
    real<lower=0> sigma_y;                         // total error
    matrix[2,J] e_betaj;

    vector<lower=0>[2] sigma_b;
    real gamma; // effect of electrode count on slope
}

transformed parameters{

    vector[N] y_hat;
    vector[J] beta0_raw;
    vector[J] beta1_raw;
    vector[J] beta0;
    vector[J] beta1;

    beta0_raw = beta_mu[1] + sigma_b[1] * e_betaj[1]';

    beta1_raw = beta_mu[2] + sigma_b[2] * e_betaj[2]';

    beta0 = beta0_raw; // No evidence of an effect of electrode count on Intercept and given limited data exclude estimation
    beta1 = beta1_raw + e * gamma;

    for (i in 1:N)
        y_hat[i] = beta0[s[i]] + beta1[s[i]] * x[i];

}

model {
    //Priors
    sigma_y ~ cauchy(0, 2.5);
    sigma_b ~ cauchy(0, 2.5);

    beta_mu ~ normal(0, 1); // Need tighter prior

    gamma ~ normal(0,1);
    to_vector(e_betaj) ~ normal(0, 1);

    y ~ student_t(4, y_hat, sigma_y);
}

Would be great if you could post the resulting inferences for sigma_y, sigma_b, beta_mu, and gamma. If still getting results that aren't sensible then making the change to a multivariate prior for the intercept and slope should hopefully fix it.

messages.body_plain:
Thanks for sending all the files over. It took a direct comparison to actually find the problem.

You have to use the for loop. It's because of this:
bg_At[2:Nx] = bg_At[1:(Nx-1)] + bg_At_raw[2:Nx]*bg_sig2At;

Stan is imperative. Before the loop, you've only defined bg_At[1]. bg_At[2:Nx] is NaN, so when you use bg_At[1:(Nx-1)] elements bg_At[2:(Nx-1)] are NaN and that'll result in the assignment being NaN.

For things like this, Stan isn't slow. Using loops are just as fast as vectorizing it. It's not like Matlab, R, or Python in that aspect. In this case, you have to loop because it's the right thing to do.

And for future reference, it really helps to send Stan programs with data. Just in case it's useful to anyone else, I debugged this by:
1. Running both programs without changing anything. Verifying the behavior.
2. Inspecting both programs for consistency.
3. Reducing the number of iterations. I wanted to make sure the problem occurred with the Stan program.
4. Copying over the working code into the non working code and comparing results. This verifies that everything was the same.
5. Changing one of the three assignments. It's always easier for me to reason about one change over multiple changes.
6. Verifying failure with one change.
7. Digging through the logic for the one change. If I didn't spot it, I would have modified the program to print.

I couldn't have done any of that with the trickle of changing programs strewn across multiple emails. I was only able to help once you actually sent programs and data over. As an exercise, try going back through your this thread and only use the info you provided to debug. Hopefully you'll see why I kept asking you to send full programs. If everything was attached at the very beginning, we would have been able to find this much sooner.

And try using print to debug. It's useful.

Daniel

Hi David,

Re "beta_mu [...] // Need tighter prior" than normal(0, 1)" -- it was previously normal(0,5) which is quite wide, normal(0,1) was a change I'd made and the comment was just noting why. Tighter prior helps with sampling, although need to demean data so intercept becomes closer to 0.

The model is on the right track, and can see how useful a multivariate prior is. Overall mean negative intercept and negative slope for the relationship between signal and distance matches the data.

One thing is that gamma is the opposite sign to what it should be (and can't be any other way with the constraint that gamma has a lower bound of zero ;-). As you increase the number of electrodes the plot indicates that the slope becomes more negative. Hence as I assume ec[j] is positive, gamma should be negative. Thus change to real<upper=0> for gamma. A negative gamma can be interpreted as the amount that the slope becomes more negative per extra electrode, and definitely makes sense to look at. I assume the beta_raw's will be compensating for the current constraint, hence the other variable that would be useful to see is beta_raw as can match with plot to check that estimates are correct.

The results are looking promising, a few more tweaks to the model and I think will be close.

Regards,

Daniel

> > in order to optimize the model (i.e. increase its efficiency) I tried to implement the multivariate non-centered parameterization of the model. Following the examples in the manual and various suggestions in the mailing list the code looks as follows (only the changes are illustrated, the rest of the code is equivalent to the code above):
> >
> > "
> > parameters {

> >   to_vector(xi_tilde) ~ normal(0,1);
> >   [...]
> > }
> >
> >
> > While model results are equivalent to those of the cholesky-model, the non-centered parameterization substantially increases the effective sample size of all parameters and helps with convergence. Moreover, it eliminates practically all divergent transitions (which was only possible in the cholesky-model by tuning the sampler. Hence, I hope I managed to implement the non-centered parameterzation correctly.
> >
> > What I am unsure of, however, is the following statement in the model block:
> >
> > to_vector(xi_tilde) ~ normal(0,1);
> >
> >  What does this statement imply exactly?
>
> It increments the log density with an independent normal prior on
> each entry of the xi_tilde matrix.  So basically, it's the unit
> normal basis that provides z scores, which then get transformed by
> rotating (correlation) and scaling (scale/variance).
>

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Does Stan have functionality for Bayesian Optimization?
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Does Stan have functionality for Bayesian Optimization?
messages.body_plain:
Hi Daniel. The answer, as far as I'm aware is no, but just to get a
sense of how hard it'd be to do, what are you imagining:

1) using Stan as the workhorse for doing the Gaussian process
regression on which Bayesian Optimization relies? or...

2) Are you hoping to write a model in Stan and then optimize it using
Bayesian Optimization instead of, say, BFGS?

For (1), Stan does GPs (see examples in manual), so you could
certainly consider replacing whatever GP implementation
rBayesianOptimization uses with a Stan-based approach. Or just writing
your own thing entirely. For (2), you can access the likelihood of a
Stan program in R, so you could probably wrap rBayesianOptimization
around it. (I have a project that hasn't gotten off the ground yet to
do this--actually Bayesian Optimization + Bayesian Quadrature--and
also use the gradient information that Stan provides for speeding up
the optimization, since you can put that into your GP as well. If
anyone is interested let me know...)

Seth
P.S. Nothing special about R/rBayesianOptimization in these
examples--the python BO packages are better developed.

On Saturday, October 8, 2016 at 1:40:57 AM UTC-7, Seth Flaxman wrote:

> 1) using Stan as the workhorse for doing the Gaussian process
> regression on which Bayesian Optimization relies? or...
>
> 2) Are you hoping to write a model in Stan and then optimize it using
> Bayesian Optimization instead of, say, BFGS?

I think it's (1). Since Gaussian Processes are a workhorse of Bayesian Optimization, I could use Stan to fit the GP.
But then I would need an implementation in Stan for the Expected Improvement (EI) algorithm, to select evaluation points for my "Acquisition function". (as described in this paper: https://arxiv.org/pdf/1206.2944.pdf)

The leapfrog algorithm is a stepwise algorithm updating
momentum based on the gradient of the log density and then
stepping in the direction of the momentum.  That
has a hard time following high curvature, like in the neck
of the funnel.  Higher-order methods, like Riemannian HMC,
use higher-order derivatives to better approximate
the curvature (though RHMC doesn't use the leapfrog algorithm).

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
This part is wrong:

  else if (cens[n] == 2)
        target += exponential_lcdf(rcens[n] | eta[n]) -
                  exponential_lcdf(Y[n] | eta[n]);

Check out the discussion in the manual and how we generate intervals.
You want the diff of the lcdfs to be on the linear scale, so you
need

  log_diff_exp(exponential_lcdf(rcens[n] | eta[n]),
               exponential_lcdf(Y[n] | eta[n]));

with basic definition

  log_diff_exp(a, b) = log(exp(a) - exp(b))

You also have to be careful with discrete distributions because
the cdf is inclusive and the ccdf exclusive of bounds, and it
matters with discretes (I'm fixing the bug in Stan related to this
right now).

- Bob

I see.  That's a problem for how things are defined
now in terms of constraints.  The only things that constrain
source of variables right now are the integrate_ode expressions
(not ordinary functions).

All of the functions have been designed to operate on any
inputs, which is why a function that calls integrate_ode
can't be compiled---it can't guarantee that the argument it will
try to pass in will be data.

This is another one that's easy to fix if we let the C++
compiler blow up on the user, but I don't see offhand how to
fix it so that well-formed Stan programs always compile in C++.

messages.body_plain:
Hi David,

As an update, I've had a chance (finally) to implement your code and everything seems to be working great!  The estimates are comparable between survival::clogit and stan_clogit across multiple datasets.  However, my need is limited to a single 'case' per stratum so I can't speak to the accuracy beyond this constraint.

As Jeff pointed out, the code as implemented didn't scale well for large datasets.  I've attached a very simple modification (lines 112-113) that improves speed by an order of magnitude or more when dealing with much larger datasets than in the 'infert' example.  Please NOTE that the data needs to be sorted by stratum/group for this produce accurate results!  I'm going to continue to tailor it towards my specific needs, but I thought this might be helpful for Jeff and others that are hoping for faster model fitting/convergence.

Once again, I really appreciate all the help!
Peter

Even IRT-like models could be done this way with a part that models how many times a question will be answered correctly, and then conditional on that, a part that models which students are the successful ones for each question.
> > >
> > > Ben
> >
> > That's an interesting idea. It should be straightforward to add  a negative binomial or binomial regression on the number of successes at the group level. It's a bit outside any application that I would use at the moment, so I can't really justify spending the time to do so, but perhaps someone else who is interested in that kind of model will jump in.
> >
> > David

messages.body_plain:
Firstly, looking at point estimates is rarely if never helpful.
Bayes is about uncertainty, which means when you judge
a model you want to look at _intervals_, not points.  The
question is wether, say, the 5-95% credible interval captures
the true value.

Secondly, neither of your models are correct.  Please read
the section of the manual on truncation and censoring.  To
build these models correctly you have think _generatively_
and match how you simulated the data.  The latent x is
generated from a truanted normal, and then the measured
x is generated from the latent x.  Also, don’t use bounds
and uniform priors.

data {
  int<lower=0> N;     // Number of samples
  vector[N] x_meas;   // Measured values
  vector<lower=0>[N] uncertainty; // Uncertainty in values
}

parameters {

  real mu;
  real<lower=0> sigma;
  real xmin;
  vector<lower=xmin>[N] xtrue;
}

model {
  mu ~ normal(0, 10);
  sigma ~ cauchy(0, 5);
  xmin ~ normal(0, 10);

  // First model the latent x

  for (i in 1:N) xtrue[i] ~ normal(mu, sigma)T[xmin,];

  // Then model the observation, note the swap
  x_meas ~ normal(xtrue, uncertainty);

}

By thinking generatively you’ll also find that you want to model
the observation variability and not assume that you know it
absolutely.  Even for a population based model like you mention
you have to consider that those populations are themselves
measured with uncertainty.

On Oct 10, 2016, at 8:06 PM, Steven and Jeanette Murray <steven.j...@gmail.com> wrote:

>
> Hi all,
>
> I have asked this question before, but with a complicated model so it was hard to see the actual problem. I have done a bit more work on it and realised that the same problem occurs in much simpler models, so I'm hoping someone can help me :)
>
> Let say I produce a set of samples by the following code (I'm using pystan, but this shouldn't matter...):
>
> ### Parameters
> xmin = 5     # Truncation location of data
> mu = 4       # Mean of data
> scale = 2.0  # Standard deviation of data
>
> ### Produce samples (final size ~5000)
> xint = np.random.normal(loc=mu,scale=scale,size=15000)
> xint = xint[xint>xmin]
>
> ### Add some measurement uncertainty
> n = 2 + np.random.poisson(10**((xint-mu-0.5)))
> sd = 2*np.clip(1 - 0.43*np.log10(n), 0.02, np.inf)
> xobs = xint + np.random.normal(scale=_sd)
>
> The addition of the uncertainty is a bit strange but corresponds in some rough way to how I add uncertainty to my real problem, where each variate represents a (dark matter) halo mass, and the halo mass is correlated with the number of galaxies within it, and the number of galaxies yields the measurement uncertainty. Basically you can think of it as adding large uncertainty to low-valued variates, and much less to high-valued variates. In any case, the final distribution looks like
>

> <Auto Generated Inline Image 1.png>

>
> Of course, there is some probability mass outside the shown range for the uncertain case (stuff that got scattered down). Also, the reason for the turnover in the intrinsic curve is just because it's a KDE. It really peaks at 5 or very close to it.
>
> Anyway, to me the obvious way to code the Stan for parameter estimation is:
>
> data {
>     int<lower=0> N;     // Number of samples
>     vector[N] x_meas;   // Measured values
>     vector<lower=0>[N] uncertainty; // Uncertainty in values
> }
>
> parameters {
>     real<lower=0,upper=8> mu;
>     real<lower=0> sigma;
>     real<lower=0,upper=10> xmin;
>     vector<lower=xmin,upper=30>[N] xtrue;
> }
>
> model {
>     xtrue ~ normal(x_meas,uncertainty);
>     for (i in 1:N) xtrue[i] ~ normal(mu,sigma)T[xmin,];
> }
>
> The interesting part is that xtrue has a  lower bound which is a parameter. When I run this through Stan (I ran 700 warmup and 2000 iterations for 4 chains), the first thing I notice is that it has a hard time converging -- each chain seems to settle in a different spot. But none of these spots are very close to the solution. In fact, they are all biased to high mu and low sigma. The median values for all chains are:
>
> {u'lp__': -3491.0188530263313,
>  u'mu': 6.33030908325631,
>  u'sigma': 1.1798037697816155,
>  u'xmin': 4.9482856755250273,
>  u'xtrue': 6.5643129692386513}
>
> The thing is, the iteration with highest likelihood has much higher likelihood than the "true" answer does. If "gaussmode" is the highest-likelihood iteration, then
>
> print gauss_fit.log_prob(gauss_fit.unconstrain_pars({'mu':mu,"sigma":scale,"xmin":xmin,"xtrue":xint})) - gauss_fit.log_prob(gauss_fit.unconstrain_pars(gaussmode))
>
> gives  -2518.74677702.
>
> However, another way to formulate the model might be the following:
>
> data {
>     int<lower=0> N;     // Number of samples
>     vector[N] x_meas;   // Measured values
>     vector<lower=0>[N] uncertainty; // Uncertainty in values
> }
>
> parameters {
>     real<lower=0,upper=8> mu;
>     real<lower=0> sigma;
>     vector<lower=0,upper=30>[N] xtrue;
> }
>
> transformed parameters {
>     real xmin;
>     xmin <- min(xtrue);
> }
>
> model {
>     xtrue ~ normal(x_meas,uncertainty);
>     for (i in 1:N) xtrue[i] ~ normal(mu,sigma)T[xmin,];
> }
>
> This time, xtrue is left free, and xmin is chosen as the minimum of xtrue. This means that there is not a heavy jacobian adjustment on xtrue (since in the previous model, most of xtrue should be close to xmin, the jacobian adjustment becomes large and negative). Using this model, and doing exactly the same calculation as above (i.e. the log_prob at the truth minus the log_prob at the mode of the other model) gives a positive number, i.e. the truth is more likely.
>
> Of course, just because it is more likely doesn't mean that that is where the probability density is. So, I then ran the same length chains with the "no mmin" model. This model ran a lot slower than the first (not sure why?). Again, each chain settles in a different place, so I guess I'd have to run longer to get convergence (or maybe it will never converge?), but here is the Stan summary:
>
> Inference for Stan model: anon_model_2d2e212313b2a3b52815285bebd934ce.
> 4 chains, each with iter=2000; warmup=700; thin=1;
> post-warmup draws per chain=1300, total post-warmup draws=5200.
>
>               mean se_mean     sd   2.5%    25%    50%    75%  97.5%  n_eff   Rhat
> mu            5.79    0.18    0.4    4.8   5.54   5.88   6.09   6.31    5.0   2.38
> sigma         1.44    0.09   0.17    1.2   1.32   1.41   1.57   1.86    4.0   2.52
>
> xmin          4.81    0.04   0.08   4.67   4.74   4.82   4.88   4.92    4.0    2.5
> lp__        3167.5   57.93 129.53 2935.1 3058.7 3181.9 3255.7 3414.5    5.0   2.07
>
>
> This is a little closer to the truth than the first model in all but xmin. Still not very good though. The thing is, the mean likelihood is higher than the likelihood at the truth.
>
> The last thing to see is the density plot of xtrue for each model. To plot, I just chose the highest likelihood iteration, but I don't think this choice affects the qualitative judgment of the outcome:
>

> <Auto Generated Inline Image 2.png>

>
> It seems like the second model does "better". I was wondering if there is any reason it *should* do better, or in fact if it should be different at all from the first model?
>
> Cheers,
> Steven

On Monday, October 10, 2016 at 11:23:22 PM UTC-4, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> Is there a way to stream the draws to disk in RStan

There has been since before we moved to GitHub: Specify the sample_file argument to sampling() or stan()

> An optional character string providing the name of a file. If specified the draws for all parameters and other saved quantities will be written to the file. If not provided, files are not created. messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Jacobian adjustments...
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Jacobian adjustments...
messages.body_plain:
Overall, I'd urge you to think more generatively in
terms of generating the parameters from priors and the data
from the parameters.  See below.

> On Oct 10, 2016, at 6:24 AM, Charles Driver <cdriv...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> Given the following, where I want to put a prior on on a) the mean of a set of parameters, and b) the relation between various transformations of parameters,
> the need for jacobian adjustment is not clear to me. I appreciate that much has been written on this general topic here in the past, and there are many cases where it is clear to me thanks to such... but I somehow find these two elusive! any help would be very appreciated.

It's elusive because it's not a typical generative model!
Usually when we transform parameters and put a prior on
the transform, we're really thinking of things the other way
around in more generative terms and just using the transform
for convenience.

> This is an incomplete toy problem that attempts to represent the issues - if I just want to encode my knowledge about the expected mean of y, and it's relation to some transformation of x, is there some way the jacobian should be adjusted? At present I think not, but can't convince myself either way...
>
> data{
> vec[z] mydata[n]
> }
> parameters{
> vec[n] y;
> real x;
> }
> model{
>
> mean(y) ~ normal(0, 1) ;

You probably don't want two priors on the same parameter y.
And putting a distribution on a sum isn't identified---see
the manual chapter on problematic posteriors for a simple
example of why.

In general, if

  for (i in 1:n)
    z[i] ~ normal(0, sigma);

then

  sum(z) ~ normal(0, sqrt(n) * sigma);

and

  sum(z) / n ~ normal(0, sqrt(n) * sigma / n);

and mean(z) = sum(z) / n, so you can take

  y ~ normal(0, sqrt(n));

and you will get

  mean(y) ~ normal(0, 1)

as a consequence.  But this is *not* the same thing as
just writing the statement for the mean.  That statement
for the mean gives y[1] = 1e20 and y[2] = -1e20 and
y[1] = 1 and y[2] = -1 the same probability, which probably
isn't what you want.

> mean(y) / x^2 ~ normal(1, 0.1);

I didn't understand why you'd want to do this.
What exactly are you trying to accomplish with these two
priors on y?  In Stan terms, the densities just multiply.

> for(i in 1:n){
> mydata[i] ~ normal(y[i],x)
> }

For efficiency, this should just be

  mydata ~ normal(y, x);

- Bob

P.S.  We like to use y for modeled data, x for predictors,
and lower case n for loop indices and capital N for sizes,
then loop for (n in 1:N) so that the index matches the bound
so it's less things to remember when trying to read the code.

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Beta Regression - Needs more restrictions but why, where, and how?
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Beta Regression - Needs more restrictions but why, where, and how?
messages.body_plain:
Why are you constraining a and b to be positive here?  They're
inside the inverse logit transform, so it'd be more typical to let
them be unconstrained.  The default random inits for positive constrained
values will be exp(uniform(-2, 2)) or roughly in (1/9, 9).
If these all pile up to produce large mu values, then it's possible
beta_b is just being driven to 0.  Reducing the range may help, but
if you choose 1, the inits will be in (1/3, 3) or thereabouts, which may
still be a problem.

You could always try custom inits, which shouldn't be too hard
for this problem.

And why lower=0.1 on phi?  We only recommend constraints where
physically/logically necessary.  Otherwise, they can cause probability
mass to pile up at the boundary, which will cause computational
issues because of the logit transform to unconstrained space taking
these to large absolute negative values.  That may not be a problem
here, though.

I also embedded some comments on efficiency of the program.

> On Oct 10, 2016, at 10:57 PM, Ilan Strauss <ilans...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> Hi,
>
> I am modelling a proportion (a real number between 0 and 1) - my y[N] - using, at the moment, a single regressor (my X) - which is also a real number between 0 and 200.  Im trying to model this using a Bayesian beta regression in Stan. Eventually we will want to make it a more complex model (hierarcichal and quadratic?) But this simple version keeps giving me grief. It doesn't run unless I put constraints on everything (which requires moving things to be parameters even when in theory they shouldn't really). I can't see why this model below would need more restrictions. And if so where and how? Many thanks in advance for any assistance.
>
> Current error message:
>
> R CODE AND ERROR OUTPUT
> ---
>
> N <- nrow(ds)               \\we have 100 data points (N=100)
> y <- as.numeric(ds$usage_p)
> Xvar <- as.matrix(ds$distance)
> x1 = as.numeric(Xvar)
> K <- ncol(x1)
>
> data2 <- list(N=N,x1=x1,y=y)
> model_2 <- stan(file = "beta6.stan", data = data2, iter = 2000, chains = 5)
>
>
> Exception thrown at line 28: beta_log: Second shape parameter is 0, but must be > 0!    38
>   Error evaluating the log probability at the initial value.                            32
> Rejecting initial value:                                                                32
> ---
>
> STAN CODE:
> ---
> data {
>   int<lower=1> N;                   // sample size
>   real<lower=0,upper=1> y[N];     // response
>   vector[N] x1;                    // predictor matrix
> }
>
> parameters {
>   real<lower=0.1> phi;
>   real<lower=0> a;
>   real<lower=0> b;
>     }
>
> model {
>    real beta_a;
>    real beta_b;
>    real mu;
>
>     for (i in 1:N) {
>         mu = inv_logit(a + b*x1[i]);
>         beta_a = mu * phi;
>         beta_b = (1-mu) * phi;
>        y[i] ~ beta(beta_a, beta_b);
>     }
>
>    phi ~ cauchy(0, 2.5); // half-cauchy priors
>     a ~ cauchy(0, 2.5);
>     b ~ cauchy(0, 2.5);
> }
> ---
>
> I know it would be more efficient to increment the log posterior myself.

Not sure what you mean by that.  The sampling statements are at least
as efficient as target += ...  It'd be a bit more efficient to collect
the beta_a and beta_b up as vectors beta_as and beta_bs
and write y ~ beta(beta_as, beta_bs);  But given there are no shared
computations, it might not help much.

> I've tried to look for posts on similar(ish) issues. Found a few but nothing which helped me sufficiently on this specific issue.
>
> Many thanks!
>
> Ilan Strauss

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] fifth argument to integrate_ode_bdf (real data) must be data only and not reference parameters
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] fifth argument to integrate_ode_bdf (real data) must be data only and not reference parameters
messages.body_plain:
> On Oct 10, 2016, at 5:34 PM, Daniel Lee <bea...@alum.mit.edu> wrote:
>
> Hi Linas,
>
> integrate_ode() (and the other integrate_ode_*() functions) are special because they are.

There are two reasons:

1.  integrate_ode() takes the name of another function as an argument
which isn't supported for general-purpose Stan functions, and

2.  integrate_ode() restricts its data argument to be data only, meaning
that it can only use values that are defined in data or transformed data
or only involve constants (but the latter case can't arise with an array,
so it really needs to be defined in the data or transformed data block).

> In this case, it comes down to how we've implemented the C++.

Specifically, it's a custom expression in the parser, not a general
function application.

But the real problem is that there's no way for Stan to figure out
in the context of a function that an argument to the function is
data only.  That's because function arguments are allowed to be
any mix of data and parameters.

We could relax the constraint in the parser for integrate_ode()
and make it a run-time check that the values are not parameters
and instead issue a warning at compile time.  That might be a good
idea here.  I'll bring it up at our next meeting.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Identifying a constant that may be dropped for sampling
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Identifying a constant that may be dropped for sampling
messages.body_plain:
Missed this the first time around.

> On Oct 5, 2016, at 6:40 PM, terrance savitsky <tds...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> Hi, The following statement in the manual defines a parameter, transformed parameter or local model variable as not constant - and therefore required - for updating the sampling joint log-probability.

Right.  Those will all be of type stan::math::var (an autodiff variable)
instead of double in the C++ code.    We drop the double arguments using
some template traits programming in C++ at compile time.

> "The second difference is that if lambda is not a parameter, transformed parameter, or local model variable, the sampling statement is clever enough to drop the log(lambda) term."
>
> I sometimes get confused as to when something is a constant with respect to updating the sampling log-probability;

It's exactly as defined.  It's not about literally being constant,
it's about where it's defined.  If I do this:

transformed parameter {
  real a;
  a = 4;
}

then Stan can't tell that a is a constant and will not be able to
drop terms involving a from the log density.  If a value really is
constant, it should be defined as a transformed data variable and reused.

> for example, if i impose a Gaussian prior on a model parameter where the covariance matrix contains no parameters, then it is constant and i can drop the additive logdet term from the log-probability update.

If that covariance matrix is defined as a data or transformed data
variable or an expression that produces such, then it'll be dropped.

>  however, I'm currently building an lpdf function where it is not clear to me.

Nothing gets dropped from user-defined functions.  We don't have
a way to inject the relevant C++ traits code.

> I want to update the log-probability for the asymmetric lapace distribution, AL(mu,tau,p) with density function, f(x|mu,tau,p) = tau*p*(1-p)*exp(-tau*rho_{p}(x-mu)),where rho_{p}(u) is the so-called check function.   Here "p" denotes the skewness.  mu, x and tau are parameters.  Suppose I bring "p" into the model in the data block.  Then will the log(p) + log(1-p) terms drop out as constants?

Not automatically.  But you can drop them yourself manually.

Stan (and most MCMC and optimization routines) only require the log
density up to an additive constant.

- Bob

a partial pooling model, where there's a prior covariance structure on

Thanks!

Here's what I've done: load the rstanarm package and the elections88 data. Then
(actually I'm using a sample of 1000 from the data, just to speed things up).

SEED<-12345
t_prior <- student_t(df = 7)

# achieved nothing.
all.equal(fixef(M1),fixef(M2))
all.equal(ranef(M1),ranef(M2))
all.equal(VarCorr(M1),VarCorr(M2))

messages.subject: Re: using stan_glmer
messages.subject_clean: using stan_glmer
messages.body_plain:
I don't think this is specific to stan_glmer, but rather to the glmer function in lme4 on which stan_glmer is based. If you run the same model with glmer there is no covariance matrix estimated because there's only a varying intercept and no varying slope. So for example, if you had (1+x|state) you would have varying intercepts by state as well as varying slopes (on whatever variable x is) by state, and a covariance matrix would be estimated. In your case you can think of it as estimating 1x1 covariance matrix, that is, just the variance of the state-specific intercept shifts. In that situation only a subset of the arguments to decov() have any effect, although it's a bit hidden in the doc in the last sentence in the Covariance matrices section in help("priors", "rstanarm"):

> A one-by-one covariance matrix is just a variance and thus does not have regularization or concentration parameters, but does have shape and scale parameters for the prior standard deviation of that variable.

Hope that helps,

Jonah

messages.subject: intel compiler and Stan...
messages.subject_clean: intel compiler and Stan...
messages.body_plain:
Hi!

... be warned: You have to use the right compiler options; otherwise you will not see divergences!

I am using the Intel compiler 15.0.3 and I just ran a model for which I know that divergences do happen, but I did not get any. I went back and noticed that my model was compiled with the defaults which is to use optimization as per default from Intel. This leads to failures of the stan-math unit tests AND it seems to be the root cause for stopping Stan to report divergences. So to get the behavior which makes stan-math unit tests succeed you must use the options

-fp-model precise -fp-model source

Note that the Intel compiler is not an "official" compiler, but be warned when using it. This means you need to include this into your ~/.R/Makevars file in the definition of the CXXFLAGS, respectivley for cmdstan.

Best,
Sebastian

On Tuesday, October 11, 2016 at 3:25:28 PM UTC-4, Jonah Gabry wrote:
> I don't think this is specific to stan_glmer, but rather to the glmer function in lme4 on which stan_glmer is based. If you run the same model with glmer there is no covariance matrix estimated because there's only a varying intercept and no varying slope. So for example, if you had (1+x|state) you would have varying intercepts by state as well as varying slopes (on whatever variable x is) by state, and a covariance matrix would be estimated. In your case you can think of it as estimating 1x1 covariance matrix, that is, just the variance of the state-specific intercept shifts. In that situation only a subset of the arguments to decov() have any effect, although it's a bit hidden in the doc in the last sentence in the Covariance matrices section in help("priors", "rstanarm"):
>
> > A one-by-one covariance matrix is just a variance and thus does not have regularization or concentration parameters, but does have shape and scale parameters for the prior standard deviation of that variable.
>
> Hope that helps,
>
> Jonah

messages.body_plain:
There weren't any errors per se, just compiler warnings
and some numerical exceptions at runtime:

Exception thrown at line 34: lkj_corr_log: y is not positive definite.                                   9
Exception thrown at line 40: multi_normal_log: LDLT_Factor of covariance parameter is not positive d     1

Those will probably go away if you set adapt_delta higher, say to 0.9, or 0.95
or 0.99.  It may also help to set stepsize=0.01 or 0.1 (that's the initial
step size).

But the better way to solve the numerical issues for efficiency sake
is to use Cholesky-factor parameterizations.  There's an example in the
regression chapter of the manual.

Also, this

vector[3] p; // Choice probabilities
p[1] <- exp(x1_c[n] * beta[r[n]]);
p[2] <- exp(x2_c[n] * beta[r[n]]);
p[3] <- exp(x3_c[n] * beta[r[n]]);
#p[4] <- exp(x4_c[n] * beta[r[n]]);
p <- p / sum(p);
y[n] ~ categorical(p); // Model for choice

can be more economically (in computation and lines of code) be written
by declaring x_c to replace x1_c, x2_c, and x3_c as

  matrix[3, K_c] x_c[N];

then replacing all of the above with

  y[n] ~ categorical_logit(x_c[n] * beta[r[n]]);

The softmax operation,  exp(u) / sum(exp(u)),  is built into the
categorical_logit.

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
Sebastian,

I think I know the reason. It is my feeling - not scientific knowledge yet. PBPK models are essentially mass balances. If mass balance is satisfied then we have a feasible solution and model is close to finite differences. Otherwise it may not because outside of feasible region we may have really non physical behavior.

Below are examples of using jacobian and just stan's automatic diff.
Jacobian:
Log probability=-41.8827

 param idx           value           model     finite diff           error
         0         -1.2627         97.9315         97.9315    8.75615e-009
         1        -1.53898        -369.631        -369.631   -4.16072e-005
         2        0.449458         295.861         295.861   -3.10076e-005
         3      -0.0548587         372.812         372.813    -0.000499954
Automatic diff:
Log probability=-41.8827

param idx           value           model     finite diff           error
         0         -1.2627         97.9315         97.9315    8.53206e-009
         1        -1.53898        -369.631        -369.631    3.28921e-005
         2        0.449458         295.861         295.861    2.45195e-005
         3      -0.0548587         372.812         372.813    -0.000546025

Thus dMod produces right Jacobians!!!
This output is based on the same seed. But if seed is random sometimes it happens that initial value for parameter is infeasible and you get output like this:
Informational Message: The current Metropolis proposal is about to be rejected because of the following issue:
Exception thrown at line 111: stan::math::normal_log: Location parameter[9] is 1.#QNAN, but must be finite!
If this warning occurs sporadically, such as for highly constrained variable types like covariance matrices, then the sampler is fine,
but if this warning occurs often then your model may be either severely ill-conditioned or misspecified.

Rejecting initial value:
  Error evaluating the log probability at the initial value.

TEST GRADIENT MODE

 Log probability=-48.7114

 param idx           value           model     finite diff           error
         0         1.15616         51.0152         51.0152    5.99495e-009
         1        -1.81621        -65.8447        -120.561         54.7161
         2        -1.23776         46.1017        -5.26329          51.365
         3       -0.303782         80.0362         24.2669         55.7692

Please note that even for infeasible initial values the error might be very small. It seems there are many moving parts...

An aggressive thought. Instead of specifying ODE system in stan I rather keep it as original ode.c (attached). It would be cool if stan could grab external c functions and their jacobians (attached).

Linas

I don't know what a mass balance is, but finite diffs
can have very low precision when there is high curvature, which
can happen even in a well-specified model for the data, especially
in the tails.  That's in addition to their problems with rounding
which limits their precision overall.  Autodiff can run into
all the usual problems with numerical computations in terms of
precision.

Initialization can help avoiding those issues.  That's
affected by either doing one by hand, or by being careful with
constraints and where initialization happens by default, or
by using the control parameters to reduce diffuseness.

- Bob

What can happen is that a value goes off to infinity due to
improper posteriors or bad numerical problems, then you get
an infinite gradient and multiplication gives you NaN.

You can track down what's going wrong with print().

You can also reduce adapt_delta if it only happens occasionally
and that might solve the problem by making the Hamiltonian
simulation more accurate (if the problem is numerical rather
than an improper posterior).

- Bob

The ODE integrators are sufficiently imprecise that if the true concentrations
get anywhere close to zero then rounding errors will hit zero and the bound
will cause the transition to be rejected, so it’s usually a bad idea.  If you really
want to get precise close to zero concentration then you want to rewrite the
system of ODEs in terms of log concentrations and then solve that.

messages.body_plain:
Hi!

I did go to log-concentrations myself in mass-balance systems when using an ODE. This does, of course, solve the positivity problem at a potentially high price. The thing is that in log-space you have to (i) choose what zero is for you and (ii) you may end up getting huge changes on the log-scale which correspond to meaningless small absolute changes. For (i) you have to say, for example, that 1e-10 is zero for you which I would find ok (depending on units, of course). However, those states which don't carry mass will fall even lower until you have a dosing event, for example. Then you have a dosing event which adds maybe a dose of order unity. As a result you have a gigantic jump on the log-scale which renders the ODE system extremely stiff and you will almost certainly run into numerical issues.

As a hack I always try to make sure that by whatever means the concentration in any compartment never falls below some reasonable but low value which I am willing to accept as being close enough to zero yet small enough that I can ignore its presence.

I know that Nonmem does "turn off" compartments when they are close to zero, but we cannot do this. At least that's not obvious to me for now.

Another possibility could be to test in the ODE RHS function if the absolute value of that compartment is below some threshold. If it is below that, then you simply set dy_dt equal to 0. That's a hack which should work from a numerical perspective, but you need to be careful about this, of course.

Finally, we should maybe consider to allow Stan communicate with the sundials solver. This is possible, but currently not implemented. That would allow the ODE RHS to check if things are still OK and if not raise an error which gets processed by the CVODES library. So in your case that would mean to test if any y is smaller than 0. In that case you know that the ODE solver approximations did something bad for you and you can then tell the solver to redo the BDF iteration with higher precision.

Ok, that was now a lot of stuff; I hope it helps.

Best,
Sebastian

messages.body_plain:
Dear all,

I  have a problem understanding discrepancies between different model comparison results for a hierarchical vs. non-hierarchical instantiation of the same model and I can't think of what could have caused the problem.

I've got two models (for a reinforcement learning task in humans) that, when I fit my 30 participants individually, e.g. using matlab's fminsearch, I find that model A is vastly better than B (BIC difference is ~200, for the BIC summed across all participants). When I fit people individually in Stan, I see similarly that the log likelihood for each person massively favours model A.

But, when I use a hierarchical model in Stan, model B is strongly favoured. This is both the case when I do a leave-one participant-out cross validation (i.e. getting the log likelihood for the left out participant, by drawing his parameters randomly using the group priors in the generated quantities block) or when I fit all participants together hierarchically and just look at their log likelihoods.

As an aside, when I compare parameters for people either generated by a hierarchical or an independent model, they correlate strongly (r is ~0.8-0.9).

I am not sure whether this model fit result is even possible or whether it means that I must have made a coding error somewhere??

The only other thing that I have come up with so far is that maybe it's a problem with the parameters not being normally distributed on the group level? (though i am not sure whether this could even explain the model fit discrepancy). For many of the parameters I assume that they are normally distributed on one scale (e.g. from - to + infinity) and then I transform them to another scale (e.g. from 0 to 1). I've attached a figure that shows in the top row all the parameters from individual participants after i've adjusted them and the bottom row is the parameters before i've adjusted them. It looks like maybe there is a problem for 'lrnw' (which means 'how much you weight what you have learnt when you make a decision'). I'm sampling this as lrnw and then transform it so that lrnw_adj=1/(1+lrnw). And I'm assuming that lrnw is normally distributed, but this is clearly not true.

I would be very grateful for any advice
Jacquie

messages.body_plain:
Hi!

My basic question is: Can I drop chains which show a divergency if I am quite sure that these chains failed to warmup appropriately?

The thing is, I just came across a model and data situation which required huge care to avoid those divergencies. The model is a hierarchical logistic regression and I had to scale things right, use NCP and start stan with adapt_delta=0.99 and a stepsize of 0.01. Under these very conservative settings I still get from time to time 1-4 divergencies.

I suspect that Stan did not succeed during warmup to find conservative enough sampling parameters for some of the chains. As a result some of the chains (but not all) suffer from divergencies. Is it OK to drop those chains in question from the results?

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] divergency fun
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] divergency fun
messages.body_plain:
No.

Rarely does poor warmup lead to divergences — it almost always causes
the step size to drop to very small values at which point the sampler slows
to a crawl and you hit max treedepth warnings.

But more importantly, if you suspect that warmup is an issue than you can
easily inspect it by looking at the mass matrices (apparently only available
in CmdStan right now).  If they are the same for all chains then there is no
indication that anything when wrong, but if one chain has a mass matrix
with particularly small or large values _then_ you can be suspect of the
warmup procedure.  In that case you can tweak the warmup procedure
using the window length parameters described in the manual.

If you step back and analyze the posterior I bet you’ll find that the problem
is simpler than you have concluded.  In the non-centered parameterization
there are strong correlations between the population mean and population
standard deviation: when the population standard deviation is large the
mean can vary more, causing a tilt of the typical funnel geometry.  In particular,
if you plot the population mean vs the population standard deviation you’ll
see a skewed triangle with long corners when the standard deviation is large
and positive and the mean is large (either positive or negative).  It’s there
that the divergences usually occur.

The simple answer is to tighten your priors a little bit.  Adding more regularization
to the population standard deviation is always helpful, but if you are weary of
that then you can try tightening the population mean prior a bit and that should
clean up the stray divergences quickly.

data-dependent values, such as the true values in a measurement-error model

is just

or use a sum if the latent values are discrete.  I think the latent here
is smoking_rate_actual and I don't know how to integrate it out.  Others might.

messages.subject: Bayesian Variable Selection models
messages.subject_clean: Bayesian Variable Selection models
messages.body_plain:
Hello all,

I am looking to fit the following variable selection for linear regression models (Kuo & Mallick, 1998 <http://citeseerx.ist.psu.edu/viewdoc/download?doi=10.1.1.54.9573&rep=rep1&type=pdf>) in Stan:

y_i ~ N(gamma_1 * beta_1 * X_{i1} + ... + gamma_p * beta_p * X_{ip}, sigma^2)
beta_j ~ N(0, 100)
gamma_j ~ Bern(0.5)
sigma ~ some weakly informative prior

i = 1,...,n
j = 1,...,p

The gamma are indicator variables denoting whether or not that covariate should be included in the model. The posterior samples of gamma are of interest, as we can compute posterior model probabilities from the samples. E.g., gamma_1 = ... gamma_p = 1 is the "full model" where all variables are included, and we can calculate the proportion of this model occurring in the posterior state space of models, which gives an estimate for the posterior model probability of the full model.

While this can be implemented in BUGS or JAGS using Gibbs sampling, this of course can't be done in Stan because sampling from discrete distributions is not possible. There are two ways I can think of to make this happen in Stan:

APPROACH 1: Marginalise over gamma

As suggested in the manuals, one could marginalise the model over the gamma variables, and use the generated quantities block to obtain posterior samples for gamma.

ISSUE: Scalability, as p gets large. If I understand correctly, marginalising over all gamma variables requires the calculation of (the log-likelihood value of) all possible 2^p models. I am concerned about efficiency - I don't know how to code this marginalisation without having to call p nested loops.

APPROACH 2: Latent continuous variable

Assume for each gamma_j there is an underlying continuous latent variable Z_j which has a standard normal distribution. Define gamma_j = 1 if Z_j >= 0 and gamma_j = 0 otherwise. This should be an equivalent representation of the original model, at least in intention, because P[Z_j >= 0] = P[gamma_j = 1] = 0.5.

ISSUE: I am not sure I have implemented this correctly in Stan. For this simple example <https://gist.github.com/haziqjamil/6840d02a49fc8fb85013c021f45567a8> (p = 5, variables 1 and 2 not included in true model) it gives good results, in the sense that the posterior model probability of the true model does turn out to be the highest of all. The concern here is that the samples turn out to be severely autocorrelated, and sometimes divergent transitions also occur.

-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Would anybody care to give any input as to whether Approach 1 or 2 is better, or neither, and if so, what's a better way of fitting this variable selection model in Stan? Thanks in advance.

C++ is pass by value, but the values can be references (don't
blame me, I just wrestle with C++).

In the C++ translation of a Stan function call, primitives are
passed by pure value, as in (double x) or (int x), whereas any structures
(arrays or matrices) are passed by const reference, as in
(const Eigen::Matrix<T, L, R>& x).

If you do

X = foo(X)

then X is only set after foo(X) is evaluated.

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Bayesian Variable Selection models
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Bayesian Variable Selection models
messages.body_plain:
Right.  Your approach 1 is what you need to do, but it's
intractable, requiring 2^N evaluations for N variables.

Your approach 2 won't work because it will break derivatives.

You'll also find that while you can write these models with
Gibbs sampling, you can't easily sample over the posterior
because it's highly multimodal.  Instead, what will happen is
that your sampler will likely get stuck if there are two
correlated variables, sometimes eliminating one and sometimes
the other.

We don't worry much about these priors because the applications
people want for them are usually not fully Bayesian. That is,
they want to use this to eliminate variables.  But if you set up
the proper Bayesian inference, you'll find there's still some
posterior weight on gamma_j = 1, and so you can't drop the variable
itself.  At least not for full Bayes.

Aki's worked on some approaches to variable selection in
some more complex models:

https://users.aalto.fi/~ave/

Or, you can just put a reasonable prior on them and let them fall
where they fall.  They might shrink close to zero.  And if they
do shrink close to zero, you might be able to eliminate them because
they'll have no effect on model predictions.

- Bob

> On Oct 13, 2016, at 3:49 PM, Haziq Jamil <haziq...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> Hello all,
>
> I am looking to fit the following variable selection for linear regression models (Kuo & Mallick, 1998) in Stan:
>
> y_i ~ N(gamma_1 * beta_1 * X_{i1} + ... + gamma_p * beta_p * X_{ip}, sigma^2)
> beta_j ~ N(0, 100)
> gamma_j ~ Bern(0.5)
> sigma ~ some weakly informative prior
>
> i = 1,...,n
> j = 1,...,p
>
> The gamma are indicator variables denoting whether or not that covariate should be included in the model. The posterior samples of gamma are of interest, as we can compute posterior model probabilities from the samples. E.g., gamma_1 = ... gamma_p = 1 is the "full model" where all variables are included, and we can calculate the proportion of this model occurring in the posterior state space of models, which gives an estimate for the posterior model probability of the full model.
>
> While this can be implemented in BUGS or JAGS using Gibbs sampling, this of course can't be done in Stan because sampling from discrete distributions is not possible. There are two ways I can think of to make this happen in Stan:
>
> APPROACH 1: Marginalise over gamma
>
> As suggested in the manuals, one could marginalise the model over the gamma variables, and use the generated quantities block to obtain posterior samples for gamma.
>
> ISSUE: Scalability, as p gets large. If I understand correctly, marginalising over all gamma variables requires the calculation of (the log-likelihood value of) all possible 2^p models. I am concerned about efficiency - I don't know how to code this marginalisation without having to call p nested loops.
>
> APPROACH 2: Latent continuous variable
>
> Assume for each gamma_j there is an underlying continuous latent variable Z_j which has a standard normal distribution. Define gamma_j = 1 if Z_j >= 0 and gamma_j = 0 otherwise. This should be an equivalent representation of the original model, at least in intention, because P[Z_j >= 0] = P[gamma_j = 1] = 0.5.
>
> ISSUE: I am not sure I have implemented this correctly in Stan. For this simple example (p = 5, variables 1 and 2 not included in true model) it gives good results, in the sense that the posterior model probability of the true model does turn out to be the highest of all. The concern here is that the samples turn out to be severely autocorrelated, and sometimes divergent transitions also occur.
>
> -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
>
> Would anybody care to give any input as to whether Approach 1 or 2 is better, or neither, and if so, what's a better way of fitting this variable selection model in Stan? Thanks in advance.
>

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Bayesian Variable Selection models
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Bayesian Variable Selection models
messages.body_plain:
You can only fit a hard spike-and-slab variable selection model
in Stan with small numbers of variables.

It's also very hard to fit in JAGS or other Gibbs samplers.
They will tend to get stuck in modes and not mix well on the
Bernoulli variate indicating if a variable is selected or not.
The true posterior is not going to be 100% on or off (that is,
full Bayes won't do variable selection), and there are likely
to be many modes.  You can see that analytically if you write out
the posterior for the value of a coefficient.

There's a vast MCMC literature on the problems posed by
combinatorial models like variable selection, with Ising spin models
making up the bulk of that because they have real physical
analogues.

You will be able to diagnose this using multiple chains if
you give them diffuse initializations.  I can't recall how
JAGS initializes, but I think it may be deterministically by
default.  Masanao and Yu-Sun and Andrew built dealing with multiple
chains into R2jags, but I can't recall how inits work.

- Bob

If many of your predictors are highly correlated, I would first ask *why* they are correlated, try reducing some of the 41 down to a smaller number of constructs. You can do this via PLS-like combined variables or CFA-like latent variables, but I would certainly hesitate to throw 41 predictors into a model, ESPECIALLY if they are highly correlated. Aside from the label-switching problem inherent in bayesian mixtures, you're going to hit some multicollinearity problems.
