messages.subject: Re: Bayesian Variable Selection models
messages.subject_clean: Bayesian Variable Selection models
messages.body_plain:
Just curious, but could you just say all gamma_p ~ beta(.5,.5) or something? It'd estimate one model and, I think, drop out any variables that seem to just contribute noise to the likelihood.

On Thursday, October 13, 2016 at 2:49:46 PM UTC-5, Haziq Jamil wrote:
> Hello all,
>
> I am looking to fit the following variable selection for linear regression models (Kuo & Mallick, 1998 <http://citeseerx.ist.psu.edu/viewdoc/download?doi=10.1.1.54.9573&rep=rep1&type=pdf>) in Stan:
>
> y_i ~ N(gamma_1 * beta_1 * X_{i1} + ... + gamma_p * beta_p * X_{ip}, sigma^2)
> beta_j ~ N(0, 100)
> gamma_j ~ Bern(0.5)
> sigma ~ some weakly informative prior
>
> i = 1,...,n
> j = 1,...,p
>
> The gamma are indicator variables denoting whether or not that covariate should be included in the model. The posterior samples of gamma are of interest, as we can compute posterior model probabilities from the samples. E.g., gamma_1 = ... gamma_p = 1 is the "full model" where all variables are included, and we can calculate the proportion of this model occurring in the posterior state space of models, which gives an estimate for the posterior model probability of the full model.
>
> While this can be implemented in BUGS or JAGS using Gibbs sampling, this of course can't be done in Stan because sampling from discrete distributions is not possible. There are two ways I can think of to make this happen in Stan:
>
> APPROACH 1: Marginalise over gamma
>
> As suggested in the manuals, one could marginalise the model over the gamma variables, and use the generated quantities block to obtain posterior samples for gamma.
>
> ISSUE: Scalability, as p gets large. If I understand correctly, marginalising over all gamma variables requires the calculation of (the log-likelihood value of) all possible 2^p models. I am concerned about efficiency - I don't know how to code this marginalisation without having to call p nested loops.
>
> APPROACH 2: Latent continuous variable
>
> Assume for each gamma_j there is an underlying continuous latent variable Z_j which has a standard normal distribution. Define gamma_j = 1 if Z_j >= 0 and gamma_j = 0 otherwise. This should be an equivalent representation of the original model, at least in intention, because P[Z_j >= 0] = P[gamma_j = 1] = 0.5.
>
> ISSUE: I am not sure I have implemented this correctly in Stan. For this simple example <https://gist.github.com/haziqjamil/6840d02a49fc8fb85013c021f45567a8> (p = 5, variables 1 and 2 not included in true model) it gives good results, in the sense that the posterior model probability of the true model does turn out to be the highest of all. The concern here is that the samples turn out to be severely autocorrelated, and sometimes divergent transitions also occur.
>
> -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
>
> Would anybody care to give any input as to whether Approach 1 or 2 is better, or neither, and if so, what's a better way of fitting this variable selection model in Stan? Thanks in advance.

While Stephen's suggestion is more sensible than what I am going to suggest, there are other things you could do. I never haven been able to use it myself but Andrew published a paper  <http://www.stat.columbia.edu/~gelman/research/published/parameterization.pdf>which suggests a Bayesian approach to your problem (section 5.2.3). If you have multiple variables x1, x2, x3 that are measuring a similar construct e.g. economic performance of a country as measured by (GDP, employment, ...), you can model their contribution with the parameters a, b1, b2, b3 and a strong prior on b1, b2, b3.

y = a (b1 x1 + b2 x2 + b3 x3)
b1, b2, b3 ~ normal(1/3, sigma)

and a suitable prior for a. a is than the contribution of economic performance to your outcome and b1, b2, b3 are the contribution of your variables to economic performance. The joint prior for b1, b2, and b3 should help with potential multicollinearity issues.

Stijn

> y_i ~ N(gamma_1 * beta_1 * X_{i1} + ... + gamma_p * beta_p * X_{ip}, sigma^2)
> beta_j ~ N(0, 100)
> gamma_j ~ Bern(0.5)

>
> i = 1,...,n
> j = 1,...,p
>

Right, it's certainly not perfect, and the betas will be incorrectly estimated (overestimated --- you'd have to multiply the posterior estimates by the gamma value I think), but intuitively it seems like crappy predictors will have lower gamma values, and better predictors higher values. > On Oct 14, 2016, at 3:18 PM, Stephen Martin <hwki...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> Right, it's certainly not perfect, and the betas will be incorrectly estimated (overestimated --- you'd have to multiply the posterior estimates by the gamma value I think),

That's right.  And you get the implied prior on that product from the
independent priors on beta and gamma.

> but intuitively it seems like crappy predictors will have lower gamma values, and better predictors higher values.

> Could probably play with the gamma priors to highly, highly encourage the model to force a near-0 or near-1 probability value  (e.g., using very wide logistic as a prior and converting the logistic to probability; that samples better than using high-valued, inverted beta distributions like beta(.001,.001)). Once you do that, you'd have gamma values closer to .98 and .02, essentially dropping the predictor from the model, I think.

As soon as you start making the priors very sharp to push the gamma
toward 0 and 1, you'll get problems with sampling due to energy wells
(local density maxima) that are too deep to climb out of with HMC (or
Gibbs).

This is good for thinking about variable selection.  Which variable
do you select if two variables x[i] and and x[j] are highly correlated?
It depends on amount of regularization and how much better you'll do
at predicting y.  Consider the limit where x[i] and x[j] are identical.
You only need one predictor.  But the posterior of which one you get isn't
identified.  When there are multiple things like this going on, the combinatorics
add up to make it pretty much impossible to solve this problem tractably
in the general case.

With the following, you can see that the posterior density is very skewed,
with half the draws for gamma[2] and gamma[3] being very close to 0 and
others being uch higher to lead to the final posterior means of 0.13 and
0.18.

- Bob

Stan doesn't do Metropolis by default---it's using the NUTS
algorithm.  The adapt_delta is not targeting "acceptance rate"
in the Metropolis sense, but the points along the Hamiltonian
simulation.  See our manual or: http://www.jmlr.org/papers/v15/hoffman14a.html

But even basic HMC, which is a Metropolis algorithm, wants
an acceptance rate much higher than the one for Metropolis (and
keep in mind the Metropolis number was assming a normal posterior).
See:  https://arxiv.org/abs/1312.0906

- Bob

messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Bayesian Variable Selection models
messages.body_plain:
On Friday, 14 October 2016 16:45:20 UTC+1, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> You can only fit a hard spike-and-slab variable selection model
> in Stan with small numbers of variables.
>
> It's also very hard to fit in JAGS or other Gibbs samplers.
> They will tend to get stuck in modes and not mix well on the
> Bernoulli variate indicating if a variable is selected or not.
> The true posterior is not going to be 100% on or off (that is,
> full Bayes won't do variable selection), and there are likely
> to be many modes.  You can see that analytically if you write out
> the posterior for the value of a coefficient.
>

In a Gibbs sampling procedure of the original model above, the conditional density for the betas is Gaussian, and Bernoulli for the gammas. I'm not sure what you mean by multimodal? Also, when you say the Bernoulli variates get stuck and not mix well, e.g. gamma_j keeps on being sampled as 1, 1, 1, 1, ... with some occasional zeroes, then surely the model is telling us that this variable is important, don't throw it out? If you mean the betas don't mix well, then sure it's a problem. But the Gibbs conditionals seem to be nice distributions, I'm failing to see how it can be an issue.

The posterior mean of the gamma_j samples are interpreted as the posterior inclusion probabilities for each variable X_j (Ntzoufras, 2011 <https://books.google.co.uk/books?id=1yZnwnOxXsEC&pg=SA10-PA60&lpg=SA10-PA60&dq=posterior+inclusion+probabilities+ntzoufras&source=bl&ots=ZIVKHbkdLG&sig=JRo7J5J2IPI_-kdKfbGsXLhTrzg&hl=en&sa=X&ved=0ahUKEwiv0MC2j9vPAhVLKcAKHStRC4QQ6AEIKjAB>). So yes agreed that Bayes doesn't turn variables 100% on or off, but inference on variable or model selection is done based on probabilities, and one could choose the model with the highest posterior probability or median probability models (Barbieri and Berger, 2004 <http://projecteuclid.org/download/pdfview_1/euclid.aos/1085408489>).

> There's a vast MCMC literature on the problems posed by
> combinatorial models like variable selection, with Ising spin models
> making up the bulk of that because they have real physical
> analogues.

> You will be able to diagnose this using multiple chains if
> you give them diffuse initializations.  I can't recall how
> JAGS initializes, but I think it may be deterministically by
> default.  Masanao and Yu-Sun and Andrew built dealing with multiple
> chains into R2jags, but I can't recall how inits work.
>
> - Bob
>
>
> > On Oct 14, 2016, at 3:36 AM, Haziq Jamil <haziq...@gmail.com> wrote:
> >
> > Thanks both for your responses.
> >
> > Without getting into too much of a discussion on the merits of these types of models and their applicability in real life situations, I am interested in these particular models as it ties in with some work I've been doing lately. I was hoping to change the MCMC engine from JAGS to Stan, but I guess there doesn't seem to be a way to do this at the moment.
> >
> > Haziq

Stephen, thanks for the example. It is an interesting alternative to the original model. Initially I did try making the gammas continuous using Uniform(0,1) priors but that gave terrible results. Your suggestion of a horseshoe-like prior is closer to the original model, since the Bernoulli(0.5) on the gammas are supposed to give this apriori indifference on being selected in the model or not.

What I find attractive about the original Kuo & Mallick model is the ability to do subset selection, something which is not possible with continuous gammas, I don't think. Sure we can get estimates for the coefficients as beta * gamma, but if that's the interest then probably a reasonable prior on beta would do the trick (as Bob pointed in the first reply to my original post). Sometimes, there is a desire to know what's the most "reasonable" parsimonious and interpretable model - a goal which is achieved through model selection.

> > > The gamma are indicator variables denoting whether or not that covariate should be included in the model. The posterior samples of gamma are of interest, as we can compute posterior model probabilities from the samples. E.g., gamma_1 = ... gamma_p = 1 is the "full model" where all variables are included, and we can calculate the proportion of this model occurring in the posterior state space of models, which gives an estimate for the posterior model probability of the full model.
> > >
> > > While this can be implemented in BUGS or JAGS using Gibbs sampling, this of course can't be done in Stan because sampling from discrete distributions is not possible. There are two ways I can think of to make this happen in Stan:
> > >
> > > APPROACH 1: Marginalise over gamma
> > >
> > > As suggested in the manuals, one could marginalise the model over the gamma variables, and use the generated quantities block to obtain posterior samples for gamma.
> > >
> > > ISSUE: Scalability, as p gets large. If I understand correctly, marginalising over all gamma variables requires the calculation of (the log-likelihood value of) all possible 2^p models. I am concerned about efficiency - I don't know how to code this marginalisation without having to call p nested loops.
> > >
> > > APPROACH 2: Latent continuous variable
> > >
> > > Assume for each gamma_j there is an underlying continuous latent variable Z_j which has a standard normal distribution. Define gamma_j = 1 if Z_j >= 0 and gamma_j = 0 otherwise. This should be an equivalent representation of the original model, at least in intention, because P[Z_j >= 0] = P[gamma_j = 1] = 0.5.
> > >
> > > ISSUE: I am not sure I have implemented this correctly in Stan. For this simple example (p = 5, variables 1 and 2 not included in true model) it gives good results, in the sense that the posterior model probability of the true model does turn out to be the highest of all. The concern here is that the samples turn out to be severely autocorrelated, and sometimes divergent transitions also occur.
> > >
> > > -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
> > >
> > > Would anybody care to give any input as to whether Approach 1 or 2 is better, or neither, and if so, what's a better way of fitting this variable selection model in Stan? Thanks in advance.
> > >

messages.subject: Memory accumulation in simulation replications despite using RM()
messages.subject_clean: Memory accumulation in simulation replications despite using RM()
messages.body_plain:
I am writing to ask about possible sources of and remedies for memory accumulation issues in RStan.

In my program there are several students currently running simulations to investigate the performance of multilevel models using R and RStan, but students are routinely running into difficulties when running multiple replications: after a handful of replications (2-5), students are encountering errors where there is insufficient memory to allocate vectors, or when models are run using RStudio on AWS instances, the servers crash as a result of insufficient memory.

A common feature of the models that myself and other students are running is the existence of parameters which covary, and the use of multi_normal or multi_normal_cholesky draws within the Stan code. There are several posts on various message boards related to memory accumulation in RStan, but the issue with memory accumulation when running the multi_normal function was said to be addressed in the most recent version of the program (https://github.com/stan-dev/rstan/issues/130).

We are currently running RStan Version 2.12.1, packaged: 2016-09-11 13:07:50 UTC, GitRev: 85f7a56811da, and still encountering issues with memory accumulation.

Details from a specific use case (code and original dataset) are contained in this Google Drive link:
​​https://drive.google.com/open?id=0B0iDFf0080xBaXlpNV9Ib1ZWVWs

- Raw data matrices are approximately 300 MB in size.
- Per discussions on Google Groups (https://groups.google.com/forum/#!searchin/stan-users/memory%7Csort:date/stan-users/HpdXNz2iA7E/T-eFvQq9BQAJ) the rm() command was included in the code. No reduction of memory usage wa observed when “rm(fit)” was used before starting the next replication; using “rm(list=ls())” reduced memory accumulation by approximately 50% per replication but doe not address the problem in full.
- Prior to the inclusion of an rm() command, only two replications could be run before the program terminated with the error, “Error: cannot allocate vector of size 935.3 Mb."

Is CmdStan the solution to the accumulation problem? Could a different placement of the rm() command help address memory accumulation? Are the draws from the multinormal distribution likely the issue?

Given that students often run tens or sometimes hundreds of replications per cell in statistical simulations, this problem is one we are eager to solve and would appreciate any insight.

messages.body_plain:
Hi Krishna,

> Choice conjoint data set with 30 respondents and 20,000 iterations took 48 minutes to complete.

Why do you need 20,000 draws. Based on my experience this is complete overkill for these models. What's your effective sample size? Or... how many samples do you need for inference in your case? Do you use chains in parallel? What kind of machine are you using for computing? Renting a nice amazon machine for 2 hours isn't that expensive!

Most of the time I use 4 chains, 1,000 draws for warmup (check the trace plots!) and then 2,500 draws for each chain (== total post-warmup draws = 10,000). All R̂ R^s are < 1.0051.005. neffneff is > 2,000 for all relevant params... that's ok for me.
> I'm now running the current successful code with another data set with 1,000 respondents and 20,000 iterations (alpha = 0.99 and stepsize = 0.1). It is still stuck on the 1 iteration of the sampling for the past 2.5 hours.

Again... why 20,000 draws? What about parallelization? And I don't think that you literally mean the first iteration, right?!? I never tried Choice Based Conjoint with more than 500 respondents (to expensive for me)... However, do you really need that many respondents in the analysis? What is the goal of the analysis? Are you interested in the estimated multivariate normal distribution of the utility parameters of do you need the individual level ββs?
> Question: Is this typical?

This is difficult to answer.. see above!

In another mail you asked:

> Question: How do I extract individual level part-worths for each respondent from a stanfit object into a CSV file?

My hunch is you are indeed interested in the individual ββs. Given the example I posted earlier you need to do the following (and I think Ben already answered the question):
beta <- extract(res_stan, pars = "beta")[[1]]
str(beta) # array: n_draws x n_respondents x n_coef
means <- apply(beta, 2:3, mean)
str(means) # matrix: n_respondents x n_coef
write.csv(means, file = "means.csv")

I urge you not to use only the posterior means in the next steps of your analysis because one nice feature of the HB estimation is that you get the full posterior distribution. I guess you're not only going show the posterior means in a big table in your paper but you are running (also) some sort of non-linear transformations (e.g., market simulation, What'if simulation, profit maximization, ...). The uncertainty in your individual level estimates will be quite large because of the low number of obs. for each respondet. Hence plugging in your posterior means in your non-linear transformations might actually be misleading...

One last point regarding speed: maybe for you it is worth considering classical methods (=> maximum simulated likelihood). mlogit is nice and very fast in R, because you integrate the heterogeneity out of your likelihood. In a second step you can use importance sampling to derive the conditional estimates of each respondent given his/her choices and the estimated heterogeneity distribution (see Kenneth Trains book chapter 11 here <http://eml.berkeley.edu/books/choice2nd/Ch11_p259-281.pdf>. AFAIK this is even implemented in gmnl (see Sarrias / Daziano (2015) <http://msarrias.weebly.com/uploads/3/7/7/8/37783629/gmnl_v2_vignette.pdf>). Don't get me wrong... I'm not saying this is the best way but it will do the job in your case (because you only want a point estimates), it is easy to implement and it is quite fast (even with many respondents). Once you have estimated the (“representative”) heterogeneity distribution this procedure scales linearly with the number of respondents.

Hope this helps!

Best,
Daniel

PS: whoever is interested in discrete choice models + R ... contact me via “daniel.guhl at hu-berlin.de <http://hu-berlin.de>“

messages.body_plain:
On Saturday, October 15, 2016 at 7:52:41 AM UTC-4, Shauna Sweet wrote:
> Is CmdStan the solution to the accumulation problem? Could a different placement of the rm() command help address memory accumulation? Are the draws from the multinormal distribution likely the issue?

The biggest difference between CmdStan and RStan is that CmdStan by default does not save the warmup iterations whereas RStan does. But you can pass save_warmup = FALSE to stan() and it will not save the warmup. Another difference is that if you are using 4 parallel chains in RStan, it holds 4 copies of the data in R and 4 copies in C++ whereas 4 parallel chains in CmdStan will only hold 4 copies of the data in C++.

You can also pass pars = character(0) and sample_file = "my_model" to stan(), in which case it will write everything to the disk like CmdStan does. You can read the resulting csv files (called my_model_1, my_model_2, my_model_3, and my_model_4) into R via read_stan_csv(), but you may still have the problem that you can't load all the draws with the available memory.

Possibly some memory is used by having the DLL loaded into R. You could try executing

dyn.unload(file.path(tempdir(), paste0(get_stanmodel(posterior)@dso@dso_filename, .Platform$dynlib.ext)))

where posterior is an object produced by stan() that you don't need anymore, but do that before calling rm().

Ben

messages.subject_clean: How to build a Rstan package? Particularly what's the best way to save compiled model files?
messages.body_plain:
I want to say that I had some similar problems and thought I'd share my experience.

1) When adding a Stan model to an existing package that contains C/C++/Fortran code and uses R's native routine registration, it is necessary to either explicitly register the name of the Rcpp Module boot functions for every model that you wish to compile, or to make sure that dynamic symbol lookup is set to true. Errors on loading the package such as:

Error in .doLoadActions(where, attach) :
  error in load action .__A__.1 for package PACKAGENAME: is(module, "character"): object 'm' not found

can be traced to this. I think that using dynamic symbol lookup is the default, but turning it off can yield a performance benefit if the package makes frequent use of native routines. To add boot functions, the package needs a C/C++ file with contents similar to:

// if C and not C++, ignore the extern "C" part and replace the casts with C-style ones
extern "C" {
  // declarations matches Modules.cpp, but that file has to be preprocessed first to actually see definition
  extern SEXP _rcpp_module_boot_stan_fit4MODELNAME1_mod();
  extern SEXP _rcpp_module_boot_stan_fit4MODELNAME2_mod();

  R_CallMethodDef R_callMethods[] = {
    { "_rcpp_module_stan_fit4MODELNAME1_mod_init",
      reinterpret_cast<DL_FUNC>(&_rcpp_module_stan_fit4MODELNAME1_mod_init),
      0 },
    { "_rcpp_module_stan_fit4MODELNAME2_mod_init",
      reinterpret_cast<DL_FUNC>(&_rcpp_module_stan_fit4MODELNAME2_mod_init),
      0 },
    { "ordinaryNativeRoutine", reinterpret_cast<DL_FUNC>(&ordinaryNativeRoutine), 10 },
    ...
    { NULL, NULL, 0 }
  };

  void R_init_PACKAGENAME(DllInfo* info)
  {
    R_registerRoutines(info, NULL, R_callMethods, NULL, NULL);
    R_useDynamicSymbols(info, static_cast<Rboolean>(FALSE));
  }
}

2) The system and user library paths in instances spawned by parallel::makeCluster in the sampling function can be reversed from the parent R session. If you happen to have an old version in the system library path with the one containing the stan model in your user library path (say, release and development versions), sampling can fail with an error such as:

Error in checkForRemoteErrors(val) :
  NUMCHAINS nodes produced errors; first error: object 'model_MODELNAME' not found

This will only happen with more than one chain, as when there is only one sampling happens in your current R session. I filed an issue on this, but an obvious workaround is to just work with a single version of your package.

Vince

On Saturday, October 15, 2016 at 11:24:37 AM UTC-4, Ben Goodrich wrote:
> On Saturday, October 15, 2016 at 7:52:41 AM UTC-4, Shauna Sweet wrote:
> > Is CmdStan the solution to the accumulation problem? Could a different placement of the rm() command help address memory accumulation? Are the draws from the multinormal distribution likely the issue?
>
> The biggest difference between CmdStan and RStan is that CmdStan by default does not save the warmup iterations whereas RStan does. But you can pass save_warmup = FALSE to stan() and it will not save the warmup. Another difference is that if you are using 4 parallel chains in RStan, it holds 4 copies of the data in R and 4 copies in C++ whereas 4 parallel chains in CmdStan will only hold 4 copies of the data in C++.
>
> You can also pass pars = character(0) and sample_file = "my_model" to stan(), in which case it will write everything to the disk like CmdStan does. You can read the resulting csv files (called my_model_1, my_model_2, my_model_3, and my_model_4) into R via read_stan_csv(), but you may still have the problem that you can't load all the draws with the available memory.
>
> Possibly some memory is used by having the DLL loaded into R. You could try executing
>
> dyn.unload(file.path(tempdir(), paste0(get_stanmodel(posterior)@dso@dso_filename, .Platform$dynlib.ext)))
>
> where posterior is an object produced by stan() that you don't need anymore, but do that before calling rm().
>
> Ben

messages.subject: Re: Error terms - lme4 vs rstanarm
messages.subject_clean: Error terms - lme4 vs rstanarm
messages.body_plain:
Hi Paul,

The estimates from rstanarm are not intended to always mirror those from lme4. lme4 is doing a type of maximum likelihood estimation giving you point estimates at the mode of the likelihood. rstanarm is doing full Bayesian inference, which means we're estimating the full joint posterior distribution of all parameters, which is a compromise between the likelihood and the prior, and then if we summarize the posterior we typically look at expectations, which can give you something quite different than the mode of the likelihood. So even before estimating anything we shouldn't necessarily expect to the get the same answers, especially if those answers are point estimates. For some model+data combinations there won't be much difference and for others there might be substantial differences. In most cases I would trust the estimates from Stan over those from lme4 when there are important differences (and not only for the estimates of the parameters themselves but also for prediction). Assuming of course that there were no red flags when running the MCMC.

If you do want to reproduce the lme4 standard deviation this should come closer

stan_glmer(

  DV1 ~ VarF1 + VarF2 + VarF3 + VarF4 + VarF5 +
    VarF6 + VarF7 + VarF8 + VarF9 + VarT1 +
    VarT2 + VarT3 + (1 | Level1),

  data = mydata,
  QR = TRUE,
  prior = normal(0,1),
  prior_covariance = decov(scale = 0.25),
  prior_intercept = priorI,
  adapt_delta = 0.99,
  cores = 2
)

although I'm not sure whether or not it's the right thing to do in this particular case. Often with only a few group levels it's good to be skeptical of the lme4 estimate of the standard deviation of the "random effects". The uncertainty estimates are probably too small.

Hope that helps,

Jonah

P.S. See this recent thread <https://groups.google.com/forum/#!category-topic/stan-users/rstanarm/j0FQReuORi4> for more on why Ben's P.S. is true

Hi Sebastian,

The easiest way is to first clone or download stan-mode: https://github.com/stan-dev/stan-mode.

Inside your .emacs file, add this:

(add-to-list 'load-path "<path-to-stan-mode>/stan-mode")
(require 'stan-mode)
(add-to-list 'auto-mode-alist '("\\.stan$" . stan-mode))

Note the first path has a stan-mode within the path. That's intended. From within the repo, the actual stan-mode emacs file is in stan-mode/stan-mode.el

Daniel

Hi Daniel

Thanks for getting back with these details. Here are answers to your questions:

1. The 20,000 draws is to establish an apples to apples comparison and benchmark against Sawtooth CBC/HB and R packages ChoiceModelR and mlogit. Both Sawtooth and ChoiceModelR allow conjugate priors so from an every day tool to use I found that ChoiceModelR does extremely well relative to Sawtooth. I'm also quite happy with mlogit. I'm testing RSGHB and RStan so that I have more tools to tackle extremely complex designs I run into with clients, "who want what they want". I'm working on a study now where there are 16 attributes ranging from 3 levels to 6 levels. It is insanity.

2. My interest is absolutely in individual level betas as you stated, to set up forecasts and predictions of future market shares. Hence my request to extract individual level betas.

3. I'm running the simulations now with total of 2000 runs, split equally between warmup and sampling. I'm also trying to get a dedicated, beefed up machine with 32GB of RAM so I can use it just for these type of simulations.

4. Is there a way to specify to Stan that I need only individual level betas and associated variance and not all the output Stan would generate by default. Another forum member mentioned that saving all of these parameters is probably stretching the limits of my machine and RStan.

5. I will keep you posted how these turn out.

Krishna

Are you interested in the estimated multivariate normal distribution of the utility parameters of do you need the individual level ββs?
> > Question: Is this typical?
>
> This is difficult to answer.. see above!
>
> In another mail you asked:
> > Question: How do I extract individual level part-worths for each respondent from a stanfit object into a CSV file?
>
> My hunch is you are indeed interested in the individual ββs. Given the example I posted earlier you need to do the following (and I think Ben already answered the question):
> beta <- extract(res_stan, pars = "beta")[[1]]
> str(beta) # array: n_draws x n_respondents x n_coef
> means <- apply(beta, 2:3, mean)
> str(means) # matrix: n_respondents x n_coef
> write.csv(means, file = "means.csv")
>
> I urge you not to use only the posterior means in the next steps of your analysis because one nice feature of the HB estimation is that you get the full posterior distribution. I guess you're not only going show the posterior means in a big table in your paper but you are running (also) some sort of non-linear transformations (e.g., market simulation, What'if simulation, profit maximization, ...). The uncertainty in your individual level estimates will be quite large because of the low number of obs. for each respondet. Hence plugging in your posterior means in your non-linear transformations might actually be misleading...
>
> One last point regarding speed: maybe for you it is worth considering classical methods (=> maximum simulated likelihood). mlogit is nice and very fast in R, because you integrate the heterogeneity out of your likelihood. In a second step you can use importance sampling to derive the conditional estimates of each respondent given his/her choices and the estimated heterogeneity distribution (see Kenneth Trains book chapter 11 here <http://eml.berkeley.edu/books/choice2nd/Ch11_p259-281.pdf>. AFAIK this is even implemented in gmnl (see Sarrias / Daziano (2015) <http://msarrias.weebly.com/uploads/3/7/7/8/37783629/gmnl_v2_vignette.pdf>). Don't get me wrong... I'm not saying this is the best way but it will do the job in your case (because you only want a point estimates), it is easy to implement and it is quite fast (even with many respondents). Once you have estimated the (“representative”) heterogeneity distribution this procedure scales linearly with the number of respondents.
>
> Hope this helps!
>
> Best,
> Daniel
>
> PS: whoever is interested in discrete choice models + R ... contact me via “daniel.guhl at hu-berlin.de <http://hu-berlin.de>“
> > Am 15.10.2016 um 04:46 schrieb krishna mohan <krish4...@gmail.com>:
> >
> > An update:
> > 1. Choice conjoint data set with 30 respondents and 20,000 iterations took 48 minutes to complete.

> >
> > Question: Is this typical?
>
>

messages.body_plain:
Hi Jonah and Ben,

Thank you for taking the time to clarify some important points: it was really helpful. I re-ran the model with prior_covariance = decov(scale = 0.25) and the the standard deviation of the random intercept is now in line with what I was expecting.

In my random intercept model that regularisation=2 was a left-over of a previous model with random slopes, and I was not expecting it to play any role in the new one. So Jonah thank you for pointing out that prior_covariance can indeed be applied to a 1x1 covariance matrix scenario.

Best regards,
Paul

On Sunday, October 16, 2016 at 11:10:32 PM UTC+1, Jonah Gabry wrote:
> Hi Paul,
>
> The estimates from rstanarm are not intended to always mirror those from lme4. lme4 is doing a type of maximum likelihood estimation giving you point estimates at the mode of the likelihood. rstanarm is doing full Bayesian inference, which means we're estimating the full joint posterior distribution of all parameters, which is a compromise between the likelihood and the prior, and then if we summarize the posterior we typically look at expectations, which can give you something quite different than the mode of the likelihood. So even before estimating anything we shouldn't necessarily expect to the get the same answers, especially if those answers are point estimates. For some model+data combinations there won't be much difference and for others there might be substantial differences. In most cases I would trust the estimates from Stan over those from lme4 when there are important differences (and not only for the estimates of the parameters themselves but also for prediction). Assuming of course that there were no red flags when running the MCMC.
>
> If you do want to reproduce the lme4 standard deviation this should come closer
>
> stan_glmer(
>   DV1 ~ VarF1 + VarF2 + VarF3 + VarF4 + VarF5 +
>     VarF6 + VarF7 + VarF8 + VarF9 + VarT1 +
>     VarT2 + VarT3 + (1 | Level1),
>   data = mydata,
>   QR = TRUE,
>   prior = normal(0,1),
>   prior_covariance = decov(scale = 0.25),
>   prior_intercept = priorI,
>   adapt_delta = 0.99,
>   cores = 2
> )
>
> although I'm not sure whether or not it's the right thing to do in this particular case. Often with only a few group levels it's good to be skeptical of the lme4 estimate of the standard deviation of the "random effects". The uncertainty estimates are probably too small.
>
> Hope that helps,
>
> Jonah
>
> P.S. See this recent thread <https://groups.google.com/forum/#!category-topic/stan-users/rstanarm/j0FQReuORi4> for more on why Ben's P.S. is true
>
> On Sunday, October 16, 2016 at 1:15:27 PM UTC-4, Ben Goodrich wrote:
> > On Sunday, October 16, 2016 at 12:59:48 PM UTC-4, Paul Scutti wrote:
> > > I am running a basic random intercept model both in lme4 and rstanarm. While I am getting identical results for the fixed effects, the same cannot be said for the random effects. The standard deviation for the residual is ok (0.74 for both), but for the intercept I get 0.31 in lme4 and more than double (0.63) in rstanarm. Any thoughts?
> >
> > Prior on the standard deviation, only having two groups with which to estimate that standard deviation, mode of likelihood vs. mean of posterior, the irrelevance of comparing point estimates, etc.
> >
> > Ben
> >
> > P.S. Setting regularization = 2 does not do anything when there is only one hyperparameter to estimate.
> >

messages.subject: Re: Improving Code Efficiency (Discrete Choice Analysis)

messages.body_plain:
100% memory usage is definitely no good.

If you move those parts to the model section, they will not be saved in the output. However, everything in the transformed parameters is determined by your parameters and data, so you could extract the parameters at the end of the model run, and then in R calculate each of the transformed parameters. It is definitely a bit of work, and just saving what the model calculates is certainly the easiest path. But it is a good trick to avoid saving intermediate variables you are not concerned about, or if you are trying to reduce the size of the output.

As for using Cmdstan, the cmdstan guide has a great getting started section which should get you most of the way there. The only slightly tricky thing is preparing the data. For this, I get the data prepared in R similar to using Rstan, and then use the Rstan function stan_rdump() to save all the data to a file that cmdstan can read. After the run, you will have a .csv which can be read into R using the RStan function read_stan_csv(). From there everything is pretty much the same as working with the output of RStan.

I always start running a model in Stan with 200 warmup, 200 samples per chain, and then increase if it appears I need better warmup or more N_eff. In my experience, with 4 chains and a straightforward, well identified model this typically is more than enough.

Matt

constraints saving draws.

This can be simplified to:

  log_lambda = rows_dot_product(x, beta[jj]);

but it's not going to be much if any faster.

messages.subject: Re: Error terms - lme4 vs rstanarm
messages.subject_clean: Error terms - lme4 vs rstanarm
messages.body_plain:
Hi Paul,

you might be interested in having a look at
http://www.ling.uni-potsdam.de/~vasishth/pdfs/BatesEtAlParsimonious2015.pdf
They show that "even under convergence, overparameterization may lead to uninterpretable models" in lme4.

Bests,
Bruno

On Monday, October 17, 2016 at 5:45:38 PM UTC+2, Paul Scutti wrote:
> Hi Jonah and Ben,
>
> Thank you for taking the time to clarify some important points: it was really helpful. I re-ran the model with prior_covariance = decov(scale = 0.25) and the the standard deviation of the random intercept is now in line with what I was expecting.
>
> In my random intercept model that regularisation=2 was a left-over of a previous model with random slopes, and I was not expecting it to play any role in the new one. So Jonah thank you for pointing out that prior_covariance can indeed be applied to a 1x1 covariance matrix scenario.
>
>
> Best regards,
> Paul
>
>
>
> On Sunday, October 16, 2016 at 11:10:32 PM UTC+1, Jonah Gabry wrote:
> > Hi Paul,
> >
> > The estimates from rstanarm are not intended to always mirror those from lme4. lme4 is doing a type of maximum likelihood estimation giving you point estimates at the mode of the likelihood. rstanarm is doing full Bayesian inference, which means we're estimating the full joint posterior distribution of all parameters, which is a compromise between the likelihood and the prior, and then if we summarize the posterior we typically look at expectations, which can give you something quite different than the mode of the likelihood. So even before estimating anything we shouldn't necessarily expect to the get the same answers, especially if those answers are point estimates. For some model+data combinations there won't be much difference and for others there might be substantial differences. In most cases I would trust the estimates from Stan over those from lme4 when there are important differences (and not only for the estimates of the parameters themselves but also for prediction). Assuming of course that there were no red flags when running the MCMC.
> >
> > If you do want to reproduce the lme4 standard deviation this should come closer
> >
> > stan_glmer(
> >   DV1 ~ VarF1 + VarF2 + VarF3 + VarF4 + VarF5 +
> >     VarF6 + VarF7 + VarF8 + VarF9 + VarT1 +
> >     VarT2 + VarT3 + (1 | Level1),
> >   data = mydata,
> >   QR = TRUE,
> >   prior = normal(0,1),
> >   prior_covariance = decov(scale = 0.25),
> >   prior_intercept = priorI,
> >   adapt_delta = 0.99,
> >   cores = 2
> > )
> >
> > although I'm not sure whether or not it's the right thing to do in this particular case. Often with only a few group levels it's good to be skeptical of the lme4 estimate of the standard deviation of the "random effects". The uncertainty estimates are probably too small.
> >
> > Hope that helps,
> >
> > Jonah
> >
> > P.S. See this recent thread <https://groups.google.com/forum/#!category-topic/stan-users/rstanarm/j0FQReuORi4> for more on why Ben's P.S. is true
> >
> > On Sunday, October 16, 2016 at 1:15:27 PM UTC-4, Ben Goodrich wrote:
> > > On Sunday, October 16, 2016 at 12:59:48 PM UTC-4, Paul Scutti wrote:
> > > > I am running a basic random intercept model both in lme4 and rstanarm. While I am getting identical results for the fixed effects, the same cannot be said for the random effects. The standard deviation for the residual is ok (0.74 for both), but for the intercept I get 0.31 in lme4 and more than double (0.63) in rstanarm. Any thoughts?
> > >
> > > Prior on the standard deviation, only having two groups with which to estimate that standard deviation, mode of likelihood vs. mean of posterior, the irrelevance of comparing point estimates, etc.
> > >
> > > Ben
> > >
> > > P.S. Setting regularization = 2 does not do anything when there is only one hyperparameter to estimate.
> > >

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Error terms - lme4 vs rstanarm
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Error terms - lme4 vs rstanarm
messages.body_plain:
Yes, more and more I've been convinced of the effectiveness of informative priors in these situations.
A

> On Oct 17, 2016, at 1:52 PM, Bruno Nicenboim <bruno.n...@gmail.com> wrote:
>

> Hi Paul,
>
> you might be interested in having a look at
> http://www.ling.uni-potsdam.de/~vasishth/pdfs/BatesEtAlParsimonious2015.pdf
> They show that "even under convergence, overparameterization may lead to uninterpretable models" in lme4.
>
> Bests,
> Bruno
>
> On Monday, October 17, 2016 at 5:45:38 PM UTC+2, Paul Scutti wrote:
> > Hi Jonah and Ben,
> >
> > Thank you for taking the time to clarify some important points: it was really helpful. I re-ran the model with prior_covariance = decov(scale = 0.25) and the the standard deviation of the random intercept is now in line with what I was expecting.
> >
> > In my random intercept model that regularisation=2 was a left-over of a previous model with random slopes, and I was not expecting it to play any role in the new one. So Jonah thank you for pointing out that prior_covariance can indeed be applied to a 1x1 covariance matrix scenario.
> >
> >
> > Best regards,
> > Paul
> >
> >
> >
> > On Sunday, October 16, 2016 at 11:10:32 PM UTC+1, Jonah Gabry wrote:
> > > Hi Paul,
> > >
> > > The estimates from rstanarm are not intended to always mirror those from lme4. lme4 is doing a type of maximum likelihood estimation giving you point estimates at the mode of the likelihood. rstanarm is doing full Bayesian inference, which means we're estimating the full joint posterior distribution of all parameters, which is a compromise between the likelihood and the prior, and then if we summarize the posterior we typically look at expectations, which can give you something quite different than the mode of the likelihood. So even before estimating anything we shouldn't necessarily expect to the get the same answers, especially if those answers are point estimates. For some model+data combinations there won't be much difference and for others there might be substantial differences. In most cases I would trust the estimates from Stan over those from lme4 when there are important differences (and not only for the estimates of the parameters themselves but also for prediction). Assuming of course that there were no red flags when running the MCMC.
> > >
> > > If you do want to reproduce the lme4 standard deviation this should come closer
> > >
> > > stan_glmer(
> > >   DV1 ~ VarF1 + VarF2 + VarF3 + VarF4 + VarF5 +
> > >     VarF6 + VarF7 + VarF8 + VarF9 + VarT1 +
> > >     VarT2 + VarT3 + (1 | Level1),
> > >   data = mydata,
> > >   QR = TRUE,
> > >   prior = normal(0,1),
> > >   prior_covariance = decov(scale = 0.25),
> > >   prior_intercept = priorI,
> > >   adapt_delta = 0.99,
> > >   cores = 2
> > > )
> > >
> > > although I'm not sure whether or not it's the right thing to do in this particular case. Often with only a few group levels it's good to be skeptical of the lme4 estimate of the standard deviation of the "random effects". The uncertainty estimates are probably too small.
> > >
> > > Hope that helps,
> > >
> > > Jonah
> > >
> > > P.S. See this recent thread <https://groups.google.com/forum/#!category-topic/stan-users/rstanarm/j0FQReuORi4> for more on why Ben's P.S. is true
> > >
> > > On Sunday, October 16, 2016 at 1:15:27 PM UTC-4, Ben Goodrich wrote:
> > > > On Sunday, October 16, 2016 at 12:59:48 PM UTC-4, Paul Scutti wrote:
> > > > > I am running a basic random intercept model both in lme4 and rstanarm. While I am getting identical results for the fixed effects, the same cannot be said for the random effects. The standard deviation for the residual is ok (0.74 for both), but for the intercept I get 0.31 in lme4 and more than double (0.63) in rstanarm. Any thoughts?
> > > >
> > > > Prior on the standard deviation, only having two groups with which to estimate that standard deviation, mode of likelihood vs. mean of posterior, the irrelevance of comparing point estimates, etc.
> > > >
> > > > Ben
> > > >
> > > > P.S. Setting regularization = 2 does not do anything when there is only one hyperparameter to estimate.
> > > >
>

> On Monday, October 17, 2016 at 12:33:26 PM UTC-4, Matt Espe wrote:
> > 100% memory usage is definitely no good.
> >
> > If you move those parts to the model section, they will not be saved in the output. However, everything in the transformed parameters is determined by your parameters and data, so you could extract the parameters at the end of the model run, and then in R calculate each of the transformed parameters. It is definitely a bit of work, and just saving what the model calculates is certainly the easiest path. But it is a good trick to avoid saving intermediate variables you are not concerned about, or if you are trying to reduce the size of the output.
> >
> > As for using Cmdstan, the cmdstan guide has a great getting started section which should get you most of the way there. The only slightly tricky thing is preparing the data. For this, I get the data prepared in R similar to using Rstan, and then use the Rstan function stan_rdump() to save all the data to a file that cmdstan can read. After the run, you will have a .csv which can be read into R using the RStan function read_stan_csv(). From there everything is pretty much the same as working with the output of RStan.
> >
> > I always start running a model in Stan with 200 warmup, 200 samples per chain, and then increase if it appears I need better warmup or more N_eff. In my experience, with 4 chains and a straightforward, well identified model this typically is more than enough.
> >
> > Matt

> > > Hi Matt

If I move them to the section you mentioned, will I still be able to extract these parameters at the end of the run? Alternatively I do not need to save the sigma estimates, how can I move them to the model portion and prevent them from being saved.
> > > I will definitely rerun reducing from 20,000 to may be 2000 and observe what happens. My current laptop has 8GB RAM, but my memory usage is at 100% when I run this model and I'm sure the reason why it is crashing.
> > > I have not used CmdStan before. How do I specify the code that I'm currently doing with a R code file. For RStan, I have an estimation.R and an estimation.stan file. Will I still use both of them in Cmdstan.
> > >
> > > Thank you for your help.
> > >
> > > Krishna
> > >
> > > On Sunday, October 16, 2016 at 11:16:18 PM UTC-4, Matt Espe wrote:
> > > > Hi,
> > > >
> > > > First, RStan can use quite a bit of memory, especially when you are running a complex model. Have you monitored your computer's memory use when you start the model?
> > > >
> > > > Assuming the issue is RAM usage, one solution is to avoid saving parameters you don't care about or can re-construct. I am guessing this bit is causing RStan to save a lot of parameters like that.
> > > >
> > > > transformed parameters {
> > > >   matrix[I,K] beta;                               // utility parameters (individual level)
> > > >   cholesky_factor_cov[K] L;                       // cholesky factors
> > > >   vector[J] v[N];                                 // utility vector for each choice set
> > > >   vector<lower=0>[K] tau;                         // scale
> > > >
> > > >   for (k in 1:K) tau[k] = 2.5 * tan(tau_unif[k]);
> > > >
> > > >   L = diag_pre_multiply(tau, L_Omega);
> > > >
> > > >   beta = d * mu + (L * alpha)';                   // individual level parameters
> > > >
> > > >   for (n in 1:N) {
> > > >     v[n] = x[n] * beta[id[n]]';
> > > >   }
> > > > }
> > > >
> > > >
> > > >
> > > > Moving this to the "model" section will result in them not being saved in the output, and should reduce the memory usage of the model.
> > > >
> > > > Second, is there a reason you are running 20,000 iterations? While this can be the default in JAGS, it is probably overkill for Stan by an order of magnitude. Saving that many samples might also cause issues with memory usage.
> > > >
> > > > Lastly, if you really need to record thousands or tens of thousands of variables but are not running on a machine with a lot of RAM, you might explore cmdstan, as it saves the results to disk rather than in memory. For me, running a fairly complex model with 30,000 observations in cmdstan will rarely use more than 0.5 GB RAM per chain.
> > > >
> > > > Hope that helps,
> > > >
> > > > Matt
> > > >
> > > >
> > > >

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Specify a prior when using LKJ
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Specify a prior when using LKJ
messages.body_plain:
Why do we prefer LKJ?

It's only a prior on the correlation matrix --- you need
a seperate prior on the scales.

We like LKJ because it has a natural interpretation of
controlling how much we expect the result to look like an
identity matrix.

The inverse Wishart has the nice property of looking like
prior data (it's conjugate for covariance matrices, so
it has to look like previously observed data).

For more info, see:

http://andrewgelman.com/2012/08/30/visualizing-distributions-of-covariance-matrices/

- Bob

>
> L_Omega ~ lkj_corr_cholesky(4);
>
> Eg. I know the parameter is in the range of mean + sd.
> With "new" data this doesn't changes "much".
>
> With the inverse wishart distribution I could specify a prior.
> With the preferred lkj not.
>
> I changed the model for every "non-fixed" parameter p_ij of the
> correlation L_Omega to:
>
> p_ij_raw ~ normal(mu_ij, sigma_ij);
> p_ij = tanh(p_ij_raw);
>
> Why is the preferred "gold-standard" of this case?

messages.body_plain:
The parens cause problems for me clicking through, but the
page is there:

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rectifier_(neural_networks)

The rectifier is

  f(x) = max(0, x)

which looks an awful lot like "hinge loss" from SVMs;  the
"soft" version the Wikipedia suggests is:

  f(x) = log(1 + exp(x))

Stan has a builtin for this:

  log1p_exp(x) = log(1 + exp(x)).

And the derivative is also built-in:

  log1p_exp'(x) = 1/(1 + exp(x)) * exp(x) = inv_logit(x)

So the log Jacobian is also a built-in:

  log_inv_logit(x)

I think I did that right.

- Bob

> On Oct 18, 2016, at 6:25 PM, Dustin Tran <dustinv...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> as bob notes, the error output is a result of the parameterization. ADVI uses stochastic gradients to optimize its objective and will drop samples that produce infinite values; such infinite values can occur when taking the exp of very large values. usually this is not a problem.
>
> one suggestion is to set the argument which increases the maximum number of dropped gradients.
>
> another suggestion is to use the softplus transformation (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rectifier_(neural_networks)). i’ve found this to be more stable than exp transformations in practice. (to manually define the transformation, you need to perform the transformation in the transformed parameters block, and then manually add the log det to your model block.)
>
> dustin

Yup, it is the hinge loss used in SVMs.

In general I like softplus because its gradient doesn’t increase as quickly as exp. More details and discussion of transformations are also here: https://groups.google.com/forum/#!topic/stan-dev/6iP0DzW5Yec

> Le mardi 18 octobre 2016 07:47:27 UTC+2, krishna mohan a écrit :
> > Thanks Ben. I have already examined the warnings documentation (which as a beginner user of RStan I do not find it to be useful - it is too brief in my naive opinion). I stopped panicking and began looking at my stan file.(see below). The message said that if L is covariance matrix then it should not be a big concern. As you can see below, L represents the cholesky factor covariance matrix. I also checked the output.csv file and I verified the coefficients generated.
> >
> > My apologies for not doing the due diligence on my part with patience.
> >
> > Krishna
> >
> > data {
> >   int<lower=1> N;                                 // number of choice sets
> >   int<lower=1> K;                                 // number of parameters (utility)
> >   int<lower=1> D;                                 // number of parameters (beta)
> >   int<lower=2> J;                                 // number of alternatives
> >   int<lower=1> I;                                 // number of respondents
> >   int<lower=1,upper=J> y[N];                      // alternative selected
> >   int<lower=1,upper=I> id[N];                     // respondent index
> >   matrix[J,K] x[N];                               // array of design matrices
> >   matrix[I,D] d;                                  // matrix of demographics
> > }
> >
> > parameters {
> >   matrix[D, K] mu;                                // means for beta
> >   matrix[K, I] alpha;                             // std normal draws
> >   cholesky_factor_corr[K] L_Omega;                // cholesky factors
> >   vector<lower=0,upper=pi()/2>[K] tau_unif;
> > }
> >
> > transformed parameters {
> >   matrix[I,K] beta;                               // utility parameters (individual level)
> >   cholesky_factor_cov[K] L;                       // cholesky factors
> >   vector[J] v[N];                                 // utility vector for each choice set
> >   vector<lower=0>[K] tau;                         // scale
> >
> >   for (k in 1:K) tau[k] = 2.5 * tan(tau_unif[k]);
> >
> >   L = diag_pre_multiply(tau, L_Omega);
> >
> >   beta = d * mu + (L * alpha)';                   // individual level parameters
> >
> >   for (n in 1:N) {
> >     v[n] = x[n] * beta[id[n]]';
> >   }
> > }
> >
> > model {
> >   to_vector(alpha) ~ normal(0, 1);

> >   to_vector(mu) ~ normal(0, 10);                  // prior for mean parameters
> >
> >   for (n in 1:N) {
> >     y[n] ~ categorical_logit(v[n]);
> >   }
> > }
> >
> > generated quantities {
> >   cov_matrix[K] Sigma;                            // cov matrix
> >   real<upper=0> log_lik;                          // log_lik for each sample
> >
> >   Sigma = tcrossprod(L);
> >
> >   log_lik = 0;

data {
  int N; // number of bins
  vector[N] x; // bin midpoints
  vector[N] dx; // bin widths
  int counts[N]; // binned Poisson counts
}

transformed data {
  matrix[N,N] sq_dist; // matrix of pairwise squared distances

  for (j in 1:N) {
    for (k in 1:N) {
      sq_dist[j,k] = (x[k] - x[j]) ^ 2;

  real<lower=0> lengthscale;
  real beta;           // linear slope
  real<lower=0> sigma; // log standard deviation
  real mu;             // GP mean (here a constant function)
  vector[N] latents;   // latent GP values
}

model {
  matrix[N, N] Cov; // covariance matrix for the GP
  // squared exponential covariance plus linear covariance, with fudge factor 0.001 added to diagonal
  Cov = sigma^2 * exp(- sq_dist / lengthscale^2) + beta^2 * x * (x') + diag_matrix(rep_vector(0.001, N));

  lengthscale ~ lognormal(0, 5);
  sigma ~ lognormal(0, 5);
}

generated quantities {
  vector[N] rates;

  rates = exp(latents + mu) .* dx;
}
"""

messages.body_plain:
Hi Daniel,

kind of - using new priors means now that model 1 has better log likelihoods for the fitted participants, but in terms of log likelihoods for the left out participant, model 4 is still better. Now of course that could mean that model 4 is the better model; but I would be surprised because if I fit each participant individually the BIC massively favours model 1 (and some other analyses do as well). I've attached a screenshot of how the model fits looks; the column of numbers are the log likelihoods for the 26 participants I used to fit the model (StanAll.n26loglik) and the number at the bottom is the leave-one out log likelihood for the remaining participant (StanAll.loologlik)

I've attached the scripts. I'm sorry the model is quite long. It's a basic reinforcement learner where people learn about reward magnitudes and probabilities and effort magnitudes. The two models just differ in how they compute the value of the two options that the participants compare and choose between:
it's either
util <- relRe*lrnW*rmp[t,o]+ (1-lrnW)*prob[is,t,o] - (1-relRE)*lrnW*emp[t,o]    {M1}
which means:
utility of an option is the weighted some of reward magnitude (rmp), probability (prob) and effort magnitude (emp).

and in model 4 it is:
util <- (1-effW)*rmp[t,o]*prob[is,t,o]/100 - effW*emp[t,o]    {M4}
so here reward magnitude and probability are multiplied together.

I'm not sure whether the error could be anything to do with how I draw parameters in the generated quantities block?
I use the normal_rng and then transform the parameters as in the model.

I would be very grateful for advice on this
Jacquie

On Mon, Oct 17, 2016 at 5:54 AM, Daniel Lee <bea...@alum.mit.edu> wrote:

> Hi Jacquie,
>
> Did the prior solve the problem? If not and you're still having trouble debugging, please post your updated code.
>
>
> Daniel
>
>
> On Thursday, October 13, 2016 at 12:43:41 PM UTC-4, jacquie...@gmail.com wrote:
> > so yes, turns out that if I put a hierarchical prior on a parameterisation of the parameter that is normally distributed (based on having fitted individual participants separately), the log likelihoods look much more like what I would have expected.
> >
> > On Thursday, October 13, 2016 at 2:53:39 PM UTC+1, jacquie...@gmail.com wrote:
> > >
> > > Dear all,
> > >
> > > I  have a problem understanding discrepancies between different model comparison results for a hierarchical vs. non-hierarchical instantiation of the same model and I can't think of what could have caused the problem.
> > >
> > > I've got two models (for a reinforcement learning task in humans) that, when I fit my 30 participants individually, e.g. using matlab's fminsearch, I find that model A is vastly better than B (BIC difference is ~200, for the BIC summed across all participants). When I fit people individually in Stan, I see similarly that the log likelihood for each person massively favours model A.
> > >
> > > But, when I use a hierarchical model in Stan, model B is strongly favoured. This is both the case when I do a leave-one participant-out cross validation (i.e. getting the log likelihood for the left out participant, by drawing his parameters randomly using the group priors in the generated quantities block) or when I fit all participants together hierarchically and just look at their log likelihoods.
> > >
> > > As an aside, when I compare parameters for people either generated by a hierarchical or an independent model, they correlate strongly (r is ~0.8-0.9).
> > >
> > > I am not sure whether this model fit result is even possible or whether it means that I must have made a coding error somewhere??
> > >
> > > The only other thing that I have come up with so far is that maybe it's a problem with the parameters not being normally distributed on the group level? (though i am not sure whether this could even explain the model fit discrepancy). For many of the parameters I assume that they are normally distributed on one scale (e.g. from - to + infinity) and then I transform them to another scale (e.g. from 0 to 1). I've attached a figure that shows in the top row all the parameters from individual participants after i've adjusted them and the bottom row is the parameters before i've adjusted them. It looks like maybe there is a problem for 'lrnw' (which means 'how much you weight what you have learnt when you make a decision'). I'm sampling this as lrnw and then transform it so that lrnw_adj=1/(1+lrnw). And I'm assuming that lrnw is normally distributed, but this is clearly not true.
> > >

> > > Jacquie

messages.body_plain: I've dealt with some models where Stan / NUTS gets to roughly the right region within a few iterations, and others where it might take 500 or 1000 very low treedepth iterations, and then move on to treedepth 10 or 12. It's difficult to specify the right number of iterations for such problems. I realise there may be ways to parameterise the model to change this behaviour, but it would also be pleasant if one could pass an additional parameter delineating some sort of variable length init phase, that ended once x iterations have passed since observing the highest likelihood.

messages.body_plain:
On Wednesday, October 19, 2016 at 2:13:18 AM UTC-4, andre.p...@googlemail.com wrote:
> I made a test with the inverse_wishart. If I know a prior-covariance matrix in cov_prior,
> do I specify cov_prior*scale or cov_prior?

The second argument to inv_wishart should be S rather than S / (nu - k - 1). But the poor performance is one of the reasons we don't recommend using inv_wishart. If you were going to use it, I would probably use the transformed parameters block to take the inverse of a matrix that has a Wishart prior.

Ben

> http://www.ling.uni-potsdam.de/~vasishth/pdfs/BatesEtAlParsimonious2015.pdf
> They show that "even under convergence, overparameterization may lead to uninterpretable models" in lme4.
>
> Bests,
> Bruno
>
> On Monday, October 17, 2016 at 5:45:38 PM UTC+2, Paul Scutti wrote:
> > Hi Jonah and Ben,
> >
> > Thank you for taking the time to clarify some important points: it was really helpful. I re-ran the model with prior_covariance = decov(scale = 0.25) and the the standard deviation of the random intercept is now in line with what I was expecting.
> >
> > In my random intercept model that regularisation=2 was a left-over of a previous model with random slopes, and I was not expecting it to play any role in the new one. So Jonah thank you for pointing out that prior_covariance can indeed be applied to a 1x1 covariance matrix scenario.
> >
> >
> > Best regards,
> > Paul
> >
> >
> >
> > On Sunday, October 16, 2016 at 11:10:32 PM UTC+1, Jonah Gabry wrote:
> > > Hi Paul,
> > >
> > > The estimates from rstanarm are not intended to always mirror those from lme4. lme4 is doing a type of maximum likelihood estimation giving you point estimates at the mode of the likelihood. rstanarm is doing full Bayesian inference, which means we're estimating the full joint posterior distribution of all parameters, which is a compromise between the likelihood and the prior, and then if we summarize the posterior we typically look at expectations, which can give you something quite different than the mode of the likelihood. So even before estimating anything we shouldn't necessarily expect to the get the same answers, especially if those answers are point estimates. For some model+data combinations there won't be much difference and for others there might be substantial differences. In most cases I would trust the estimates from Stan over those from lme4 when there are important differences (and not only for the estimates of the parameters themselves but also for prediction). Assuming of course that there were no red flags when running the MCMC.
> > >
> > > If you do want to reproduce the lme4 standard deviation this should come closer
> > >
> > > stan_glmer(
> > >   DV1 ~ VarF1 + VarF2 + VarF3 + VarF4 + VarF5 +
> > >     VarF6 + VarF7 + VarF8 + VarF9 + VarT1 +
> > >     VarT2 + VarT3 + (1 | Level1),
> > >   data = mydata,
> > >   QR = TRUE,
> > >   prior = normal(0,1),
> > >   prior_covariance = decov(scale = 0.25),
> > >   prior_intercept = priorI,
> > >   adapt_delta = 0.99,
> > >   cores = 2
> > > )
> > >
> > > although I'm not sure whether or not it's the right thing to do in this particular case. Often with only a few group levels it's good to be skeptical of the lme4 estimate of the standard deviation of the "random effects". The uncertainty estimates are probably too small.
> > >
> > > Hope that helps,
> > >
> > > Jonah
> > >
> > > P.S. See this recent thread <https://groups.google.com/forum/#!category-topic/stan-users/rstanarm/j0FQReuORi4> for more on why Ben's P.S. is true
> > >
> > > On Sunday, October 16, 2016 at 1:15:27 PM UTC-4, Ben Goodrich wrote:
> > > > On Sunday, October 16, 2016 at 12:59:48 PM UTC-4, Paul Scutti wrote:
> > > > > I am running a basic random intercept model both in lme4 and rstanarm. While I am getting identical results for the fixed effects, the same cannot be said for the random effects. The standard deviation for the residual is ok (0.74 for both), but for the intercept I get 0.31 in lme4 and more than double (0.63) in rstanarm. Any thoughts?
> > > >
> > > > Prior on the standard deviation, only having two groups with which to estimate that standard deviation, mode of likelihood vs. mean of posterior, the irrelevance of comparing point estimates, etc.
> > > >
> > > > Ben
> > > >
> > > > P.S. Setting regularization = 2 does not do anything when there is only one hyperparameter to estimate.
> > > >

messages.body_plain:
After the refactor to the low-level commands, we'll have
much more flexibility in starting and stopping so will be
able to start exploring some more flexible adaptation
strategies.  What we'll want to do is something like split
R-hat to assess whether the adaptation paths
have "converged" (they're not Markov chains, so the usual
definitions don't quite apply).

Our adaptation is enough like sampling that this may work.

Just doing something in a single adaptation path
based on the log density (it's usually log likelihood + log prior)
is tricky because we're looking for the high mass volume of the
posterior for sampling, not the mode.

I really need to finish my case study on typical sets and
the curse of dimensionality so we have some clear examples
to illustrate why the mode is often atypical.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Initialisation suggestion
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Initialisation suggestion
messages.body_plain:
We're happy to have people experiment with alternative
initialization schemes.  We need to estimate a step size
and mass matrix (diagonal by default).  The mass matrix
is basically an inverse covariance --- in the diagonal case,
it determines step sizes in each parameter dimension.

It'd be great if we could get to the typical set more quickly.
The challenge is the usual chicken-and-egg problem:  in order
to move efficiently, we need the mass matrix and step size
and in order to get the mass matrix and step size, we need to
be able to move efficiently.  The problem is exacerbating
by models with varying posterior curvature, as the optimal
mass matrix and step size will vary by region, so we really need
something conservative enough to work globally in the typical
set of the posterior.

What we do now is alternate running the sampler for increments
of exponentially increasing size, estimate the covariance
from the last increment, then find a step size that meets
the acceptance rate criterion (not simple Metropolis for NUTS),
then keep going.  We want to keep adapting until the covariance
and step sizes reach equilibrium.

We could try something like finding a posterior mode, but the
problem with that is most of the multilevel models we use don't have
posterior modes---the density is unbounded as you head to
zero multilevel variance.  So it's not clear where to stop.

- Bob

> On Oct 19, 2016, at 11:37 AM, Charles Driver <cdriv...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> Ok sounds good. I understand your point that it's difficult to determine convergence given a single path and log density - my suggestion was not to determine convergence, more to amend this as a first variable length initialization stage, and to move on to 'regular initialisation / warmup' after a few iterations where the log density is no longer increasing. But I'm happy if you have bigger and better plans for this sort of problem. In the meantime for the times when this is a problem I've decided to optimize, with hyper variances fixed at a medium to high values, to determine start values... something that will probably induce head shaking from a few but is working well in these cases.

>
> On Wednesday, October 19, 2016 at 5:26:40 PM UTC+2, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> After the refactor to the low-level commands, we'll have
> much more flexibility in starting and stopping so will be
> able to start exploring some more flexible adaptation
> strategies.  What we'll want to do is something like split
> R-hat to assess whether the adaptation paths
> have "converged" (they're not Markov chains, so the usual
> definitions don't quite apply).
>
> Our adaptation is enough like sampling that this may work.
>
> Just doing something in a single adaptation path
> based on the log density (it's usually log likelihood + log prior)
> is tricky because we're looking for the high mass volume of the
> posterior for sampling, not the mode.
>
> I really need to finish my case study on typical sets and
> the curse of dimensionality so we have some clear examples
> to illustrate why the mode is often atypical.
>
> - Bob
>
> > On Oct 19, 2016, at 6:53 AM, Charles Driver <cdriv...@gmail.com> wrote:
> >
> > I've dealt with some models where Stan / NUTS gets to roughly the right region within a few iterations, and others where it might take 500 or 1000 very low treedepth iterations, and then move on to treedepth 10 or 12. It's difficult to specify the right number of iterations for such problems. I realise there may be ways to parameterise the model to change this behaviour, but it would also be pleasant if one could pass an additional parameter delineating some sort of variable length init phase, that ended once x iterations have passed since observing the highest likelihood.

messages.body_plain:
> On Oct 17, 2016, at 10:13 AM, krishna mohan <krish4...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> Hi Daniel
>
> Thanks for getting back with these details. Here are answers to your questions:
>
> 1. The 20,000 draws is to establish an apples to apples comparison and benchmark against Sawtooth CBC/HB and R packages ChoiceModelR and mlogit.

If you're measuring efficiency, then you want to measure
n_eff / second.

If you're measuring accuracy, you need to compare using MCMC std
error.

I'd strongly recommend using our posterior analysis tools as
they are more robust than a lot of the other ones out there and
more conservative in their n_eff calculations, especially for
chains with long-range correlations and for multiple chains that
haven't quite converged to the same stationary distribution.

> Both Sawtooth and ChoiceModelR allow conjugate priors so from an every day tool to use I found that ChoiceModelR does extremely well relative to Sawtooth. I'm also quite happy with mlogit. I'm testing RSGHB and RStan so that I have more tools to tackle extremely complex designs I run into with clients, "who want what they want". I'm working on a study now where there are 16 attributes ranging from 3 levels to 6 levels. It is insanity.
>
> 2. My interest is absolutely in individual level betas as you stated, to set up forecasts and predictions of future market shares. Hence my request to extract individual level betas.
>
> 3. I'm running the simulations now with total of 2000 runs, split equally between warmup and sampling. I'm also trying to get a dedicated, beefed up machine with 32GB of RAM so I can use it just for these type of simulations.

Be careful in comparisons here.  Stan usually converges much
faster than 1000 iterations---our default is very conservative.

So there's really two things to measure:

1) how fast does the system adapt and converge (warmup, burnin, whatever)

2) what is the mixing rate after adaptation.

> 4. Is there a way to specify to Stan that I need only individual level betas and associated variance and not all the output Stan would generate by default. Another forum member mentioned that saving all of these parameters is probably stretching the limits of my machine and RStan.

Yes, you can choose the parameters to save in RStan.

> 5. I will keep you posted how these turn out.

OK.  And please include the evaluation methodology.

Of course, in the end what really matters is what lets you
get your work done the fastest.  Much of the real time is
spent in developing and debugging models and critiquing and
comparing their outputs, not in actually running them.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] cov_exp_quad performance test
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] cov_exp_quad performance test
messages.body_plain:
real eta_sq_plus_noise ;
        eta_sq_plus_noise = (eta^2) + noise ;

        rho = 1/inv_rho ;

        covMat = cov_exp_quad(x,eta,rho) ;

        ...
        for(n in 1:N){
        	covMat[n,n] = eta_sq_plus_noise ;
        }

I think you can replace all of the above (and remove
the declaration of rho) with:

  covMat = cov_exp_quad(x, eta, inv(inv_rho));
  for (n in 1:N)
    covMat[n, n] = covMat[n, n] + noise;

I take it cov_exp_quad doesn't have a way to add jitter, which
seems like a drawback given that the noise term here is just
a scalar so there are shared derivative calcs.

- Bob

messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Marginalized latent discrete chgpt for piecewise models - cause for concern?
messages.body_plain:
Once you've defined the model, the posterior is whatever
you've defined.  Stan helps you diagnose if you've accurately
reconstructed the posterior with R-hat and n_eff calculations.

You can try to debug your model code (in case you defined the
wrong posterior) by simulating data from your model and then
fitting it to ensure the model's well calibrated and recovering
the true parameters in the proper posterior intervals.

- Bob

However, the parameters for all other potential values of the changepoint are not well estimated, and have posterior distributions that essentially match the prior distributions. This raises some doubts for me as to whether the posterior probability of each value of the changepoint is well represented by the model runs. Should I be worried about using these results? Might there be a better way of specifying this model to accurately explore the posterior distribution?

If the posterior distribution looks essentially like your prior distribution, why is that a bad thing? When you say "essentially," what do you mean?

>
>

messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Where is source code of HMC?
messages.body_plain:
Source and doc for everything in Stan is linked from
our home page:  http://mc-stan.org

You can use Stan through its interfaces to change the
target Metropolis accept rate of static HMC.  But given

messages.subject: RStan suggestion: don't look in global environment for data variables
messages.subject_clean: RStan suggestion: don't look in global environment for data variables
messages.body_plain:
Currently, when using rstan, you can either package the data variables in a list that is then supplied as the value of the "data" argument to rstan::sampling(), OR you can define your data variables in the global environment and rely on rstan::sampling() to find them there. While the latter behaviour makes for fewer keystrokes, I encountered a scenario while teaching today that I believe strongly argues against it.

I had students run the same model twice, once with the data in its raw format, once after rescaling the data (using scale() in R) . The .stan file expected a data variable called Y for the outcome data, and the first time students packaged the data, in its raw format, they indeed named an element in the list "Y". But the second time around, having created a rescaled version of Y they called Y_rescaled, and erroneously created a list that had an element named "Y_rescaled" instead of the expected "Y". However, since an object called Y still existed in the global environment, when stan::sampling couldn't find an entry in the list called "Y", it went and found the object called "Y" still in the global environment, yielding no warning or error and subsequent samples for which the priors were dramatically ill posed (since the priors were specified expecting scaled data).

The only reason we caught this error is because some students didn't make the error and some did, yielding different results for different students despite everyone using the same seed. Had they been home working alone, I think it unlikely that they would have caught it.

Admittedly, you can never prevent all user errors, but since seeking variables in the global environment is a convenience feature that frankly defies expected behaviour from well-contained programming systems, I wonder if it might be considered for removal.

Cheers,

Mike

--
Mike Lawrence
Graduate Student
Department of Psychology & Neuroscience
Dalhousie University

~ Certainty is (possibly) folly ~

>> Currently, when using rstan, you can either package the data variables in a list that is then supplied as the value of the "data" argument to rstan::sampling(), OR you can define your data variables in the global environment and rely on rstan::sampling() to find them there. While the latter behaviour makes for fewer keystrokes, I encountered a scenario while teaching today that I believe strongly argues against it.
>>
>> I had students run the same model twice, once with the data in its raw format, once after rescaling the data (using scale() in R) . The .stan file expected a data variable called Y for the outcome data, and the first time students packaged the data, in its raw format, they indeed named an element in the list "Y". But the second time around, having created a rescaled version of Y they called Y_rescaled, and erroneously created a list that had an element named "Y_rescaled" instead of the expected "Y". However, since an object called Y still existed in the global environment, when stan::sampling couldn't find an entry in the list called "Y", it went and found the object called "Y" still in the global environment, yielding no warning or error and subsequent samples for which the priors were dramatically ill posed (since the priors were specified expecting scaled data).
>>
>> The only reason we caught this error is because some students didn't make the error and some did, yielding different results for different students despite everyone using the same seed. Had they been home working alone, I think it unlikely that they would have caught it.
>>
>> Admittedly, you can never prevent all user errors, but since seeking variables in the global environment is a convenience feature that frankly defies expected behaviour from well-contained programming systems, I wonder if it might be considered for removal.
>>
>> Cheers,
>>
>> Mike
