On Wednesday, October 19, 2016 at 4:32:05 PM UTC-4, Andrew Gelman wrote:
> What I would like is for the stan() call in R to take variables from the local environment.  Thus, if you're operating in the R console entering commands one at a time, it would use the global environment; if you're calling stan() from within a function, it will take variables from the local environment; etc.  It should also be possible to input the data as a list.

It already does all that. The problem is that the global environment is an ancestor of all environments (except package namespaces). So, even if you first look in the local environment, that only works if the thing is in the local environment. Otherwise, it will continue looking in the next environment up until it finds a R object with the same name. Also, it wouldn't make any difference in the OP's case because stan() was being typed in the global environment.

Ben

messages.subject_clean: Beta Regression: problems with initial values (?) causes chain to fail in creating replicated values
messages.body_plain:
I'm attempting to implement beta regression in Stan and am using the package betareg as gut check. I am using the parameterization in terms of mean and precision and my goal is to be able to regress on both the mean and precision parameters. In betareg package for example, this is implemented with the formula convention (y ~ x1 + x2 ... | z1 + z2 ...) where the x's are covariates for mean term using a logit link and z's are the covariates for the precision term using a log link.

I have coded this up in Stan along with a minimal code to simulate and fit data in both betareg and Stan: https://github.com/daltonhance/stan_beta_reg

The problem I am encountering started occurring when I tried to implement a posterior predictive check in the generated quantities block by creating replicated data. It appears that initial values for the regression coefficients are frequently causing an issue with the beta_rng() call resulting in NaN values for the y_rep. If I run multiple chains, for about half the chains I get the following error:
[37] "Error in eval(substitute(expr), envir, enclos) : "
[38] "  Exception thrown at line 50: beta_log: Random variable is nan, but must not be nan!"
[1] "error occurred during calling the sampler; sampling not done"

This causes that chain to fail and not return any samples. For chains that are able to run, I can confirm that they are quickly settling on appropriate values in that they match the betareg output and the simulated values. For example, to create README.md on stackoverflow it took a few tries, but I was able to successfully get MCMC draws when rstan hit upon good initial values.

I've tried playing around a bit with initialization functions but haven't hit on a solution as of yet. Any advice on minimizing this issue? Is this a bug with beta_rng?

Andrew's right.  It reads the global environment.

If I run this R code in RStan 2.12.1:

stan_program <- "data { real mu; } parameters { real y; } model { y ~ normal(mu, 1); }";
mu <- 5;
run_program <- function (x) { mu <- -5; stan(model_code=stan_program); }
mu <- 0;
fit <- run_program();
print(fit);

I see this:

      mean se_mean   sd  2.5%   25%   50%   75% 97.5% n_eff Rhat
y     0.00    0.02 1.03 -1.95 -0.72  0.00  0.68  1.99  3225    1

So the no-arg version is just reading mu out of the global environment, not out of
the function's.

On the other hand, if I do this:

run_program <- function (x) { mu <- -5; stan(model_code=stan_program, data=c("mu")); }

then I get

      mean se_mean   sd  2.5%   25%   50%   75% 97.5% n_eff Rhat
y    -5.01    0.02 1.02 -6.99 -5.69 -4.99 -4.33 -2.99  2958    1

So the one that reads by name uses the local environment.

I'd prefer the local environment behavior in both places.

- Bob

I don't know the betareg package or what it's doing.

Which line number is causing the problem?  It's a call
to either beta_lpdf(...) or ~ beta(...).  The error message
is terrible now because it refers to our deprecated name
for the underling density function, beta_log.

And the problem is the first argument to beta_lpdf or the
argument before the ~ to beta(...).

The explicit exp() operations or the one implicit in
inv_logit() can lead to overflow or underflow, which can lead
to NaN values on further operations.

You can test for is_nan(x) before computing in the generated
quantities block and just set the value to not_a_number() in
those cases.  If it's only an issue with inits and warmup, it's
not a problem.  This is just getting caused by our functions
throwing exceptions in generated quantities that would otherwise
cause a rejection of a draw, but there's no way to reject at
the point generated quantities are being calculated.  We don't
want the generated quantities to influence the model.  But it'd
be nice if in the generated quantities block we just propagated
NaN instead of throwing exceptions (but that's a lot of work).

- Bob

Hi all,

we presented some first results regarding the performance of Stan for discrete choice models („mixed logit“) at the eRum (European R user meeting) 2016 in Poznan (Poland) last week. Slides are available here: https://github.com/eRum2016/Presentations-participants/blob/master/13.10/Methodology%202/eRum_GG2016.pdf

Bottom line is that Stan outperforms bayesm and ChoiceModelR if the model is not super simple. These are only preliminary results, we’re about to write up everything in the next few weeks. For computing the effective sample size we used rstan:::ess_rfun (bayesm and ChoiceModelR results) or directly n_eff from summary(stanfit)$summary (RStanresults).

PS: The model on slide 7 was not the model used in the simulation study. We only included this slide to show how easy it is to set up a first version (MVP <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minimum_viable_product> style). For the simulations we used the model that we posted here on the mailing list.

Best,

Daniel

messages.subject: hyperprior horseshoe prior
messages.subject_clean: hyperprior horseshoe prior
messages.body_plain:
Dear developers,

Juho Piironen and Aki Vehtari recently published a very nice paper regarding the hyperprior for the global shrinkage parameter in the horseshoe prior (https://arxiv.org/pdf/1610.05559v1.pdf). They showed that the default choice for the global shrinkage parameter (half-cauchy with scale 1) is suboptimal. To my best knowledge, it is currently not possible to adjust the scale of this half-cauchy in the horseshoe prior using rstanarm. Are you planning to make this possible? Or can I do it myself? I think the only thing that needs to be adjusted (for glm's in rstanarm/inst/chunks/priors_glm.stan) is line 16:
target += normal_lpdf(global[1] | 0, 1);
to
target += normal_lpdf(global[1] | 0, scale_global);
in which scale global is a user defined real.

Thanks!

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Model comparison favours different models for hierarchical and non-hierarchical set-up?
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Model comparison favours different models for hierarchical and non-hierarchical set-up?
messages.body_plain:
I've found a possible solution: I've noticed that some parameters that are fitted are correlated. However, when I generate new parameters for the left out participant (in generated quantities block) they will not be correlated. I was wondering whether this might be an explanation why log likelihoods for the fitted participants are as expected (and parameters are recovered well by the model for simulated data) but log likelihoods for the left out participants are not as expected?

To address this, I've thought of two possibilities, I've tried one now, I've fitted my model on half the data from each participant (which in my case made sense because the data was collected in two independent sessions for each person). I use the parameter estimates from that to then compute the log likelihoods for the second half of the data set. This shows the pattern that I would predict.

The second solution which I have not tried yet (and I'm not sure whether it would be better) is a leave-one-out cross validation in several steps: 1) Fit models to data of n-1 participants to get estimates of mean and standard deviations for hyper parameters. 2) Use these to simulate say 1000 new participants (they will have uncorrelated parameters). 3) Fit the data of these 1000 new participants with the model. This will give me somewhat correlated parameter estimates. 4) Use these 1000 estimated parameter sets to compute the log likelihood for the left out participant [the main advantage now is that I will have realistic parameter sets with some correlations between parameters]. Repeat all steps, leaving out a different participant each time. I am not sure whether this method has any advantage over what I've done now? (I guess it would answer my question whether the problem was that I'm not capturing correlations between parameters?)

--> My main question is now whether in general a leave-one-out cross validation for hierarchical models (leaving out participants rather than trials within participants) is problematic when parameters are somewhat correlated?

Even though the log likelihoods for the participants that I'm using to fit the model (i.e. n-1 = 29) do consistently favour the model I used to create the data.
> >

messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Beta Regression: problems with initial values (?) causes chain to fail in creating replicated values
messages.body_plain:
Hey Bob,

betareg is an R package that implements MLE beta regression. I'm simply using it as a point of comparison.

The line number throwing the error is line 50. This is second call to beta_lpdf() which takes y_rep as an argument. This leads me to believe that beta_rng is returning NaN values for at least some elements of y_rep and that feeding these NaN to beta_lpdf is what causes the error.  I've confirmed this by commenting out log_lik_rep and it associated variables. Upon doing that I still get errors causing chains to fail, but those errors are of the from  "y_rep[70] is nan, but must be greater than or equal to 0; error occurred during calling the sampler; sampling not done".

I'm only using this step as part of a posterior predictive check of the model, using the total likelihood of observed and replicated data as an omnibus assessment of fit. So I could easily comment this out for drawing from the posterior once I'm satisfied the model is performing well.

But it sounds like what I should be doing is to check whether beta_rng is returning an nan and if so have it draw another random beta value for that element of the replicated data vector?

On Wednesday, October 19, 2016 at 4:54:24 PM UTC-7, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> I don't know the betareg package or what it's doing.
>
> Which line number is causing the problem?  It's a call
> to either beta_lpdf(...) or ~ beta(...).  The error message
> is terrible now because it refers to our deprecated name
> for the underling density function, beta_log.
>
> And the problem is the first argument to beta_lpdf or the
> argument before the ~ to beta(...).
>
> The explicit exp() operations or the one implicit in
> inv_logit() can lead to overflow or underflow, which can lead
> to NaN values on further operations.
>
> You can test for is_nan(x) before computing in the generated
> quantities block and just set the value to not_a_number() in
> those cases.  If it's only an issue with inits and warmup, it's
> not a problem.  This is just getting caused by our functions
> throwing exceptions in generated quantities that would otherwise
> cause a rejection of a draw, but there's no way to reject at
> the point generated quantities are being calculated.  We don't
> want the generated quantities to influence the model.  But it'd
> be nice if in the generated quantities block we just propagated
> NaN instead of throwing exceptions (but that's a lot of work).
>
> - Bob
>
>
> > On Oct 19, 2016, at 6:44 PM, Dalton Hance <dalton...@gmail.com> wrote:
> >
> > I'm attempting to implement beta regression in Stan and am using the package betareg as gut check. I am using the parameterization in terms of mean and precision and my goal is to be able to regress on both the mean and precision parameters. In betareg package for example, this is implemented with the formula convention (y ~ x1 + x2 ... | z1 + z2 ...) where the x's are covariates for mean term using a logit link and z's are the covariates for the precision term using a log link.
> >
> > I have coded this up in Stan along with a minimal code to simulate and fit data in both betareg and Stan: https://github.com/daltonhance/stan_beta_reg
> >
> > The problem I am encountering started occurring when I tried to implement a posterior predictive check in the generated quantities block by creating replicated data. It appears that initial values for the regression coefficients are frequently causing an issue with the beta_rng() call resulting in NaN values for the y_rep. If I run multiple chains, for about half the chains I get the following error:
> > [37] "Error in eval(substitute(expr), envir, enclos) : "
> > [38] "  Exception thrown at line 50: beta_log: Random variable is nan, but must not be nan!"
> > [1] "error occurred during calling the sampler; sampling not done"
> >
> > This causes that chain to fail and not return any samples. For chains that are able to run, I can confirm that they are quickly settling on appropriate values in that they match the betareg output and the simulated values. For example, to create README.md on stackoverflow it took a few tries, but I was able to successfully get MCMC draws when rstan hit upon good initial values.
> >
> > I've tried playing around a bit with initialization functions but haven't hit on a solution as of yet. Any advice on minimizing this issue? Is this a bug with beta_rng?

>

If so, then if the models are the same, Stan's optimize
should return the same (penalized) MLE.

> The line number throwing the error is line 50. This is second call to beta_lpdf() which takes y_rep as an argument. This leads me to believe that beta_rng is returning NaN values for at least some elements of y_rep and that feeding these NaN to beta_lpdf is what causes the error.

That's the only way that error should be able to arise on that line.
Our beta_rng shouldn't be returning NaN though.  If you could trap the
inputs that cause beta_rng to return NaN that'd be super helpful.  If
that's what's going on, it should be easy to fix, or at least trap on
our side with a warning message.

>   I've confirmed this by commenting out log_lik_rep and it associated variables. Upon doing that I still get errors causing chains to fail, but those errors are of the from  "y_rep[70] is nan, but must be greater than or equal to 0; error occurred during calling the sampler; sampling not done".

You can kill that problem by removing the constraint on y_rep.  It's
only there for error checking in generated quantities.

> I'm only using this step as part of a posterior predictive check of the model, using the total likelihood of observed and replicated data as an omnibus assessment of fit. So I could easily comment this out for drawing from the posterior once I'm satisfied the model is performing well.
>
> But it sounds like what I should be doing is to check whether beta_rng is returning an nan and if so have it draw another random beta value for that element of the replicated data vector?

You can just trap this in Stan this way:

  if (is_nan(y_rep[n]))
     print("A[n]=", A[n], "; B[n]=", B[n]);

to see what the parameters are causing the problem.

- Bob

returning 0 or 1 with proportion A/(A + B), though those don't

messages.body_plain:
I don't see how to do it linearly because of the mass
arising from not moving when z(t) = 0.

- Bob

> On Sep 26, 2016, at 3:24 PM, Michael Betancourt <betan...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> Won’t it be linear because the z(t) are independent?
>
> Also, the model we eventually used was constant
> as one theta was used to turn on or off all of the z(t).
> To get the linear version there would be one theta
> for each t.
>
> On Sep 26, 2016, at 6:54 PM, Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com> wrote:
>
>> Agree with Michael that you want to think generatively.  What
>> you really have is a discrete parameter:
>>
>> z(t) ~ bernoulli(theta);
>>
>> which will be 1 if x(t) != x(t-1) [equivalently r(t) != 0]
>> and 0 otherwise.
>>
>> Marginalizing out the z(t) is exponential in the number
>> of time steps because there are 2^T paths for t in 1:T.
>>
>> I don't see how you can fit the model in less than exponential
>> time in the number of time steps in Stan.
>>
>> - Bob
>>
>>
>>> On Sep 26, 2016, at 8:39 AM, James Savage <jav...@gmail.com> wrote:
>>>
>>> Hi all,
>>>
>>> Let's say I have a time series whose growth is either 0 or positive. Some values of the time series are
>>> missing and so I want to use a state-space representation.
>>>
>>> The state model is:
>>>
>>> x(t) = x(t-1) with probability theta
>>>
>>> x(t) = x(t-1) + r(t) with probability 1- theta
>>>
>>> and the "growth bump" r(t) is always non-negative
>>>
>>> r(t) ~ normal_{+}(0, sigma)
>>>
>>> Another way of putting it is that r(t) is 0 with probability theta, and takes the above distribution with probability
>>> 1- theta. There's then a measurement model:
>>>
>>> observation(t) ~ normal(x(t), sd_measurement_error)
>>>
>>> The question is how to implement the structure? At the moment, I'm hacking it, by simply stating that rather than
>>> being precisely 0 in the first case, r(t) is small.
>>>
>>> model {
>>>  // priors for theta and sigma
>>>
>>>   target += log_sum_exp(log(theta) + normal_lpdf(r[t] | 0, 0.01), // r[t] very small rather than precisely 0
>>>                                         log(1-theta) + normal_lpdf(r[t] | 0, sigma);
>>> }
>>>
>>> Is there a better way of doing this?
>>>
>>> Cheers,
>>> Jim
>>>

messages.subject_clean: rstanarm for survey data
messages.body_plain:
Hi Corey

Could you estimate the weights as parameters in addition to the model parameters using RStan or rstanarm? I also work with survey data a lot and the application of weights, I often do after developing the (predictive) models.

If you have weights, say by an age or an ethnicity variable, those weights could also be additionally estimated (makes the model hierarchical in some ways as your weights will differ by a grouping variable). You could set your prior to be between 0,1 and the sum of weights (/priors) to be equal to 1.

Let me know how it works out. I will see if I can set up example model with and without weights for starters.

Krishna

> On Oct 21, 2016, at 1:35 PM, Matt Espe <lck...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> Hi,
>
> This is a case of multiplicative non-identifability. As you have the model now, the product term does not have a solution, since you can multiply and divide either term by a constant and arrive at the same product. One solution is to put priors on your coefficients so they are constrained.  There is a section in the manual on this.
>

The problematic priors chapter discusses the additive case and
I think also the multiplicative case for IRT.  Something has
to define the scale.

The other problem is that with multiplicative non-identifiability
in the likelihood (even with a prior for weak identification),
you tend to get banana-shaped marginal posteriors in the non-identified
parameters which is very hard to sample because the covariance
varies around the banana.

> Matt
>

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Rstan gaussian mixture model 'Scale parameter is 0, but must be > 0'
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Rstan gaussian mixture model 'Scale parameter is 0, but must be > 0'
messages.body_plain:
sigma is occassionally hitting 0 due to underflow in the transforms.

There's a problem with mixture models in general that they don't have
maximum likelihoods.  If you put one mixture component be responsible
for one data item, as the scale (std dev param) goes to zero and the location
(mean param) goes to the data item's value, the likelihood grows.

One way to avoid this is to force the components to have more responsibility.
You can do this with a prior on the simplex.  Something like Dirichlet(alpha)
where alpha is a vector values >> 1 can help.  Also putting a prior on the
scales that explicitly avoids zero (like a lognormal) can help.

- Bob

messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Model comparison favours different models for hierarchical and non-hierarchical set-up?
messages.body_plain:
Parameters are correlated by design in a hierarchical model.
That's where the partial pooling comes from.

Also, see Wei and Andrew's paper on the topic:

http://www.stat.columbia.edu/~gelman/research/published/final_sub.pdf

I believe the loo package in R will do this for you.
Aki, Andrew, and Jonah have a new paper on this topic, too:

http://andrewgelman.com/2016/10/21/practical-loo/

-Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Bayesian Variable Selection models
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Bayesian Variable Selection models
messages.body_plain:
> On Oct 14, 2016, at 4:45 PM, Haziq Jamil <haziq...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
>
>
> On Friday, 14 October 2016 16:45:20 UTC+1, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> You can only fit a hard spike-and-slab variable selection model
> in Stan with small numbers of variables.
>
> It's also very hard to fit in JAGS or other Gibbs samplers.
> They will tend to get stuck in modes and not mix well on the
> Bernoulli variate indicating if a variable is selected or not.
> The true posterior is not going to be 100% on or off (that is,
> full Bayes won't do variable selection), and there are likely
> to be many modes.  You can see that analytically if you write out
> the posterior for the value of a coefficient.
>
>
> In a Gibbs sampling procedure of the original model above, the conditional density for the betas is Gaussian, and Bernoulli for the gammas. I'm not sure what you mean by multimodal?

The usual---the posterior will have local optima, based
on which of the variables is selected.

> Also, when you say the Bernoulli variates get stuck and not mix well, e.g. gamma_j keeps on being sampled as 1, 1, 1, 1, ... with some occasional zeroes, then surely the model is telling us that this variable is important, don't throw it out?

What happens is that it can do that because it gets stuck, not
because the Pr[z[n] = 1 | data] = 1 in the posterior.

> If you mean the betas don't mix well, then sure it's a problem. But the Gibbs conditionals seem to be nice distributions, I'm failing to see how it can be an issue.

:-)  Gibbs is scale invariant but not rotation invariant.
When you introduce correlations among your parameters (as
in the strong correlation between the variables being
selected), then it can fail.  There really is a huge literature
on this as I said before.  It's mainly about the kinds of
phase changes that happen among the modes.

> The posterior mean of the gamma_j samples are interpreted as the posterior inclusion probabilities for each variable X_j (Ntzoufras, 2011). So yes agreed that Bayes doesn't turn variables 100% on or off, but inference on variable or model selection is done based on probabilities, and one could choose the model with the highest posterior probability or median probability models (Barbieri and Berger, 2004).

Assuming you can put a prior on models that makes sense.
Usually it doesn't, and all this model comparison and model
weighting stuff is pretty useless.

And your choices of which variables are on or off are not
independent.  So you can't just look at the marginals.  You
get another combinatorial problem there.

> There's a vast MCMC literature on the problems posed by
> combinatorial models like variable selection, with Ising spin models
> making up the bulk of that because they have real physical
> analogues.

I would like to emphasize this point.  Seriously, check out
the Ising models as they have the exact same problems you're
going to run into.

> You will be able to diagnose this using multiple chains if
> you give them diffuse initializations.  I can't recall how
> JAGS initializes, but I think it may be deterministically by
> default.  Masanao and Yu-Sun and Andrew built dealing with multiple
> chains into R2jags, but I can't recall how inits work.

Ditto.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Ideas for Hierarchical Modeling With Partially Ordered Groups?
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Ideas for Hierarchical Modeling With Partially Ordered Groups?
messages.body_plain:
No problem posting this kind of thing and sorry
nobody answered.

I think "multilevel model" is what you want to search for.
There's a lot of discussion in the Gelman and Hill multilevel
regression book.

If you have an effect on an ordinal scale, you can
enforce monotonicity with an ordered parameter vector
in Stan or you can do it yourself by incrementing
a base value with a positive-constrained or negative-constrained
difference.  You can do priors either way, but as usual,
have to be careful about Jacobians when putting priors on
transformed parameters.

In multilevel regressions, you'd often get a whole slew of
parameters

  beta_vehicle[1:N]  categorical
  beta_abdomen[1:5]  ordinal
  beta_head[1:5]     ordinal
  beta_chest[1:5]    ordinal

and then start looking at interaction terms, which would be

beta_vehicle_abdomen[1:N, 1:5]

Unless you have a lot of data, the fine-grained parameters can
be hard to estimate.

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
Sorry nobody answered this back in July when you sent it out.
I'll try to answer some things inline.

Hopefully better late than never.

> On Jul 19, 2016, at 6:02 AM, liam....@gmail.com wrote:
>
> Hi all,
>
>
> I'm pretty new to Stan (and HMC/NUTS in general). My question is geared towards Stan, but it may be that the issue is more general than that.
>
>
>
> I'm trying to fit a model with a somewhat elaborate hierarchical form:
>
>
>
> y ~ bernoulli_logit( alpha+V*beta+Z*gamma )
>
>
>
> where Z is a kind of "latent" variable with Z ~ normal( W*tau, sigma1 )
>
>
>
> As with any typical regression, I have an N-dimensional response vector (y) and a matrix of predictor variables (X).
>
> I split the matrix of predictor variables (X) into two distinct and non-overlapping sub-matrices (V and W).
>
> V denotes a matrix with P columns and N rows.
>
> W denotes a matrix with Q columns and N rows. Along with a scale parameter sigma1, the Q columns of W are used to parametrise a "latent" variable (Z) which, when realised, is combined with the above V matrix to form a linear predictor for the response vector y.
>
>
>
> Hopefully, the following R code will be illustrative.
>
>
>
> ##########
>
>
>
> # SIMULATE FROM MODEL:
>
>
>
> # Predictors:
>
> X <- matrix( rnorm(6000), nrow=1000 ) # Predictor matrix.
>
> V <- X[,1:3] # Observed predictors.
>
> W <- X[,4:6] # Predictors of latent variable.
>
>
>
> # Initialise parameters:
>
> alpha <- 3 # Observed intercept.
>
> beta <- c(3,7,-6) # Observed slopes.
>
> tau <- c(2,3,-5) # Latent slopes.
>
> gamma <- 2 # Slope for latent variate.
>
> sigma1 <- 1.1 # Scale parameter for latent variable.
>
>
>
> # Simulate from Z:
>
> expected_Z <- W%*%tau # Mean for latent variable Z.
>
> Z <- rnorm(1000, expected_Z, sigma1) # Simulate Z from normal distribution with mean expected_Z and scale sigma1.
>
>
>
> # Simulate from y:
>
> lin_pred <- alpha + V%*%beta + gamma*Z # Linear predictor for y.
>
> pr <- 1/(1 + exp(-lin_pred)) # Map from (-inf, inf) to [0,1]; inverse logit.
>
> y <- rbinom(1000, 1, pr) # Simulate y from Bernoulli distribution with “success” parameter pr.
>
>
>
> ##########
>
>
>
> My attempt to fit this model using Stan doesn't appear to be very effective. Aside from posterior distributions which don't seem to characterise the initialized values above, n_eff is very low and Rhat is well above 1.
>
>
>
> The Stan code is:
>
>
>
> /* BEGIN STAN CODE: */
>
>
>
> data {
>
>
>
>   int<lower=0> N; // # observations.
>
>   int<lower=0> P; // # predictors in V matrix.
>
>   int<lower=0> Q; // # predictors in W matrix.
>
>
>
>   int<lower=0,upper=1> y[N]; // Response.
>
>   matrix[N,P] V; // Observed predictors.
>
>   matrix[N,Q] W; // Latent predictors.
>
>
>
> }
>
>
>
> parameters {
>
>
>
>   vector[Q] tau; // Latent slope(s).
>
>   real alpha; // Observed intercept.
>
>   vector[P] beta; // Observed slope(s).
>
>   real<lower=0> gamma; // Slope for latent variate.
>
>
>
>   real sigma1; // Scale parameter for latent variable.
>
>
>
>   vector[N] Z; // Latent variable.
>
>
>
> }
>
>
>
> model {
>
>
>
>   vector[N] expected_Z; // Declare mean for latent variable Z.
>
>   vector[N] lin_pred; // Declare linear predictor.
>
>   expected_Z <- W*tau; // Initialize mean for latent variable Z (combination of latent predictors).
>
>   Z ~ normal(expected_Z,sigma1); // Draw Z from distribution.
>
>   lin_pred <- alpha + V*beta + Z*gamma; // Initialize linear predictor for y.
>
>   y ~ bernoulli_logit(lin_pred); // Compute log probability.
>

You can just use these directly --- you don't need to
define local variables.  e.g.,

  Z ~ normal(W * tau, sigma1);

>
>
> }
>
>
>
> /* END STAN CODE: */
>
>
>
> A few things:
>
>
>
> - For the moment, I'm relying on the implicit built-in uniform priors in Stan for all model parameters; of course, placing informative priors on the parameters will alter the posterior distributions, but I want to see how the model performs in the absence of informative priors. The adapted continuous model (see below) performs very well with just the uniform priors on all parameters.

A flat prior is more informative than you may hope.  It's saying
almost all the values to be expected are extreme because there's
only finite mass inside any compact volume.

> - I've constrained the parameter gamma to non-negative values and I have neglected to include an intercept value in the expected_Z term in the interest of ensuring an identifiable model. Perhaps I haven't gone far enough in this direction? Is the model under-constrained?

Maybe.  You can look at pairs plots to see if there
are additively correlated (lines) or multiplicatively
correlated (bananas) paramters.

> - When I alter the structure of the predictor variables to contain dummy/binary variables (i.e. values in {0, 1}) and/or constrained values (e.g. values in [-1,1]), maximum tree depth issues begin to arise; is this a common issue for these kinds of variables?

No, but if you have uniform priors and run into things like
separability issues, it can be a problem.

> - When I change the structure of the model to have a continuous response (i.e. y ~ normal( alpha+V*beta+Z*gamma, sigma2 ), where sigma2 is a scale parameter for the response variable), the results become much better, so I'm guessing that the issue may lie with bernoulli_logit response.

Yes, that changes the response dramatically.  You no longer
get a separability problem where some parameters will try to
grow infinitely large.

>
> - Noting the above, according to this post, a transformation based on the normal distribution might be appropriate, but I'm not sure that these cases are like-for-like. Could anybody elaborate on this?

Not sure what kind of transformation you're talking about here.

> - In general, does anybody have any suggestions as to how I could improve the code to recover posterior distributions more representative of the values above?

I'd simulate data to see if the model's correct. It may just
be misspecified for the model.

Also, we highly recommend at least weakly informative priors.

> This post seems to have expanded beyond the compact form that I had originally intended for it. Sorry about that.

Longer posts tend not to get answered because it's too hard
to figure out the models and all the questions.  Sorry this one
took me so long.

- Bob

How should I be thinking about this?

Thanks,

messages.body_plain:
You can't do this in any direct way, as Stan does not have particle filters.  The most direct approach would be to include your old data and prior (which you used to construct your posterior) and your new data into a single model and perform Stan on all of it at once.  If you really want to first do inference and then take those simulations as a prior, I suppose you could approximate those simulations in some parametric form such as multivariate normal or mixture of multivariate normals, then use this parametric approx as your prior.
A

P.S.  In our usual notation, y would be data, not a parameter!  We usually label data as x,y, etc., and label parameters as alpha, beta, etc and a, b, etc.

messages.subject_clean: rstanarm for survey data
messages.body_plain:
Just to reiterate some of the points made a while ago in this thread, we recommend the fully Bayesian approach. This would be a multilevel model without weights estimated by MCMC, and then you can use the model to study the population of interest via the posterior predictive distribution, i.e. predicting the outcome in the relevant post-stratification cells. With that you can then calculate whatever summaries you want, and you don't need survey weights at any step in the process.

For standard multilevel (G)LMs this can easily be done in rstanarm with stan_(g)lmer() and posterior_predict(). Of course you can also write out the model and predictions in the Stan language yourself if you want.

Hope that helps,

Jonah

>

I use the parameter estimates from that to then compute the log likelihoods for the second half of the data set. This shows the pattern that I would predict.
>
>

This will give me somewhat correlated parameter estimates. 4) Use these 1000 estimated parameter sets to compute the log likelihood for the left out participant [the main advantage now is that I will have realistic parameter sets with some correlations between parameters]. Repeat all steps, leaving out a different participant each time. I am not sure whether this method has any advantage over what I've done now? (I guess it would answer my question whether the problem was that I'm not capturing correlations between parameters?)
>
>
> --> My main question is now whether in general a leave-one-out cross validation for hierarchical models (leaving out participants rather than trials within participants) is problematic when parameters are somewhat correlated?

messages.body_plain:
You are on the right list for questions about Stan.
Most of our systems biology ODE experts are outside of
Columbia but are on our mailing list.  The list is high
volume, so if you're interested in ODEs, I'd start a new
thread with that in the title.

We always welcome case studies:

  http://mc-stan.org/documentation/case-studies.html

Multiplicatively non-identifiability is highly problematic as
it leads to banana-shaped posteriors that defeat our adaptation
(no fixed mass matrix is appropriate throughout the posterior).
But if that's only one of the data sets, it should be OK as it's
still providing some information constraining the relation between
a and b.

If the two data collection processes share parameters, then it
is straightforward to write the Bayesian model to handle both
jointly---just include both sets of data and model the joint
likelihood of that data and provide a single set of priors on
the parameters.

We are about to introduce a matrix exponential function specifically
for handling some steady-state computations in ODEs.  I'm hoping
it'll be ready for our 2.13 release later this year.  If not, it'll
be in 2.14.

- Bob

messages.subject: Posterior predictive simulations
messages.subject_clean: Posterior predictive simulations
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I am working on a problem of adaptive sample size. Assume we have acquired some data and estimated parameters. In my case data consists of L lots with S samples each and I am using a two-level hierarchical model for inter and intra lot variation (sigmaBetween and sigmaWithin). Then I generate predictive posterior for a Lnew lots S samples each using the technique analogous to replicated data in new schools (see BDA appendix C). The idea is for each draw from predictive posterior combine real data with simulated Lnew lots and perform the fit again to obtain posterior of sigmaBetweenNew for each draw. Then I combine all sigmaBetweenNew and get 95% credible interval. I increase Lnew until this credible interval dips below some threshold. This will tell me how many more lots I have to sample to obtain a good inter lot variability estimate. One problem is that I have to run MCMC multiple times (as many times as there are draws in sigmaBetween). Is there some more efficient way of doing this?

Thank for the insight,
Linas

The stan model for generating predictive posterior is attached.

messages.subject: Predicting outcomes with lower and upper bounds at 95% credible interval
messages.subject_clean: Predicting outcomes with lower and upper bounds at 95% credible interval
messages.body_plain:
Hi All,

The attached is the negative binomial script. I would like to predict the dependent outcome from the estimated coefficients at 95% bayesian credible interval.

>From the script I used the rbinom function and probabilities (0.025, 0.5 and 0.975) to predict the outcome. The challenge I am facing is I am getting very big results from the upper bound (0.975) whereby its deviation from the mean (0.5) is quite different from the deviation of the lower bound (0.025) to the mean. Is there something wrong with my script or is there a better approach to this objective?

I will appreciate your help. Thanks.

negbin<-"
data{
int<lower=0> N;                           # rows of data
vector[N] intervention;
vector[N] timeindicator;
vector[N] studyperiod;
vector[N] majaadt;
vector[N] minaadt;                    # predictor variable
vector[N] majlane;
vector[N] minlane;
vector[N] medianwidth;
vector[N] speed;
vector[N] landuse;
vector[N] mediantype;
int<lower=0> totalcrashes[N];            # response variable
}

parameters {
real<lower=0> phi;      # negative binomial dispersion parameter
real beta0;             # intercept
real beta1;
real beta2;
real beta3;
real beta5;
real beta6;
real beta7;
real beta8;
real beta9;
real beta10;
real beta11;
real beta12;
}

model {
### priors
phi ~    cauchy(0.001,0.001);
beta0 ~ normal(0.0,1E4);
beta1 ~  normal(0.0, 1E4);
beta2 ~  normal(0.0, 1E4);
beta3 ~  normal(0.0, 1E4);
beta5 ~  normal(0.0, 1E4);
beta6 ~ normal(0.0, 1E4);
beta7 ~ normal(0.0, 1E4);
beta8 ~ normal(0.0, 1E4);
beta9 ~ normal(0.0, 1E4);
beta10 ~ normal(0.0, 1E4);
beta11 ~ normal(0.0, 1E4);

Hey Andre, if you want to get your original code to work and prevent
overfitting, I think you just need to get rid of the
non-identifiability between jitter and sigma_sq. You might be able to
remove jitter entirely, but if not try fixing it to .00001 and see if
you get reasonable results. (And to speed things up, I would switch to
using cov_exp_quad to calculate the covariance matrix.)

Seth

At the bottom of the wiki entry on prior choice recommendations (https://github.com/stan-dev/stan/wiki/Prior-Choice-Recommendations) is a section for Gaussian Processes. messages.body_plain:
Oh, found it by delving into the source. First, you need to do the extract as:

    mu = rstan::extract(post,pars='mu',permuted=F)

so that the chains are distinguished (not mixed & shuffled as occurs when permuted=T, the default for rstan::extract).

Then you can do:

    rstan:::ess_rfun(mu)

for n_eff, and:

    rstan:::split_rhat_rfun(mu)

for rhat. If mu is a vector parameter, then you need to do

    rstan:::ess_rfun(mu[,,1])

for the 1st element of the vector, etc.

I think you mean the marginal posterior distributions in yellow are not what you expected. But your prior mean was zero, so I don't know what is the basis for that. It is quite possible that your continuous predictors are in units that such that a one-unit change has a negligible effect on the predictions, in which case you should change the units.

But the big thing is that you should pretty much always specify the QR = TRUE argument with stan_glm unless you have informative priors about the mean or only one predictor. It is quite possible that these results that use the default of QR = FALSE are not reliable.

messages.body_plain:
I haven't fit any joint survival longitudinal models myself and am not very familiar with the intricacies of these models. Can you explain why the log likelihood is not just the sum of the three likelihood components you mention? If by submodels you mean you have a model for the outcome and then models also for some or all parameters in the model for the outcome, then you just have a hierarchical model and you can use the log likelihood calculated at the observation level of the model. But that's not necessarily true if that's not what submodel means here. I think Aki has a lot of experience with similar survival models so maybe he can give some more helpful advice on this particular point.

Something else relevant for loo is what is considered to be the unit left out. Is it a single measurement? A single person (so possible multiple measurements)? Etc.

Jonah

messages.subject: Possible issue with initialization (cmdstan and rstan)
messages.subject_clean: Possible issue with initialization (cmdstan and rstan)
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I am experiencing some issues with initialization, both in CmdStan and RStan.

The model is a logistic growth model for a nut with adjustments to the asymptote and log rate constant by cultivar and site (attached w/ example data).

When the parameters are given a prior in a centered parameterization tighter than ~ normal(0, 1), during initialization the parameter is sometimes initialized very far away from the prior (e.g., prior is ~normal(0, 0.1), parameter is initialized at a value of 2), which causes the model to get stuck in an area of low probability.  Restricting the initialization values helps in some cases, but then causes parameters with priors wider than ~ normal(0, 1) to become stuck. Re-parameterizing the priors to a non-centered parameterization solves all issues and results in sampling to proceed well on all chains.

The reason I thought I should write this is that I originally ran this model over a year ago with the centered parameterization on Stan/Rstan 2.6 with no initialization issues what-so-ever.  However, on 2.12 at least one chain of four does not initialize properly.

For reference, I am currently running this on:
Arch Linux - 4.8.4
GCC - 6.2.1
R - 3.3.1
Cmdstan - 2.12.0
RStan - 2.12.1

Thanks,

Matt

This is very interesting. Thanks for sharing. I have worked with forecasting time series data (individual stock prices and of the mutual funds) in the financial sector. In the some of the models I have built with ANN, I have used leading indicators as well as opposite trending stock prices to improve upon the model fits and forecasting accuracy of the ANNs: for example, when examining the stock prices across multiple sectors during the 2008-2009 market downturn, I have used the prices of precious metals (Gold, Silver weighted combination) as well as bond market prices to use as control variables. I found that this helped the models. Did you use such variables in your models?
My modelling was fairly basic in that, I used multi-layer perceptrons for training and forecasting. For leading market indicators, I used the excellent data source from http://recessionalert.com/ (I'm only a subscriber, I still use their information to develop forecasts for my own portfolio)

Jonah

messages.subject: Is it possible to generate simulated data for model testing using Stan?
messages.subject_clean: Is it possible to generate simulated data for model testing using Stan?
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I am relatively new to Stan and to Bayesian statistics in general. I am implementing an linear regression with multiple predictors and multiple outcomes, similar to the example in based on the example provided in Chapter 6 of the stan-reference manual. In the manual it is also suggested that "One of the best ways to make sure your model is doing the right thing computationally is to generate simulated (i.e., “fake”) data with known parameter values, then see if the model can recover these parameters from the data. If not, there is very little hope that it will do the right thing with data from the wild." I would like to validate my model by generating simulated data as suggested. One can generate simulated data with R for example (it gets a little tricky if you need to have LKJ priors, but I'm sure it's doable), but since Stan has already built in functions for all the distributions, it would be very useful if Stan could also help generate the simulated data. Is that possible and if so how? I read in the manual that among other things, the generated quantities section can be used to "forward sampling to generate simulated data for model testing", but there are no examples of how this can be done. It would be great if someone could provide an example. Much thanks for your help.

Best,

Michael

messages.body_plain:
If you just want to see the correlations between all the predictors then you can just use the regular cor function in R, which I believe works for a matrix or a data frame.

Also if you set the QR argument to true when estimating your model, as Ben recommended, then the predictor matrix actually used to fit the model will have no correlations between any predictors by design. This is one reason why the QR option is nice. If you don't use QR then the correlations will be whatever cor says they are.

Hope that helps,

Jonah

messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Re: Is it possible to generate simulated data for model testing using Stan?
messages.body_plain:
The advantage of the approach Jim outlines is that it
works for any kind of model specification.  The RNG approach may
require some translation, but it's a lot more efficient computationally
and statistically (it iterates much faster and takes independent
draws by design).

- Bob

> On Oct 24, 2016, at 1:39 PM, James Savage <jav...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> Hi Michael -
>
> There are a couple of ways of doing this. The simplest might be to simulate the data like so:
>
> data {
>    int N;
>    int P; // number of predictors
>    real<lower = 0> sigma; // your "known" error scale
>    vector[P] beta; // your "known" coefficients
>    matrix[N, P] X; // your predictors, including a column of 1s
> }
> parameters {
>     vector[N] yhat;
> }
> model {
>     yhat ~ normal(X*beta, sigma);
> }
>
> If you run that, each draw would be a sample you could use to test your model with. Your question mentioned having LKJ priors (I presume for random effects on betas covariance?). So you want to provide known group-level betas to exhibit correlation consistent with your prior? If so, you could export the lkj_corr_rng() function from Stan to R. Your Stan program would be
>
> // saved as export_lkj.stan
> functions {
>     matrix lkj_rng(int size, real eta) {
>         return( lkj_corr_rng(size, eta));
>     }
> }
> model {}
>
> at the top. You can then extract the lkj rng function using
>
> rstan::expose_stan_functions(export_lkj.stan)
>
> After which the function lkj_rng() will be available for use in your R session.
>
> Hope this helps. FWIW I normally do all my fake data stuff in R.
>
> Jim
>

> Hi,
>
> I am relatively new to Stan and to Bayesian statistics in general. I am implementing an linear regression with multiple predictors and multiple outcomes, similar to the example in based on the example provided in Chapter 6 of the stan-reference manual. In the manual it is also suggested that "One of the best ways to make sure your model is doing the right thing computationally is to generate simulated (i.e., “fake”) data with known parameter values, then see if the model can recover these parameters from the data. If not, there is very little hope that it will do the right thing with data from the wild." I would like to validate my model by generating simulated data as suggested. One can generate simulated data with R for example (it gets a little tricky if you need to have LKJ priors, but I'm sure it's doable), but since Stan has already built in functions for all the distributions, it would be very useful if Stan could also help generate the simulated data. Is that possible and if so how? I read in the manual that among other things, the generated quantities section can be used to "forward sampling to generate simulated data for model testing", but there are no examples of how this can be done. It would be great if someone could provide an example. Much thanks for your help.

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Posterior predictive simulations
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Posterior predictive simulations
messages.body_plain:
Move everything in the model down to generated quantities
and use the associated rngs.

You can probably speed things up a bit with vector operations,
but it's probably not worth it:

  vector[N_SAMPLES_LOT] smp_pred[N_ADD_LOTS]

  smp_pred[l, s] = normal_rng(0, 1);

...

  smp_pred[l] = smp_pred[l] * sigmaWithin + processMean + sigmaBetween * i3;

It usually doesn't make much difference if it's not in
the context of autodiff (which generated quantities are not).

I'd think you could use the usual convergence measures.  Run estimates
in multiple batches (say four batches of 50) and see if they've
converged, then try four batches of 100 and so on until you have enough.

- Bob

In my case data consists of L lots with S samples each and I am using a two-level hierarchical model for inter and intra lot variation (sigmaBetween and sigmaWithin). Then I generate predictive posterior for a Lnew lots S samples each using the technique analogous to replicated data in new schools (see BDA appendix C). The idea is for each draw from predictive posterior combine real data with simulated Lnew lots and perform the fit again to obtain posterior of sigmaBetweenNew for each draw. Then I combine all sigmaBetweenNew and get 95% credible interval. I increase Lnew until this credible interval dips below some threshold. This will tell me how many more lots I have to sample to obtain a good inter lot variability estimate. messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Possible issue with initialization (cmdstan and rstan)
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Possible issue with initialization (cmdstan and rstan)
messages.body_plain:
We changed how the basic sampling works in NUTS, moving
from a slice sampler to a multinomial sampler, which in
general, has been more robust and less variable across
chains.  Sorry to hear it's gone the opposite way for
your problem.  This may just be that Stan's gotten better
at diagnosing a pathology in the model that was always
there.

You might want to try a lower stepsize initially if it's
getting stuck during warmup and a larger adapt_delta if
it gets stuck during sampling.

It generally helps to rescale all the parameters.  So if
you have:

  theta ~ normal(0, 0.1)

then instead take theta_raw as the parameter, modeled as

  theta_raw ~ normal(0, 1);

with a transformed parameter or local variable rescaling:

  theta = 0.1 * theta_raw;

That is just the non-centered parameterization for a fixed scale
(the non-centering is around 0 for the the mean and the sd on the
log scale).

- Bob

> On Oct 23, 2016, at 10:42 PM, Matt Espe <lck...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> Hi,
>
> I am experiencing some issues with initialization, both in CmdStan and RStan.
>
> The model is a logistic growth model for a nut with adjustments to the asymptote and log rate constant by cultivar and site (attached w/ example data).
>
> When the parameters are given a prior in a centered parameterization tighter than ~ normal(0, 1), during initialization the parameter is sometimes initialized very far away from the prior (e.g., prior is ~normal(0, 0.1), parameter is initialized at a value of 2), which causes the model to get stuck in an area of low probability.  Restricting the initialization values helps in some cases, but then causes parameters with priors wider than ~ normal(0, 1) to become stuck. Re-parameterizing the priors to a non-centered parameterization solves all issues and results in sampling to proceed well on all chains.
>
> The reason I thought I should write this is that I originally ran this model over a year ago with the centered parameterization on Stan/Rstan 2.6 with no initialization issues what-so-ever.  However, on 2.12 at least one chain of four does not initialize properly.
>
> For reference, I am currently running this on:
> Arch Linux - 4.8.4
> GCC - 6.2.1
> R - 3.3.1
> Cmdstan - 2.12.0
> RStan - 2.12.1

> Thanks,

The cauchy(0.001, 0.001) is suspicious as I said before.  You
want to try to keep all your variables around unit scale (zero mean,
unit variance) to the extent possible for good sampling.

If this isn't just to hack something to be near 0.001, what you want
to do is set

  phi_raw ~ cauchy(0, 1);

  phi = phi_raw * 0.001 + 0.001;

Given that this is controlling your dispersion parameter, it seems
like you're likely to get answers very close to poisson.

- Bob

> There's a problem with mixture models in general that they don't have
> maximum likelihoods.  If you put one mixture component be responsible
> for one data item, as the scale (std dev param) goes to zero and the location
> (mean param) goes to the data item's value, the likelihood grows.
>
> One way to avoid this is to force the components to have more responsibility.
> You can do this with a prior on the simplex.  Something like Dirichlet(alpha)
> where alpha is a vector values >> 1 can help.  Also putting a prior on the
> scales that explicitly avoids zero (like a lognormal) can help.

messages.body_plain:
Andre's point is a good one--within Stan you can save time by computing a distance matrix in transformed data:
for(i in 1:n)
  for(j in 1:n)
     d[i,j] = -squared_distance(x[i], x[j]);

and then in transformed parameters you can calculate the covariance matrix as:

K = exp(d/lengthscale^2);

But I'm not sure how this might be incorporated into the implementation of cov_exp_quad. Perhaps there could be a version that would take a precomputed distance matrix d as the argument? Daniel and Rob did the work on this function...any thoughts on that?

Seth

Over the weekend I re-ran the code with a smaller dataset and only 200 iterations on a single core.  It appears to have worked (the posterior means made sense when compared to known true values) so I'm assuming the original problem had to do with the parallelization.

I am going to work on making it faster now.  The full data requires approximately 100,000 parameters and 200 iterations was not enough to obtain convergence.  I'll let you know what happens after the using the Cholesky factor parameterization and I may look into the Variational Bayes solution as well.

Thanks again for the help, I greatly appreciate it,

Jonathon

messages.body_plain:
Just chiming in to clarify Ghislain's question, which was motivated by a discussion/disagreement we had the other day.

When designing the prior for a variability parameter, I might consider some value X as the most credible value for that parameter, with values above or below X relatively less credible, going to zero credibility at zero and positive infinity. For this scenario, I consider a lognormal to be a useful shape insofar as you can define where its peak is, how rapidly the credibility falls off away from this peak, and it's positive-bounded.

I believe that, to reflect that I have maximum credibility at X, I'd want a lognormal peaked at X (so, in stan, "lognormal(log(X),...)" ).

Ghislain notes that the expected mean of lognormal(log(X),Z) is exp(X+(Z^2)/2), and believes that if we want to reflect maximum credibility at X we'd need to set the mean and sd of the lognormal to yield an expected mean of X, not exp(X+(Z^2)/2) as the approach I suggest yields.

Which of us (if either!) is correct?

messages.body_plain:
The positive boundedness and shape of tails (and head near zero)
are all worth thinking about.  The peak isn't important, but
the probability mass in intervals is important.

Work backwards from what the prior does to your posterior
estimate.  Individual points have measure zero and all the
Bayesian quantities of interest are expectations of functions of
parameters and involve posterior expectation calculations:

  E[f(theta) | y] = INTEGRAL_theta f(theta) p(theta | y) d.theta

For example, event probabilities conditioned on the data
take f as an indicator function.

  Pr[theta[1] > 0] = INTEGRAL_theta I[theta[1] > 0] p(theta | y) d.theta

The posterior breaks down as

  p(theta | y) propto p(y | theta) * p(theta)

So this is where the prior p(theta) comes into the calculation---through
its affect on the posterior, and the only thing that matters is
the integrals over p(theta | y), not its peaks.

That's why you want to think in terms of interval probabilities,
not in terms of where the mode is.  If you reparameterize, the
location of the mode may change without affecting the expectations.

- Bob

Hi All,

Just a quick question, is it possible I can the change the logit model to multinomial logit model in rstanarm? or is there a way I can fit my data using the multinomial logit model instead of logit model in rstanarm?

Thanks

Thank you for the positive response towards the problem I posted. They are helping me a great deal.

Thank you Bob for the explanation concerning the priors,  I have been struggling in understanding the scale parameter for rstan and confusing it with that of WinBUGS, where they use tau=1/standard deviation.

What I found out currently is that rstan use the scale parameter as the standard deviation (which is the reciprocal of tau). Please correct me if I am wrong about this clarification.

Thanks.

messages.body_plain:
BUGS and JAGS use 1 / scale^2 (aka precision) for the normal parameter.
It's convenient because gamma's the conjugate prior and many operations
are easier over precision or variance than scale.

R and Stan both use scale as the normal parameter.  The scale determines
the standard deviation of a normal.  We like this parameterization better
because it's on the same scale as the location (which determines the mean)
and the random variates.

- Bob

I don't speak Mathematica, so I don't know what all the
extra arguments are.

The Stan program should sample x with density

  p(x) propto normal(x[1] | 0, 1)
              * normal(x[2] | 0, 1)
              * normal(x[3] | 0, 1)

subject to the constraint that x[n] > 0 and sum(x) = 1.

I don't think there's a problem in Stan's tails here
because if I crank the adapt_delta up to 0.99, I get
the same draws.

- Bob

Daniel and I had a brief discussion off list. Daniel writes:

> With a 1000 obs of 10 vectors, it takes ~5 seconds to do the computation 1000 times. If you
> think we have 10 leapfrog steps on average, it'll be ~50 seconds. It's still not a killer, but maybe
> it's worth it.

And my response:

That's right, and I think we're hoping eventually to be able to
routinely do 5000-10000 observations based on other speedups!

I recognize it's annoying to maintain the codebase, but from a user's
point of view it seems pretty natural for there to be this option. I
just went to see what the R package RandomFields does and the function
RFcovmatrix which creates a covariance matrix for a specified kernel
takes either x or x1 and x2 (so far just like Stan) or the lower
triangular part of a matrix of a matrix of distances. There's no lower
triangular data type, so I'd propose the following design:

data {
  int n;
  int p;
  vector[n] x[p];
}

transformed data {
  matrix[n,n] D;

  for(i in 1:n)
    for(j in 1:n)

       D[i,j] = distance(x[i], x[j]);
}
parameters {
   real lengthscale;
}

transformed parameters {
   cov_matrix[n] K;
   K = cov_exp_quad(D, 1, lengthscale);
}

Which would be a more efficient version of:

K = cov_exp_quad(x, 1, lengthscale);

Does that make sense?

> But I'm not sure how this might be incorporated into the implementation of

messages.body_plain:
The notion is one of Bayesian sampling, where the declaration of x as a simplex serves as a prior on x, creating uniform sampling within a symplex domain . The normal distribution imposed on x then serves as a likelihood. The combination of the prior with the likelihood should, in my mind, create a standard unit normal distribution whose edges are trimmed away so that it lies within the unit simplex.  In order to visualize this result more easily, I then marginalize this distribution on to the x axis.

 With my current understanding,  either my marginalization integral is not written correctly, or Stan is not sampling correctly. I appeal to this group for its insight.

messages.body_plain:
What Stan does is what I wrote the first time:

The Stan program should sample x with density

 p(x) propto normal(x[1] | 0, 1)
             * normal(x[2] | 0, 1)
             * normal(x[3] | 0, 1)

subject to the constraint that x[n] > 0 and sum(x) = 1.

Stan underlying samples over an unconstrained 2-dimensional
representation of the simplex.  This is transformed to
the simplex and the density updated with the Jacobian of
the transform (explained in the manual).  That gives you a
distribution in the unconstrained space that is uniform
on simplexes in the constrained space.

The normal model statement then makes the posterior in the
constrained space the product of the model times the
uniform on x, which is why the p(x) sampling density for
x is proportional to the above.

The density's are all implemented on the log scale up to an
additive constant.

The posterior marginal of x[1] is given by the marginalization:

  p(x[1]) = INTEGRAL_{x[2], x[3], s.t. x is a simplex}

            normal(x[1] | 0, 1) * normal(x[2] | 0, 1) * normal(x[3] | 0, 1)

            d.x[2] d.x[3]

where I'm using Stan's vectorized notation for the normal.  So each
of the x[n] has the same marginal.

Stan's posterior draws for x[1] should be according to p(x[1]) as
given above.  The joint draws of the x[n] will illustrate the
negative correlation among them.  I added a generated quantity for
the sum of x[2] and x[3], i.e., 1 - x[1].

parameters {
  simplex[3] x;
}
model {
  x ~ normal(0,1);
}

generated quantities {
  real x23;
  x23 = x[2] + x[3];
}

In RStan:

> pairs(fit)

- Bob

It's not annoying to maintain our codebase!  It's just
time-consuming to add new features, especially when the
combinatorics add up (both within a single function and
across functions).  And they add up to downstream maintenance
time, so we have to be careful to not just add things
willy nilly or we'll wind up with an unmanageable list of
functions.

Writing that new cov_exp_quad() function should be
relatively easy to write because the original one could
be implemented by computing the distance matrix and calling
this version (though that'd slow down the original one which
otherwise doesn't need to do the allocation and setting of
a distance matrix).

The best way to get this kind of code in is find someone
who'll write it and submit a pull request with doc and
reasonable code re-use.

- Bob

>> think we have 10 leapfrog steps on average, it'll be ~50 seconds. It's still not a killer, but maybe
>> it's worth it.
>
> And my response:
>
> That's right, and I think we're hoping eventually to be able to
> routinely do 5000-10000 observations based on other speedups!
>
> I recognize it's annoying to maintain the codebase, but from a user's
> point of view it seems pretty natural for there to be this option. I
> just went to see what the R package RandomFields does and the function
> RFcovmatrix which creates a covariance matrix for a specified kernel
> takes either x or x1 and x2 (so far just like Stan) or the lower
> triangular part of a matrix of a matrix of distances. There's no lower
> triangular data type, so I'd propose the following design:
>
> data {
>  int n;
>  int p;
>  vector[n] x[p];
> }
>
> transformed data {
>  matrix[n,n] D;
>  for(i in 1:n)
>    for(j in 1:n)
>       D[i,j] = distance(x[i], x[j]);
> }
> parameters {
>   real lengthscale;
> }
>
> transformed parameters {
>   cov_matrix[n] K;
>   K = cov_exp_quad(D, 1, lengthscale);
> }
>
> Which would be a more efficient version of:
>
> K = cov_exp_quad(x, 1, lengthscale);
>
> Does that make sense?
>
>

messages.body_plain:
Thanks, Bob.

I was trying to mention that there's a design issue with cov_exp_quad() and accepting matrix as the first argument. There isn't one natural way to treat a matrix. This was the second time this week that someone's asked that cov_exp_quad() accept a matrix as the first argument, but it wasn't to accept the distance matrix. Here are 3 sensible ways users might expect a cov_exp_quad() function to work accepting a matrix as the first argument:
1. treat the matrix as a distance matrix (what Seth is thinking). This might save some computation.
2. treat the columns of the matrix as observations (what Aki is thinking). This would be identical to an array of vectors as the first argument. This might save some user confusion and indexing issues.
3. treat the rows of the matrix as observations (what Ben thinks is natural and anyone that uses something like R). This would be identical to providing an array of row_vectors as the first argument. This also saves some user confusion and indexing issues.

The design issue is this: which one of these do we implement?

Once we introduce one of these implementations to our users, that's it. That's what the function means. That's why I had suggested that if you're really keen on implementing this function, that it be called something different, like cov_exp_quad_with_distance_matrix().

That said, if someone were to implement option 1 fully, there's a good chance we would just accept it as the default behavior. Actions speak much louder than words. (or option 2 or 3.)

Hope that makes sense.

Daniel

messages.subject: Hierarchical model that was supposedly difficult to fit in Stan
messages.subject_clean: Hierarchical model that was supposedly difficult to fit in Stan
messages.body_plain:
Hi--I think this came up before on the Stan list, but I'm not sure.  What I remember is that we asked what this model was that was supposedly so hard to fit in Stan, and it turned out it was very easy to fit in Stan, it did not require any "clever programming contrivances."

If someone can remind me what this model is, I could post something on it on the blog, as I'd like to dispel this confusion. If people remain confused on this point, we could write a program to have the post reappear on the blog and on other social media until eventually everyone understands.

A

> On Oct 26, 2016, at 11:42 AM, Michael Betancourt <notifi...@github.com> wrote:
>
> Easy to specify does not mean that the resulting fit will
> be fast or even right. Gibbs samplers that are easily
> implemented for models with discrete parameters can
> be very slow and and in many cases do not even explore
> sufficiently well, causing biased expectation estimation.
> Kruschke�s comment here is statistically naive and when
> taken seriously quite dangerous.
>
> When coupled with the technical difficultly of calculating
> the terms necessary for implementing Gibbs sampling or
> Random Walk Metropolis with models featuring both
> discrete and continuous parameters, we are not eager
> to support discrete parameters. Especially when with
> a little work most of these models can be implemented
> with marginalization in Stan.
>
> Of course we are actively researching and in contact
> with the vanguard of the statistical community, and
> if a robust sampler for discrete parameters is introduced
> it will be considered for Stan as soon as possible.
>
> On Oct 25, 2016, at 6:36 PM, skanskan <notifi...@github.com> wrote:
>
> > I don't speak well English but I can quote some words from the book Doing Bayesian Data Analysis:
> > "The lack of discrete parameters in Stan means that we cannot do model comparison as a hierarchical model with an indexical parameter at the top level. There might be ways to work around this restriction by using clever programming contrivances, but presently there is nothing as straight forward as the model specification in JAGS.
> >

messages.body_plain:
What's "very easy" for one person is a "contrivance" for another.
We regularly get requests to add discrete sampling
because users find the marginalizations both difficult and error prone.
As Michael and I are pointing out, there are huge advantages in
efficiency from marginalization, and in some cases it allows us to do
inference in models where discrete sampling gets stuck.  In other cases,
discrete sampling is challenging if not impossible, as in Ising models
or the combinatorially similar variable selection models.

It's come up with mixtures, the Cormack-Jolly-Seber model in
ecology, and change-point models, all of which are explained in
the manual.  All of Kery and Straub's book has been translated and
also Wagenmakers and Lee, both of which contain quite a few BUGS/JAGS
models with discrete parameters.

PyMC3 is a directed graphical modeling building language, so they were
able to combine HMC and discrete sampling.  I think there's a lot of work
to do on efficiency, but if we were to look into it seriously, we'd
probably start there.  But given that it doesn't really expand the models
we can fit reliably, it's not a high priority for us.

- Bob

> On Oct 26, 2016, at 2:41 PM, Daniel Lee <bea...@alum.mit.edu> wrote:
>
> Thanks, Bob.
>
> I was trying to mention that there's a design issue with cov_exp_quad() and accepting matrix as the first argument. There isn't one natural way to treat a matrix. This was the second time this week that someone's asked that cov_exp_quad() accept a matrix as the first argument, but it wasn't to accept the distance matrix. Here are 3 sensible ways users might expect a cov_exp_quad() function to work accepting a matrix as the first argument:
> 1. treat the matrix as a distance matrix (what Seth is thinking). This might save some computation.
> 2. treat the columns of the matrix as observations (what Aki is thinking). This would be identical to an array of vectors as the first argument. This might save some user confusion and indexing issues.
> 3. treat the rows of the matrix as observations (what Ben thinks is natural and anyone that uses something like R). This would be identical to providing an array of row_vectors as the first argument. This also saves some user confusion and indexing issues.

(3) is also the usual stats notation, which is why you can
write X * beta in regressions.  It also follows all of our
example code.  I don't think we want to do (2) because it
doesn't match our other conventions (you'd get beta' * X
in regressions).

Is it restricted to univariate now instead of multivariate
observations?  That seems very limiting, so I'd be inclined
to go with (3).  But then if you go with (1), the distance can get
computed on the outside, which is a plus for flexibility but
also defeats some of the purpose of having a built-in function.

We could then build two distance-matrix building functions, one
for univariate input, one for multivariate output, and then Aki
can just transpose for (2).  This would be good especially if what
we want to do is encourage people to use the more efficient form (1).

Longer names vs. overloading is a separate issue to which if any
of these we'll implement.

The higher level the function, the harder it is to specify a clean
interface that covers all the usages.

- Bob

If it helps, we could pass in a vector of distances for the first argument. Since a distance matrix is symmetric with zeros on the diagonal, you really only need the lower triangle. On Thursday, October 27, 2016 at 1:23:44 PM UTC-4, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> You declare Ymis but you never define it (i.e., give it a value).
> I'm not sure what you were expecting to happen.

I think he was expecting that by declaring but not defining an integer array in the model block he could work around the fact that integer arrays cannot be declared in the parameters block, which is the wrong intuition. The reason we cannot deal with integer unknowns has to do with the fact that the sampling algorithm does not support them, rather than the language. Also, integer arrays are initialized to zero rather than NaN, so there is no exception thrown.

For a model like this, you basically have to do what Gibbs samplers would call data augmentation, where you declare a continuous latent variable of length N in the parameters block that has a logistic likelihood. But the observed outcomes only, you can restrict that latent variable to be between cutpoints with a transformation (meaning you have to deal with a scalar Jacobian correction). Then you model the latent variable as a function of predictors and the sampling performance will probably be bad.

Ben

This was the second time this week that someone's asked that cov_exp_quad() accept a matrix as the first argument, but it wasn't to accept the distance matrix. Here are 3 sensible ways users might expect a cov_exp_quad() function to work accepting a matrix as the first argument:
> 1. treat the matrix as a distance matrix (what Seth is thinking). This might save some computation.

messages.body_plain:
It's missing the adjustment for the fact that a uniform
distribution on the simplex isn't marginally uniform.
For some clarification, see

  http://math.stackexchange.com/questions/391631/integrate-over-the-uniform-distribution-on-the-simplex

The linked Wikipedia article

  https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dirichlet_distribution#Marginal_distributions

may also help.  The Dirichlet([1 1 1]) is uniform on the 3-simplex,
but it's marginally Beta(1, 2) on each component.  That is, if

   p(theta) = Dirichlet(theta | [1 1 1])

then marginally

   p(theta[1]) = Beta(theta[1] | 1, 2)

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
On Friday, October 28, 2016 at 3:42:13 AM UTC-4, Dung Tran wrote:
> What I do expect, similar to Openbugs and JAGS,  is that when I specify
>
> Y~distribution(parameters*predictor) (here I mean categorical distributions)
>
> and when Y have missing values then the algorithm will used observed values to estimate the parameters and the missing values will be automatically generated from the distribution given the current parameters and predictors.

You are expecting the wrong thing. There is an appendix in the Stan manual that explains most of the differences between the Stan language and the BUGS language. This particular mistake is common and could be avoided if you utilize the newer syntax

target += ordered_logistic_lpmf(y[i] | predictors[i] * parameters, cutpoints);

which makes it more explicit that all you are doing is adding the log-likelihood of the data to the target keyword (which is originally zero).

y[i] ~ ordered_logistic(predictors[i] * parameters, cutpoints);

implicitly does the same thing.

If some of the data are missing, then y needs to be the union of y_obs and y_miss in order to evaluate the so-called complete-data log-likelihood. However, when y_miss is discrete, HMC cannot proceed because you cannot differentiate the log-posterior with respect to an integer.

> As you have said that use latent probably bad so I am wandering which is a better solution here.

There is no alternative. In parameters, declare both y_star_obs and y_star_miss as vectors or real arrays. Then transform y_star_obs[i] to be between the two cutpoints that pertain to the observed value of y_obs[i], making sure to handle the Jacobian adjustment. Combine that with the unrestricted values from y_star_miss to form y_star_complete and y_star_complete[i] is distributed standard logistic with expectation predictors[i] * parameters.

Ben

Just to add:

It's helpful to use the distribution functions in R to formulate priors for something like this. A student-t with a scale of 3 and 5 degrees of freedom might work for your example.

I usually think about truncated distributions as being conditioned on the RV being greater than 0, so in R for the t distribution, I wrote:

pt.zero.trunc <- function(q, df, mean = 0, scale=1) {
     return((pt((q - mean) / scale, df) - 0.5) / 0.5)
 }

pt.zero.trunc(2, 5, scale=3) = 0.4654908
1 - pt.zero.trunc(4, 5, scale=3) = 0.239939

Rob

and doubling in most problems until the n_eff is large enough and
all the R-hat are near 1.

- Bob

uprot <- unique(dat$protid)
nprot <- length(uprot)
set.seed(777)
protlab <- sample(1:6, nprot, replace =T)
datlabels <- protlab[match(dat$protid, uprot)]
dat <- data.frame(dat, datlabels)

dat <- dat[order(dat$protid,dat$peptide,dat$treatment),]

subdat <- by(dat, dat$datlabels, function(x) x)

################Now process the subdat by group##############
dat <- subdat[[1]]   #start with group 1

nchannel <- length(unique(dat$treatment))
channel <- as.integer(dat$treatment)
N <- length(dat$protid)
y <- dat$lratio

peps <- paste(dat$protid, dat$peptide)
npep <- length(unique(peps))
opep <- rep(NA,N)
counter <- 1
id <- peps[1]
for (i in 1:N){
  if(id == peps[i]){
    opep[i] <- counter
  }else{
    counter <- counter + 1
    opep[i] <- counter
    id <- peps[i]
  }
}

protch <- paste(dat$protid, dat$treatment)
oprotch <- as.integer(factor(protch))
nprotch <- length(unique(protch))

pepIS <- aggregate(dat$IS ~ opep, FUN = mean)
int_IS <-cbind(1,pepIS[,"dat$IS"])

SSN <- 4*(dat$totsig/max(dat$totsig)) - 4
pepSSN <- aggregate(SSN ~ opep, FUN = mean)
int_SSN <-cbind(1,pepSSN[,"SSN"])

##########################Begin Stan Code##########################
modelText <- '

data {
int<lower=0> npep ;
int<lower=0> N ;
int<lower=0> nprotch ;

real y[N] ;
matrix[npep,2] int_SSN ;
int<lower=1,upper=npep> opep[N] ;
int<lower=1,upper=nprotch> oprotch[N] ;

}

parameters{

real beta_pep[npep] ;  // pep effect
vector[2] alpha[nprotch] ;  // channel/prot averages independent

real<lower=0> tau ; // peptide effect var
real<lower=0> sigma ; // experimental error
vector<lower=0>[2] bsds ; // random int and slope SD

vector[2] mu_beta ;
cholesky_factor_corr[2] L ;

}

transformed parameters {
vector[2] beta[nprotch] ;
for (i in 1:nprotch){
  beta[i] = mu_beta + bsds .* (L * alpha[i]) ;  //int_SSN*beta gives the protch mean
}

}

model {
// First do parameters that effect the protein level
mu_beta ~ normal(0,10) ;

bsds ~ normal(0, 10) ; //This is a half-normal
L ~ lkj_corr_cholesky(1) ;

for (i in 1:nprotch){
  alpha[i] ~ normal(0,1) ;  // normal(0,1)s used to efficiently get beta
}

//Now compute peptide deviations
tau ~ normal(0, 5) ;  //peptide prior
beta_pep ~ normal(0, tau) ;

//finally add it together
sigma ~ normal(0, 5) ;
for (i in 1:N)
  y[i] ~ normal(beta_pep[opep[i]] + int_SSN[opep[i]] * beta[oprotch[i]], sigma) ;

}  // end model statement

generated quantities {

  vector[nprotch] ppred;
  for (i in 1:nprotch)
  ppred[i] =  beta[i][1] ;

}

'  # End of STAN code

compSSN <- stan(model_code = modelText, chains = 1, iter = 1000 )

rnorm(1e3) %>%
  as.data.frame %T>%
  { names(.) <- "x" } %>%
  {
    ggplot(., aes(x = x)) + geom_density()
  }
