Yes, this works... in theory.
What you're doing is something I've played with for a while: Encouraging high probability clustering by using betas and dirichlets with parameters < 1. The closer to 0, the more probability mass is placed over the extremes.
You can then say each individual has a probability, pi_i, of belonging to each cluster, where pi_i ~ dirichlet(alphas), and alphas ~ dirichlet(.1,.1,.1,...), which gives you not only individual membership probabilities, but overall membership probabilities too (as well as shrinkage).

However, HMC/NUTS is simulating a particle across the posterior surface. Sampling from betas and dirichlets where the parameters are < 1 pushes the probability mass toward the edges of the constraint. When inverted, it looks like a plateau, and the particle simulation can hit some difficulties, causing divergent transitions.
All that to say: If you want to encourage categorization with high probabilities, reparameterize your model to sample log-odds parameters (logistic regression, softmax regression) and convert to probability for the likelihood. If you do this, you can get a similar effect to 'inverted betas and dirichlets' by simply making the logistic prior very wide, such that most of the probability mass is beyond 1 and -1.

messages.subject_clean: WAIC and LOO-CV for inference including submodels
messages.body_plain:
Both following options are valid: a) leave-one-observation-out, b) leave-one-subject-out. Which one to choose depends on which prediction task is important for you a) predicting new observations for the same subjects or b) predicting new observations for new subjects. In a) you don't sum any logliks and in b) you sum all logliks of one subject (it doesn't matter if there are different number of observations and loglik terms for each subject). The case b) is however more difficult and if there are many observations for a subject it's more likely that PSIS-LOO fails (waic is even more likely to fail). Luckily loo package will report khat values so that you can check whether case b works too.

CPO is just a different name for loo log predictive density given by loo package.

DIC is relevant only if you are interested in plug-in predictive performance using the posterior mean point estimate for parameters instead predictive performance obtained by integrating over the parameters. Since you are using Stan, I assume you are integrating over the parameters and thus should not use DIC.

Aki

messages.body_plain:
On Saturday, October 29, 2016 at 6:36:10 PM UTC-4, malai...@gmail.com wrote:
>
> I am currently working on fitting the negative binomial regression using the rstanarm package.
>
> Next I would like to predict the dependent variable at lower (2.5%), median (50%), and upper bound (97.5%). I have no idea on how I can achieve that in rstanarm.

You can't because it wouldn't be a good thing. The point of posterior prediction is to integrate over the entire posterior distribution of the parameters rather than predicting given marginal quantiles of the parameters. You can look the quantiles of the posterior_predict() with summary() or quantile() or whatever.

Ben

I think we'll be introducing a function predictive_intervals that will summarize the posterior predictive distribution in the way Ben mentioned. For now you can do it in two steps with something like this:

preds <- posterior_predict(fit)
apply(preds, 2 quantile, prob = vector_of_probabilities))

posterior_predict is the most important function in rstanarm (other than the model fitting functions). It's at the core of nearly everything you'll ever need to do after fitting a model.

Hope that helps,

Jonah

messages.body_plain:
On Monday, October 31, 2016 at 6:28:27 AM UTC-4, Charles Driver wrote:
> Further, I am wondering about a justification for the decreasing prior probability of high correlations as the number of dimensions increases. If I have started with a dataset of two variables that involves a single correlation, and then add another variable to my analysis, why should that decrease the probability of a high correlation between my first two variables? Does anyone have thoughts on this?

The positive definiteness constraint means you cannot have independent prior beliefs about the correlations. In the 3x3 case, you can think of the density as

f(rho_{12} | rho_{13}, rho_{23}) * f(rho_{13}, rho_{23})

Why should f(rho_{12} | rho_{13}, rho_{23}} in the 3x3 case be the same as f(rho_{12}) in the 2x2 case? Of course, in the 3x3 case, you can also think of the density as

f(rho_{12}) * f(rho_{13}, rho_{23} | rho_{12})

but then you have to have weird beliefs about rho_{13} and rho_{23} given rho_{12} if your beliefs about rho_{12} are the same as in the 2x2 case. Basically, rho_{13} and rho_{23} have to be more concentrated near zero than rho_{12} is to satisfy the positive definiteness constraint.

For K > 6, increasing K decreases the hypervolume of correlation matrices satisfying the positive definiteness constraint and the ones that do tend to be close to the identity matrix. To construct one, you are better off using the onion method, which yields the same distribution of correlation matrices. Search for onion.stan in Google Groups.

Ben

messages.subject: beta release of new R package "bayesplot"
messages.subject_clean: beta release of new R package "bayesplot"
messages.body_plain:
Dear Stan users,

The purpose of this post is to announce the beta release of a new R package
called bayesplot and to ask you for your feedback before we release the
package on CRAN.

The bayesplot R package is a new ggplot2-based plotting package for use after
fitting models with Stan (or other packages). The functions in bayesplot are
separated into modules. Currently there is the PPC module for graphical
posterior predictive checking and the MCMC module for plotting posterior draws
and various diagnostics. Going forward we plan on adding other modules (e.g.,
plots for forecasting) and expanding the functionality of the existing PPC and
MCMC modules. The package documentation and (drafts of) the package
vignettes provide more details and many examples.

The beta release of bayesplot can be installed by following the instructions in
the README file at the stan-dev/bayesplot <https://github.com/stan-dev/bayesplot> GitHub repository. If you find bugs,
want to request a feature, or have general comments or questions about the
package, we encourage you to open an issue on GitHub and/or respond to this
post. Please don't hesitate to let us know what you like, what don't like, what
you'd like to see added to the package, etc. Your feedback is greatly
appreciated!

After the initial CRAN release later this fall we will be using the new package to unify
the underlying plotting functionality in our other R packages (particularly rstan,
rstanarm, and parts of shinystan). But bayesplot itself does not depend on any
of our other packages and is compatible with output from any package for fitting
Bayesian models. Our goal is not only to provide functionality for our own
packages, but also to offer a library of plotting functions that can be used by
developers of other R packages for Bayesian modeling (particularly, but not
exclusively, those interfacing with Stan), as well as a simple enough interface
that individual users can use the bayesplot functions interactively (as opposed
to only via wrappers provided by rstan, rstanarm, or other packages).

- The Stan Development Team

messages.body_plain:
That looks great.  I really like the increasing modularity
of the Stan moving pieces---it's the only way forward for
both development of new features and maintenance of existing
ones.

Next up, we'll be breaking the core stan-dev/stan repo into
modules for the language translator, the algorithms, and
the interface services.  And splitting the manual into a
language reference manual and user's guide.

- Bob

> On Oct 31, 2016, at 11:23 AM, Jonah Gabry <jga...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> Dear Stan users,
>
> The purpose of this post is to announce the beta release of a new R package
> called bayesplot and to ask you for your feedback before we release the
> package on CRAN.
>
> The bayesplot R package is a new ggplot2-based plotting package for use after
> fitting models with Stan (or other packages). The functions in bayesplot are
> separated into modules. Currently there is the PPC module for graphical
> posterior predictive checking and the MCMC module for plotting posterior draws
> and various diagnostics. Going forward we plan on adding other modules (e.g.,
> plots for forecasting) and expanding the functionality of the existing PPC and
> MCMC modules. The package documentation and (drafts of) the package
> vignettes provide more details and many examples.
>
> The beta release of bayesplot can be installed by following the instructions in
> the README file at the stan-dev/bayesplot GitHub repository. If you find bugs,
> want to request a feature, or have general comments or questions about the
> package, we encourage you to open an issue on GitHub and/or respond to this
> post. Please don't hesitate to let us know what you like, what don't like, what
> you'd like to see added to the package, etc. Your feedback is greatly
> appreciated!
>
> After the initial CRAN release later this fall we will be using the new package to unify
> the underlying plotting functionality in our other R packages (particularly rstan,
> rstanarm, and parts of shinystan). But bayesplot itself does not depend on any
> of our other packages and is compatible with output from any package for fitting
> Bayesian models. Our goal is not only to provide functionality for our own
> packages, but also to offer a library of plotting functions that can be used by
> developers of other R packages for Bayesian modeling (particularly, but not
> exclusively, those interfacing with Stan), as well as a simple enough interface
> that individual users can use the bayesplot functions interactively (as opposed
> to only via wrappers provided by rstan, rstanarm, or other packages).
>
> - The Stan Development Team

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] K-means clustering, constrain cluster assignment with dir(0.1, ..., 0.1)
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] K-means clustering, constrain cluster assignment with dir(0.1, ..., 0.1)
messages.body_plain:
> On Oct 29, 2016, at 12:59 AM, Stephen Martin <hwki...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> Yes, this works... in theory.
> What you're doing is something I've played with for a while: Encouraging high probability clustering by using betas and dirichlets with parameters < 1. The closer to 0, the more probability mass is placed over the extremes.
> You can then say each individual has a probability, pi_i, of belonging to each cluster, where pi_i ~ dirichlet(alphas), and alphas ~ dirichlet(.1,.1,.1,...), which gives you not only individual membership probabilities, but overall membership probabilities too (as well as shrinkage).
>
> However, HMC/NUTS is simulating a particle across the posterior surface. Sampling from betas and dirichlets where the parameters are < 1 pushes the probability mass toward the edges of the constraint. When inverted, it looks like a plateau, and the particle simulation can hit some difficulties, causing divergent transitions.

> All that to say: If you want to encourage categorization with high probabilities, reparameterize your model to sample log-odds parameters (logistic regression, softmax regression) and convert to probability for the likelihood. If you do this, you can get a similar effect to 'inverted betas and dirichlets' by simply making the logistic prior very wide, such that most of the probability mass is beyond 1 and -1.

Andrew explained this to me a while ago and it's worth emphasizing.
I'm going to add a discussion to the manual:

https://github.com/stan-dev/stan/issues/2051#issuecomment-257355399

- Bob

Here is a problem I am not sure how to deal with after reading the post <https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/rstan/vignettes/stanfit-objects.html> by the Stan team. I have a Stan model with simulation parameters set to the following:

######
parameters = c("b1", "b2", "b3", "b4", "b5", "b6", "b7", "thresh", "bmean", "bsigma", "log_lik")  # The parameter(s) to be monitored.
adaptSteps = 5000              # Number of steps to "tune" the samplers.
burnInSteps = 5000            # Number of steps to "burn-in" the samplers.
nChains = 3                   # Number of chains to run.

thinSteps=10                  # Number of steps to "thin" (1=keep every step).
nPerChain = ceiling( ( numSavedSteps * thinSteps ) / nChains ) # Steps per chain.
######

Because this is a complex model for estimation and using shorter chains have failed to reach convergence, I am using a rather long chain with a thinning step set to 10 (save one iteration out of ten). Here I request to have 100,000 iterations for one chain, and only save one out of ten iterations for a total of three chains. It converged. Now my questions are:

So when I was trying to compare the descriptive statistics produced by summarizing across all iterations with those using pring(stan_fit), it's not surprising that they are different.

2) We can use the "generated quantities { }" block in stan to produce some post-estimation statistics using those means of estimated parameters and their credible intervals. I would assume we should be able to get the same results using the simulated posterior distributions. In this case, it should be the posterior after thinning, right?

Any thoughts? Thanks a lot!

Jun Xu, PhD
Associate Professor
Department of Sociology
Ball State University
Muncie, IN

messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Rstan gaussian mixture model 'Scale parameter is 0, but must be > 0'
messages.body_plain:
Just to add to this: Yes, it's probably due to label switching. You're marginalizing over multiple modes that are equivalent in inference, but labels are switched, so everything winds up being the same when averaged.
This is *not* an issue if you have between-chain label switching, meaning that chain 1 found and explored 1 mode, and chain 2 found and explored another mode, but neither chain found the other modes.
If this is the case, your trace plots will tell you pretty quickly --- The traces of the individual chains will just be flipped from one another. In this case, just extract out individual chains or chains that converged to similar modes and look at the posterior summaries.

However, if your chains are switching modes during simulation (chain 1 explores modes 1, 2, 3, ...), you have an issue that I have no idea how to solve from MCMC output itself. I've only stopped this by applying some identifiability constraints that either creates one mode, or pushes the modes further apart so any one given chain is unlikely to 'find' the other one throughout its simulation. It's not ideal, but it works well enough.
